title: Global HipHop and Social Justice
description: Critical interrogation of the relationship between HipHop and social justice. What is "HipHop," what is "social justice," what is their relationship, how can HipHop can be an effective force for social justice, and what obstacles mitigate against this potential? Discussions will develop familiarity with important concepts in Black studies and social theory such as race and colonialism, imperialism and hegemony, structure and agency, identity and strategic essentialism. Consider the race/class/gender dimensions of weekly topics, acquire a broader familiarity with HipHop activism, and develop new conceptual tools and critical thinking skills.

title: Afro Asian Improv: From Hip Hop to Martial Arts Fusion
description: An Afro Asian perspective provides a lens through which intersections between Asian American and African American dance and martial arts are studied and practiced. Asian American and African American movement genres provide tools to explore dance fusion, choreography, and improvisation, to create dances informed by African American and Asian American legacies of struggle, innovation and transformation, while cognizant of historical forces of oppression and racism. Building connections through respectful communication with others are learned through dance practice, discussion and writing about concepts learned through readings, videos, and guest artist visits. Engagement with dance as a cultural vehicle for creative problem-solving and risk-taking occurs through guided class or smaller group activities.

title: Slavery and Capitalism in the United States
description: Addresses the relationship between slavery and capitalism in the British North American colonies and the United States of America. Drawing on recent scholarship that explores how slavery and capitalism are independent systems, examines  how the labor of enslaved people affected the development and growth of wage labor; the impact of the growth and dominance of capitalism as an economic system on the institution of slavery; and the experiences of enslaved people.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: American slavery and American capitalism developed in tandem; the two systems were interdependent. Yet, only recently have scholars (economists and historians) at mainstream institutions begun studying the many intersections of slavery and capitalism in the Americas, despite the pioneering work of Black scholars like Eric Williams who wrote Slavery and Capitalism in 1944. Until the 1990s many mainstream historians and economists at predominantly white institutions continued to write and teach slavery as pre-capitalist, situating modern capitalism as dependent only on free labor and in opposition to slave labor. We will read and discuss the intersections of slavery of modern capitalism and explore the following questions: What are the historical connections between the "new world  race-based slavery and capitalism? Why have slavery and capitalism only recently been studied as interdependent systems? How did the growth and dominance of capitalism as an economic system affect slavery as an institution and the experiences of enslaved people? How did the labor of enslaved people affect the development and growth of wage labor?
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: The Foundations of Slavery and Capitalism in British North America and the United StatesWeek 1: Lecture 1: What is slavery? What is capitalism?Lecture 2: Atlantic Plantation Complex and the Atlantic Slave TradeReading: Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (Preface and Introduction by Colin A. Palmer) AND Sven Beckert and Seth Rockman, Slavery's Capitalism: A New History of American Economic Development (Introduction) Available on Canvas under "Additional Readings Week 2:Lecture 3: The Charter GenerationsReading: Ryan Quintana "The Within Enemy: Slaves and the Production of South Carolina's Early State  (Chapter 1); Robert Olwell "Loose, Idle and Disorderly: Slave Women in the Eighteenth Charleston Century Marketplace  (Chapter 5); Christy Clark-Pujara "The Business of Slavery and the Making of Race  and "Living and Laboring Under Slavery  (Chapters 1 and 2) Available on Canvas under "Additional Readings Week 3:  Lecture 4: The Plantation GenerationsReadings: Part 1 of Ebony of IvyWeek 4:*REVIEW ESSAY DUE*Lecture 5: The Revolutionary Generations Readings: Part 2 of Ebony and Ivy

title: Global HipHop and Social Justice
description: Critical interrogation of the relationship between HipHop and social justice. What is "HipHop," what is "social justice," what is their relationship, how can HipHop can be an effective force for social justice, and what obstacles mitigate against this potential? Discussions will develop familiarity with important concepts in Black studies and social theory such as race and colonialism, imperialism and hegemony, structure and agency, identity and strategic essentialism. Consider the race/class/gender dimensions of weekly topics, acquire a broader familiarity with HipHop activism, and develop new conceptual tools and critical thinking skills.

title: Decolonial Theory
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in African societies and cultures.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Course Title: Decolonial TheoryDecolonize this, decolonize that -- but what does this all mean? In the 2010s "decolonization  became an academic buzzword, sometimes leading to significant change, and sometimes merely indicating that one was following an intellectual trend. At times, one (honestly, "I ) wondered if anyone had actually done the reading. This course will take a chronological approach to decolonial theory, beginning with writers frequently cited by present-day decolonial theorists, and then turning to those theorists writing today. This structure is meant to help students see how ideas build on one another. The readings are Africa-focused -- due to the professor's specialization -- but include writers from outside the continent. Students with various geographical foci are welcome in this class, in the hopes that learning across continents can increase solidarities and strengthen students' own research and writing. In addition, this course can be taken as part of the Graduate Certificate in Visual Cultures. If you are pursuing that certificate, I expect your writing projects to address issues in visual and/or performance studies.

Empire, Global Coloniality and African Subjectivity (2022) Tamale, Decolonization and Afro-Feminism, 2020 Ferdinand, Decolonial Ecology: Thinking from the Caribbean World (2022)Taiwo, Against Decolonization: Taking African Agency Seriously (2022)

title: Resuscitation Anesthesiology Elective
description: An expanded version of the American Heart Association's Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) course designed to provide the necessary knowledge and skills to manage the first minutes of a cardiorespiratory emergency using ACLS protocols. Opportunities to learn the proper management of the ten core cases (i.e. Asystole, Bradycardia, Tachycardia, etc.) in the three rescuer roles: lone rescuer; resuscitation team member; and resuscitation team leader. Learn essential resuscitation skills including: recognition of cardiac arrest rhythms and common bradycardias and tachycardias; proper use of conventional and automated external defibrillators (AED); use of transcutaneous pacing devices; advanced airway management; administration of drugs via intravenous and endotracheal routes; recognition of the 12-lead electrocardiogram signs of acute injury and ischemia; adult CPR.

title: Veterinary Genetics
description: The molecular basis for the inheritance of monogenic and polygenic traits related to animal disease and production. Genetic defects, their discovery, diagnosis, and treatment. Examines the molecular basis underlying the inheritance of monogenic and polygenic traits related to animal disease and production. Topics include genetic defects and their discovery, diagnosis, and treatment, as well as gene-environment interactions. Learn the molecular mechanisms of animal diseases and integrate concepts from multiple disciplines to understand how environmental factors influence gene activity and, ultimately, phenotypes. Emphasizes the role of epigenetics in livestock production, reproduction, and animal health. Explore how biomedical research can be applied to address both human and animal research questions.

title: Principles of Archaeology
description: Introduction to the methods, historical development, and scientific principles of archaeology. Discover how archaeologists generate and interpret information about the human past. Introduces scientific inquiry and provides a foundation for pursuing advanced archaeological courses and field research.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Welcome! This course is designed for students at any level who want to learn about archaeology and the study of our human history. Through a combination of lectures, discussions, and hands-on activities, you will discover how archaeologists reconstruct people's ways of life and significant cultural transformations in the past. You will learn about basic concepts in archaeological research and become familiar with methods and technologies used at field sites and in laboratories. We will also examine current issues related to the conservation of archaeological landscapes, which are invaluable sources of information about our shared human story.
instructorProvidedContent.format: This course is taught in person. Students are required to attend class meetings twice per week with Professor Clayton and a weekly section meeting with a teaching assistant. Section meetings involve hands-on activities, such as analyzing artifacts. No previous experience in archaeology is needed!

title: Dimensions of Material Culture
description: This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of material culture studies. It is intended for students interested in any professional endeavor related to material culture, including careers in museums, galleries, historical societies, historic preservation organizations, and academic institutions. During the semester, students have varied opportunities to engage with and contemplate the material world to which people give meaning and which, in turn, influences their lives. Sessions combine in some way the following: presentations from faculty members and professionals who lecture on a phase of material culture related to his/her own scholarship or other professional work; discussion of foundational readings in the field; visits to collections and sites on campus and around Madison; discussion of readings assigned by visiting presenters or the professors; and exams and short papers that engage material culture topics.

title: Ceramics Analysis: Archaeology
description: Selected areas, periods or problems in archaeology.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The class will be structured as a combination lecture/seminar and hands on technology course in which ceramic technologies that played a role in human adaptive strategies will be studied through readings, discussion, and selected films, as well as actual manufacture and examination of a wide range of artifacts, including pottery, ornaments, figurines, and other objects made from terracotta, stoneware, porcelain, and faience.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: After a brief introduction to the major themes and issues to be addressed in the course, we will study the major varieties of ceramic raw materials and their various modifications. This will be followed by a detailed study of manufacturing techniques and how these have been presented in the literature. We will then look at methods of recording, illustrating and photographing ceramics that are found in archaeological excavations and in preparation for your future projects. The subsequent sessions will focus on ethnographic and experimental studies of ceramic production, trade, use and discard, including a discussion of organic residues found in pottery and usewear on ceramic objects.  More specific topics of ceramic production such as firing techniques, use of ceramics as refractory materials in metallurgy, and the production of glazes will also be explored. The final sessions will focus on selected studies of ceramic research during the early Neolithic up through the period of early complex societies and hierarchical state level societies in the Old and New Worlds. By the end of this class you should have a broad understanding of how to examine the changing role of all major types of ceramic artifacts over time and a detailed understanding of the major types of ceramic technologies.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Combination lecture, seminar style discussion and hands on experimental replication

title: The Origins of Civilization
description: Global archaeological survey of the origins of pristine civilizations beginning with the development of food production and ending with the emergence of the world's first civilizations. Focus of attention: Near East, Egypt, the Indus Valley, North China, Mesoamerica, and Peru.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: For the vast majority of humanity's history, we lived in relatively small communities. We did not live in highly populous, urbanized, and politically centralized societies that researchers refer to as "civilizations . Today, of course, the world is a far different place. We see tremendous differences in social inequality, wealth, power, and access to materials in most societies in our contemporary world. We also see differences in how we produce food and various economic products, and how we use these materials to shape our interactions with each other and the environments around us. How and when did such major cultural transitions occur? This course explores the answers to this question, and will focus on a range of archaeological case studies from across geographic space and time. To be considered is how factors such as occupational specialization, religion, technology, trade, identity formation, and warfare have all been significant for the emergence of "civilizations  in the past. The course explores major questions and implications for humanity and the world we inhabit. How should we define civilizations? What contributed to the emergence of these kinds of societies? How are such social configurations maintained, and how do they decline, collapse, or transform? Archaeology is uniquely capable of exploring the past manifestations of these phenomena, and to understand their evolutionary trajectories throughout the history of humanity. Reviewing evidence and case studies from a global material record of varied temporal and geographical settings, the class will highlight archaeological techniques in studying ancient civilizations. We will also explore some of the most prominent anthropological and archaeological theories that have been proposed to account for the origins of civilizations, considering both cross-cultural patterning as well as unique local-historical settings. Finally, we will consider what these lessons from the past can reveal to us about our shared future.All backgrounds and perspectives are welcome.

title: Psychological Anthropology
description: Survey of psychologically oriented approaches in cultural anthropology: ethnopsychiatry, the ethnography of emotion, conceptions of the self, cognitive development, and culturally defined deviance and mental illness.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course focuses on relations between individuals and the cultures  into which they are socialized and live their lives. It offers a person-centered approach to the study of social and cultural anthropology.The course also focuses on comparative perspectives on constructions of self, person, and other and thei dynamic interactions of self and person with cultural values and social arrangements. We will draw on examples from societies ranging in scale and economy from foraging to post-industrial.  Specific topics include self, person, and individual in anthropological perspectives; ethos, worldview, values, and experience; ethnopsychologies and cultural constructions of self and person; life histories; the life course in cross-cultural perspective; gendered selves; anthropologies of childhood and youth; anthropologies of sexuality; anthropologies of aging; culture and emotion; dreaming in cross-cultural perspective; person, myth, and folklore; self, person, and religious experience; shamanism, spirit possession, and ecstatic religion; self and performance; altered states of consciousness; the anthropology of drugs; cultural constructions of mental health, mental illness, and psychic distress; ethnopsychiatries and psychotherapies. Students with diverse academic backgrounds and interests, both undergraduates and graduate students,  are very welcome to join the course. There are additional requirements for Honors Optional undergraduates and for graduate students. For more information please contact Professor Maria Lepowsky at <lepowsky@wisc.edu>

title: Art, Technology, Gender
description: Independent research in specific problems in physical anthropology, archaeology, or cultural anthropology; under supervision.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The class will be structured as a lecture/seminar and hands on technology course in which current issues in the archaeology of Art, Technology and Gender in the Old and New Worlds will be explored through class discussion, group presentations, experimental replication and Powerpoint presentations. The course will look at how archaeologists study all three topics and how they are interconnected in early state level societies. The issues of gender involve cultural choices about male, female, transvestite, homosexual, and asexual categories that are closely linked to technology, and the environment. Specific topics will include the role of gender in divisions of labor, how different ancient cultures linked gender to specific artistic and functional technologies and how social, ideological and political power was exercised by different genders. Archaeological case studies and readings will be selected from all major world areas and include the time periods leading up to and including early state level societies.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: The course will begin by exploring the definitions of art and gender as seen in ancient and modern texts and graphic representations. We will also look at examples of how cultural concepts of gender and power, are reflected or represented in both utilitarian and ornamental or artistic expression. As part of this investigation we will critically evaluate the gender biases of archaeologists and the societies that they worked in to see how this has impacted interpretations of the past. The second main focus will be on how different societies made choices about gender roles in different technologies and the role of the environment in these choices. Technologies to be considered include agriculture and pastoralism, lithic production, textile production, ceramics, art, magic, ritual and trade. An additional theme will be on how gender has been linked to power in different urban and state level societies in each major region of the world: Mesopotamia, Mediterranean, Egypt, Indus Valley, Sub-Saharan Africa, China, North America, Mesoamerica, South America. The final section of the course will focus on gender roles in early empires, with selected examples from major regions.
instructorProvidedContent.format: lecture, discussion, group presentations, hands on experimental replication

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This graduate-undergraduate course teaches students about the anthropological study of language, colonialism, and resistance. Our key questions are: how are the power relations of colonialism expressed in, on, or through language? How have people opposed these power relations, and how can people do language against white supremacy? Are there possibilities for a decolonial anthropology?During the term, we will explore these questions collaboratively, through readings and films that address language, colonialism, and resistance throughout the Indigenous Americas, and in places including (in alphabetical order) India, the Philippines, and Zimbabwe. We will learn about the varied and perhaps surprising linguistic results of colonialism, and we will analyze and question structures of colonial and linguistic racism and oppression.Reading and workload expectations in this interdisciplinary, seminar-style course are appropriate for advanced undergraduate students and graduate students from anthropology or other fields.

title: Dimensions of Material Culture
description: This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of material culture studies. It is intended for students interested in any professional endeavor related to material culture, including careers in museums, galleries, historical societies, historic preservation organizations, and academic institutions. During the semester, students have varied opportunities to engage with and contemplate the material world to which people give meaning and which, in turn, influences their lives. Sessions combine in some way the following: presentations from faculty members and professionals who lecture on a phase of material culture related to his/her own scholarship or other professional work; discussion of foundational readings in the field; visits to collections and sites on campus and around Madison; discussion of readings assigned by visiting presenters or the professors; and exams and short papers that engage material culture topics.

title: Anthropology of Gender
description: Theoretical and ethnographic approaches to the anthropology of gender, focusing on current works. instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This seminar offers a close examination of gender and embodied identities in cultural and cross-cultural perspectives.  We will explore a range of ethnographically grounded works, both classic and recent, tracing the roots and efflorescence of a subdiscipline and its current discourses within and beyond anthropology. Topics include sex/gender, race, and indigeneity in early modernist ethnography; feminist anthropologies from second-wave feminism to the 2020s, gendered histories and political economies, masculinities, nonheteronormative genders and sexualities; lesbian, gay, and transgender as globalizing  cultural constructions; anthropologies of sexuality and the body; gender and religion; gender, environment, and ecofeminisms; migrations and gendered borderlands, and gender and globalization.   This cross-listed seminar may be taken either as Anthropology 920 or Gender and Women's Studies 920.  Please contact the instructor for further information.
instructorProvidedContent.format: This seminar will meet once a week for 2.5 hours.  Seminar members will contribute regularly in seminar as well as asynchronously to reading-based Canvas discussions of seminar themes and occasionally screen and comment on seminar-related videos . Each seminar member will write a 12-15 page term paper and will present on it in seminar during the last two weeks of the semester.

title: Decolonial Theory
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in African societies and cultures.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Course Title: Decolonial TheoryDecolonize this, decolonize that -- but what does this all mean? In the 2010s "decolonization  became an academic buzzword, sometimes leading to significant change, and sometimes merely indicating that one was following an intellectual trend. At times, one (honestly, "I ) wondered if anyone had actually done the reading. This course will take a chronological approach to decolonial theory, beginning with writers frequently cited by present-day decolonial theorists, and then turning to those theorists writing today. This structure is meant to help students see how ideas build on one another. The readings are Africa-focused -- due to the professor's specialization -- but include writers from outside the continent. Students with various geographical foci are welcome in this class, in the hopes that learning across continents can increase solidarities and strengthen students' own research and writing. In addition, this course can be taken as part of the Graduate Certificate in Visual Cultures. If you are pursuing that certificate, I expect your writing projects to address issues in visual and/or performance studies.

Empire, Global Coloniality and African Subjectivity (2022) Tamale, Decolonization and Afro-Feminism, 2020 Ferdinand, Decolonial Ecology: Thinking from the Caribbean World (2022)Taiwo, Against Decolonization: Taking African Agency Seriously (2022)

title: Have Brush, Will Travel: The Italian Renaissance from Florence to Rome
description: Examines artistic developments that took place in Florence in the 15th century, and how the Florentine Renaissance paved the way to the achievements by painters, sculptors, and architects in Rome in the 16th century, many of whom traveled from Florence to Rome in pursuit of economic opportunity. Introduces the numerous important artistic works produced in Florence, Rome, and other artistic centers, and provides a basic understanding of the purposes, methodology, and terminology of art historical study.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This is a hybrid course. All levels welcome. Note: FRIDAYS will be REMOTE (asynchronous). This course explores artistic developments that took place in FLORENCE in the 15th century, and ROME in the 16th-century, and how the Florentine Renaissance paved the way to the spectacular achievements by painters, sculptors, and architects like BOTTICELLI, LEONARDO DA VINCI, MICHELANGELO, and RAPHAEL. Many of these artists traveled from Florence to Rome in pursuit of economic opportunity and fame. The production and proliferation of art in this period ran paralletlto STATE-BUILDING. We will focus on how religious art was used for POLITICAL as well as spiritual purposes. This includes learning about economic exchange, artist-patron-viewer relationships, art's power as a form of propaganda. Analyzes economic exchange and artist-patron-viewer relationships in an age of political instability and social conflict. Focusing on topics ranging from public projects, civic pride and state-funded imperial propaganda, the procurement of materials, the collective experience of viewing religious and secular art, the course tracks the upward social mobility of artists, shifting gender dynamics, and the projection of personal and professional identities.

title: The Body, Sex, & Health in Art
description: Considers the many fascinating ways in which cultures represented ideas of health, sex, disease, medicine, and death, focusing on the ways different art forms (painting, sculpture, architecture, prints, photography, textiles, decorative arts, hair, costume, music and dance, food) conveyed historically and culturally distinctive ideas about bodies.  Linking the topics will be an attention to how notions of race, gender, and disability determine representations of the body. Enjoy an introduction to basic skills in visual interpretation that are widely applicable in today's world, while covering health and body-related topics chosen from the arts of Europe, China, Japan, Africa, the Islamic World, and the United States. Our objects of study range from ancient Greece and Rome to the present, with an emphasis on nineteenth- to twenty-first century art.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Comm B Class.  This lecture course will introduce you to basic skills in visual interpretation that are widely applicable in today's world, while covering health and body-related topics chosen from the arts of Europe, China, Japan, Africa, the Islamic World, and the United States. The art we study study ranges from ancient Greece and Rome to the present, with an emphasis on nineteenth- to twenty-first century art.   We will consider the many fascinating ways in which cultures represented ideas of health, sex, disease, medicine, and death, focusing on the ways different art forms (painting, sculpture, architecture, prints, photography, textiles, decorative arts, hair, costume, music and dance, food) conveyed historically and culturally distinctive ideas about bodies.  Linking the topics will be an attention to how notions of race, gender, and disability determine representations of the body.Occasional guest experts will speak to our class and section discussions will give you a chance to explore subjects in more depth and acquire the skills of visual analysis while improving your writing and public speaking abilities. Also in sections we will view, smell, taste, hear, and touch the materials out of which art is made as well as various healing substances related to the art under study.  Be prepared to interact with your subject of study!

title: Elegant Revenge: Chinese Arts and Drama
description: Uses popular TV dramas like The Legend of Zhen Huan to explore how eighteenth-century Chinese court women's lives and material culture are reimagined today. Topics include the imperial palace's architecture, interior design, rituals, religion, idealized womanhood, women's objects, cross-cultural exchange, theater, festivals, and the full range of fine arts and crafts - from painting, calligraphy, and embroidery to textiles, glass, ceramics, furniture, jewelry, and costume design.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: AH118 ELEGANT REVENGE: CHINESE ARTS AND DRAMA Since it debuted in 2011, the Chinese television series The Legend of Zhen Huan / Empresses in the Palace (Ch. Zhenhuan zhuan) has been rated as one of the best TV productions on imperial women in Qing China (1644-1911). Based on the art historical and textual sources, the material life at the Qing court was restaged in this show. Such theatrical reimagination has generated heated discussion on the rich material practices in late imperial China in social media. The Qing empire, now often referred to as a material empire, has gained a second life in the popular culture. In these shows, imperial women's artistical talents were fancied as efficient means to facilitate their revenge and conspiracy to climb up to the imperial ladder. In this course, we will follow the episodes in The Legend of Zhen Huan and selections from several other harem dramas and explore the art forms and concepts that developed cross Qing period. Organized according to the growth of the main protagonist Zhen Huan from a lower rank imperial concubine to a powerful Empress Dowager, the course examines the  material, technique, subject and function of imperial palace from its architectural and interior design, ritual and religious practice, idealized womanhood and women's things, cultural exchange between China and the rest of the world, theater and festivals to the development of various fine arts and craft technologies such as paintings, calligraphy, prints, embroidery, woven tapestry, glass, paper objects, ceramics, furniture to costume and jewelry design.

title: History of Western Art I: From Pyramids to Cathedrals
description: Examines the arts and cultures of Europe and the Mediterranean basin before the Renaissance. Explores canonical works such as the pyramids at Giza, the Parthenon in Athens, the Venus di Milo, Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, the Book of Kells, the Great Mosque at Cordoba, Chartres cathedral, and Giotto's Arena Chapel. Define art broadly, to encompass the material culture of everyday life, including jewelry, ceramics, and textiles. Considers the social and historical contexts of art and artistic production - art and imperialism, ethnicity, technology, religious ritual and belief, and myth and storytelling, and its relationships to basic human concerns: death and the afterlife, desire and the body, self-definition and portraiture, power and propaganda, monstrosity and the supernatural, the divine and the sacred. Develops crucial skill sets: critical visual analysis, contextual interpretation, research methods and resources, historiography, and oral, written and digital communication.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course examines the arts and cultures of the broad Western tradition before the Renaissance, including the Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome, and Medieval Europe. The course focuses on the social context of art and artistic production in antiquity. We will consider the relationships between art and imperialism, ethnicity, technology, religious ritual and belief, myth and storytelling, and other considerations. We will define "art   broadly, including buildings, books, and objects meant for everyday use as well as the more traditional masterpieces of sculpture and painting, using approaches from archaeology and material culture. We will consider the role of the artist in artistic production, which was very different in pre-modern societies from what we assume today; the complex roles of state and patron; and the afterlife of works of art, how they were perceived and used by other cultures that inherited or conquered these masterpieces. We will consider the broad trajectory of the "Western  artistic tradition, and how it was used in creating definitions of self in ancient European cultures. We will also consider just what constitutes understanding and explanation in art history, and some of the ways scholars can approach a work of art and grasp its various meanings.

title: A History of the World in 20 Buildings
description: Why were the ancient Egyptians obsessed with building elaborate tombs? Was the Taj Mahal really a monument to love? Why do the Greeks want the Parthenon marbles returned? Was Frank Lloyd Wright "modern?" How have buildings reflected and shaped the historical forces of the modern age, from colonialism, to industrialization, to globalization? Take a journey through space and time and explore the history of the world through its great buildings. Learn to recognize, analyze, and question the dynamic interaction between culture, politics, religion, and architectural form. Perhaps more than any other visual art, architecture is alive. Buildings shapeshift over decades, centuries, millennia. They stand as both witnesses to and agents of historical change. Unpack our buildings' histories to reveal their role in our shared human story.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Why were the ancient Egyptians obsessed with building elaborate tombs? Was the Taj Mahal really a monument to love? How did building with iron change . . . well, everything!? Why did architects embrace Brutalism, and why have so many people come to hate it? How have buildings reflected and shaped the historical forces of the modern age, including colonialism, industrialization, and globalization? Take a journey through time and space as we explore the history of the world through monumental buildings. Learn to recognize, analyze, and question the dynamic interaction between culture, politics, religion, and architectural form. Perhaps more than any other visual art, architecture is alive. Buildings shapeshift over decades, centuries, millennia. They stand among us as both witness to and agents of historical change. Together, we will unpack our buildings' histories to reveal their role in our shared human story.

title: Making the American Landscape
description: Traces the history and evolution of the American cultural landscape from precolonial times to present. Explores how class, ethnic, and racial inequality have shaped the appearance of the American landscape over time, and how that landscape in turn has affected relationships between people and groups through the present day. Examines extraordinary things (civic structures (like our State Capitol), National Parks, War Memorials) and more ordinary kinds of places (mining towns, cotton plantations, sites of recreation and leisure, and suburban tract housing) to stimulate critical thinking about how these places have served people and groups unequally and disproportionately over time and across space. Considers complex meanings of American spaces and places to different people and groups, stimulating empathy and encouraging participation in a multicultural society.

title: Dimensions of Material Culture
description: This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of material culture studies. It is intended for students interested in any professional endeavor related to material culture, including careers in museums, galleries, historical societies, historic preservation organizations, and academic institutions. During the semester, students have varied opportunities to engage with and contemplate the material world to which people give meaning and which, in turn, influences their lives. Sessions combine in some way the following: presentations from faculty members and professionals who lecture on a phase of material culture related to his/her own scholarship or other professional work; discussion of foundational readings in the field; visits to collections and sites on campus and around Madison; discussion of readings assigned by visiting presenters or the professors; and exams and short papers that engage material culture topics.

title: Architecture as Weapon ...
description: Surveys the arts or visual culture of varying geographical regions, time periods, or cultures depending on selected topic.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Architecture as Weapon: Building the Cold WarThe Cold War is typically framed as a military and diplomatic rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union. In reality, it was the horizon against which the entire world imagined and organized itself for half a century and beyond. This course examines how architecture was implicated in the political struggles of the Cold War. Architects and planners participated in projects of military power, development, reconstruction, cultural exchange, and domestic life, advancing competing visions of modernity and the future. As a result, architecture became a tool for both domination and defiance. Not only engaging the familiar US-Soviet binary, we also adopt a non-aligned lens that recognizes the Global South as a generative force in Cold War spatial politics rather than a passive battleground. Despite global partitioning through "blocs  and the "Iron Curtain,  this period was marked by increasing interconnectivity through technological development, popular media, and knowledge exchange, reflected in transformations in the built environment. The course therefore looks beyond explicitly military architecture to seemingly ordinary spaces such as hotels, homes, and highways. We also consider environments transformed through nuclear testing, reimagined in film, and reorganized via cybernetics all of which attempted to redesign the world according to conflicting political agendas. The course includes lectures, discussion, readings, short writing assignments, and collaborative group projects. The main prerequisite is curiosity and a willingness to explore the complexity of Cold War dynamics that, in many ways, are still very much with us today.

title: The Art and Archaeology of Ancient Rome
description: Explores the art and archaeology of ancient Italy, the Roman Republic, and the Roman Empire from the Iron Age to Late Antiquity.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: In the Art and Archaeology of Ancient Rome we explore the material culture of the ancient Roman Empire from the early Iron Age through the age of Constantine the Great. This course uses archaeology to shed light on how the ancient Romans understood and explained their universe, deities, religion, gender, warfare, codes of behavior and justice, and attitudes about life and death. The course focuses on the city of Rome and its monuments and archaeological discoveries, but also on findings from urban centers and sanctuaries beyond Rome, like Ostia, Pompeii, Athens, Ephesus, Leptis Magna, Palmyra, Zeugma, and Ilion (Troy). Students learn how to recognize, describe, discuss and interpret the art of the ancient Romans, and they also learn about archaeological methods, current excavations, ethics and archaeology, modern challenges of museums and collections of antiquities; and the legacy of ancient Roman material culture and technologies in the modern era.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Examines the art and culture of Italy from the Proto-Renaissance to the High Renaissance. title: From Pollock to Warhol
description: Surveys visual art made in the United States between approximately 1945 and 1975, with a focus on movements such as Abstract Expressionism, Pop Art, and Minimalism as well as the historical context of the Cold War and emerging countercultures.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: At the end of World War II, the United States emerged as the dominant global superpower, with only the Soviet Union as its competitor. In the visual arts, the following three decades were arguably the most wildly inventive years in the nation's history. Powerful new styles revolutionized American culture, only to be eclipsed by yet more radical experiments just a few years later. In the midst of both unprecedented economic expansion and profound political upheaval, artists had to negotiate the contradictions of a capitalist democracy marred by persistent racial injustice and the violence of the Korean and Vietnam wars. Some artists, such as Jackson Pollock and Andy Warhol, would become household names. Others preferred to work in the underground.This course provides an overview of major artistic developments in the United States between the end of World War II and the mid-1970s. Movements covered include Abstract Expressionism, Pop Art, Minimalism, and Conceptual Art, as well as feminist, queer, and anti-racist practices. Several sessions will be held in the galleries of the Chazen Museum, which has a strong collection of postwar American art.Assignments:Midterm examFinal examFinal paperSeveral short (one page) reading responses and visual analysis papers

title: Cities of Asia
description: Historical overview of the built environment of cities of Asia from antiquity to the present; architectural and urban legacy in its social and historical context; exploration of common themes that thread through the diverse geographical regions and cultures of Asia. Not open to students with credit for LCA 379 prior to Fall 2019.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This semester long survey course, presents a historical overview of the built environment of the cities of Asia from antiquity to the present.  Most surveys of the city focus on the West, even though the earliest neolithic settlements are found in western Asia, and the first true cities were constructed between the Tigris and Euphrates around 3500 B.C.  Max Weber's work on the City was influential in drawing a contrast between Western and non-Western cities, arguing that 'urban communities' and hence 'true cities' were only found in the West.  This course seeks does not seek to essentialize Western or non-Western cities.  Instead, it seeks to explore and tease out common themes that thread through the diverse geographical regions and cultures of Asia.

title: Cities and Sanctuaries of Ancient Greece
description: Topics include urbanism in ancient Greece in theory and practice; the forms, technologies, patronage and use of buildings; the creation and conception of urban space; and the organization of religious sites, dedications, and rituals.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course explores the secular and religious landscapes of ancient Greece, and the sites in which Greeks lived and worshipped: their cities and sanctuaries. We will start by studying the Greek polis in theory, examining theories of city planning and the creation of the polis as an ideal society, reading the works of philosophers including Plato and Aristotle, urban planners such as Hippodamus of Miletus, and the inscriptions on stone in which laws and decrees were recorded. We will consider the historical and social factors such as colonization which led to the foundation of new cities and constitutions, and the development of concepts of citizenship, equality, and democracy in these new cities. We will then turn to the process of building a city. We will look at both monumental and domestic architecture, and consider not only the forms of architecture but also the technologies of construction, patronage, use and reuse of buildings, and the finds which are associated with such buildings which help reconstruct their chronology and use. We will consider the ancient Greek house and household, the roles of men, women, and slaves, the organization of household space and how it relates to the organization of civic space, the household and the urban economies, and the agricultural countryside of the Greek polis. Finally, in the latter part of the course we will address the religious life of the ancient Greeks within this civic context. After a brief introduction to Greek religion and cult practice, we will look at various sanctuaries in the Greek world. We will consider how sanctuaries were organized, what sorts of activities went on in them, and how they were related to civic life. We will end with an examination of religious art in its sacred context.

title: Visual Cultures of India
description: Concentrates on image complexes (art, photography, and cinema) and visual environments (architecture, urban planning, and public rituals) of India; examination of visual culture through thematic issues such as, sexuality, patronage, cultural encounter, transculturation, ways of viewing, modernism, and nationalism. Not open to students with credit for LCA 428 prior to Fall 2019.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This lecture course concentrates on the images (art, advertisements, photography, television, and cinema), material culture (such as, clothing), and environments (architecture, urban planning, and public rituals) of India.  During the semester, we will examine Indian visual cultures from the ancient to the modern periods.  This historical trajectory will be complemented by a critical focus on selected thematic issues. During these moments we will compare and contrast cases studies from across India, spatially and temporally.  These historical ruptures, or time travels, will allow us to see the continuities and discontinuities between the past and present.  Thematic issues and ideas that will be examined in this class include sexuality, the representation of women, patronage, cultural encounter and cultural synthesis, iconoclasm, the relationship between landscape and architecture, rethinking the canon, ways of seeing, art and craft, the sacred and secular, colonialism, modernism, nationalism, and the pleasures of Indian cinema. No prior knowledge of India is necessary.

title: Frank Lloyd Wright
description: An analysis of Frank Lloyd Wright's architecture and writings.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This experiential course looks at important issues surrounding the personal philosophies and projects (architectural and otherwise) by Frank Lloyd Wright. Often hailed as the best architect of all time -- which is how Wright once described himself -- Wright's work spans more than seven decades, a time when architecture and building underwent major transformations ranging from prefabrication to suburbanization to modernization (in a stylistic sense). We will examine Wright's ideas and buildings relative to these and other changes, and also consider his legacy -- for architects, for builders, for Wright's homeowners, and for his numerous fans (who assemble for annual conferences and building tours to celebrate his legacy).  Our course will do so thematically (versus strictly chronologically) and we will visit many examples of Wright's buildings and meet with experts in the Madison community. Student projects will also be focused on issues related to Wright's buildings (and those of his followers).

description: Advanced topics in Art History taught in a seminar-style format. Topics will vary as to media, geography, culture, and time frame.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: A capstone art history seminar. Considers topics and ideas in the representation of emergent scientific theories of late eighteenth to 21st centuries in American and European Art: how artists drew on, illustrated, augmented, or resisted various scientific strands of thought in their cultures, and, alternatively, how visual materials were deployed in scientific contexts. Areas of inquiry will include arts related to new discoveries in vision and optics, artists involved in genetic modification and AI, visual culture related to Charles Darwin's ideas of sexual selection and evolution, including the recent queering of this discourse; and artists engaging with botany and environmental/climate science. Other areas of consideration might be science fiction/ steampunk; photography; microscopy; natural history museums; science and the supernatural; popularizing science/science as entertainment; zoology and zoos/animal studies; neuroscience; geology, glaciology and paleontology. instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Museums the world over are filled with things that were not originally meant to be there, and which some still do not even define as "art.  In this weekly advanced seminar, we will explore issues related to caring for and displaying such objects/artworks/ancestors, be they sacred drums from Nigeria, stolen statues from Cambodia, or feather tunics from Peru. What is the duty of a museum and curator to these objects, the descendants of their original communities, and the public today? This course will focus on arts from "Non-Western  "Global South  "Global Majority  and "Formerly Colonized  countries due to the shared histories of being considered ethnographic objects to be housed in natural history museums.

title: Materialist Interpretation
description: Advanced topics in 20th Century European Art History taught in a seminar-style format.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is dedicated to materialist tendencies in the interpretation of visual art and literature, with particular attention to thinkers in the tradition of critical theory. The term "materialism  has been associated with a wide range of philosophical perspectives, including the ancient atomistic materialism of Democritus and Lucretius, the mechanistic materialism of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and modern forms of scientific physicalism. instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Architecture as Weapon: Building the Cold WarThe Cold War is typically framed as a military and diplomatic rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union. In reality, it was the horizon against which the entire world imagined and organized itself for half a century and beyond. This course examines how architecture was implicated in the political struggles of the Cold War. Architects and planners participated in projects of military power, development, reconstruction, cultural exchange, and domestic life, advancing competing visions of modernity and the future. As a result, architecture became a tool for both domination and defiance. Not only engaging the familiar US-Soviet binary, we also adopt a non-aligned lens that recognizes the Global South as a generative force in Cold War spatial politics rather than a passive battleground. Despite global partitioning through "blocs  and the "Iron Curtain,  this period was marked by increasing interconnectivity through technological development, popular media, and knowledge exchange, reflected in transformations in the built environment. The course therefore looks beyond explicitly military architecture to seemingly ordinary spaces such as hotels, homes, and highways. We also consider environments transformed through nuclear testing, reimagined in film, and reorganized via cybernetics all of which attempted to redesign the world according to conflicting political agendas. The course includes lectures, discussion, readings, short writing assignments, and collaborative group projects. The main prerequisite is curiosity and a willingness to explore the complexity of Cold War dynamics that, in many ways, are still very much with us today.

title: From Pollock to Warhol
description: Topics will vary as to media, geography, culture, and time frame.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: At the end of World War II, the United States emerged as the dominant global superpower, with only the Soviet Union as its competitor. In the visual arts, the following three decades were arguably the most wildly inventive years in the nation's history. Powerful new styles revolutionized American culture, only to be eclipsed by yet more radical experiments just a few years later. In the midst of both unprecedented economic expansion and profound political upheaval, artists had to negotiate the contradictions of a capitalist democracy marred by persistent racial injustice and the violence of the Korean and Vietnam wars. Some artists, such as Jackson Pollock and Andy Warhol, would become household names. Others preferred to work in the underground.This course provides an overview of major artistic developments in the United States between the end of World War II and the mid-1970s. Movements covered include Abstract Expressionism, Pop Art, Minimalism, and Conceptual Art, as well as feminist, queer, and anti-racist practices. Several sessions will be held in the galleries of the Chazen Museum, which has a strong collection of postwar American art.Assignments:Midterm examFinal examFinal paperSeveral short (one page) reading responses and visual analysis papers

title: Frank Lloyd Wright
description: Varied topics on American Art History.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This experiential course looks at important issues surrounding the personal philosophies and projects (architectural and otherwise) by Frank Lloyd Wright. Often hailed as the best architect of all time -- which is how Wright once described himself -- Wright's work spans more than seven decades, a time when architecture and building underwent major transformations ranging from prefabrication to suburbanization to modernization (in a stylistic sense). We will examine Wright's ideas and buildings relative to these and other changes, and also consider his legacy -- for architects, for builders, for Wright's homeowners, and for his numerous fans (who assemble for annual conferences and building tours to celebrate his legacy).  Our course will do so thematically (versus strictly chronologically) and we will visit many examples of Wright's buildings and meet with experts in the Madison community. Student projects will also be focused on issues related to Wright's buildings (and those of his followers).

instructorProvidedContent.format: This class is a 400-level course, functioning as a mixed lecture/discussion. There will be significant "content delivery" outside of class through videos, readings, and activities such that we can focus in class time on discussion and field visits to Wright buildings in Madison. Assignments will consist of a mix of "low stakes" weekly responses and activities and a large graduate-level research project (which students will work on throughout the semester).

description: This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of material culture studies. title: Cities of Asia

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This semester long survey course, presents a historical overview of the built environment of the cities of Asia from antiquity to the present.  Most surveys of the city focus on the West, even though the earliest neolithic settlements are found in western Asia, and the first true cities were constructed between the Tigris and Euphrates around 3500 B.C.  Max Weber's work on the City was influential in drawing a contrast between Western and non-Western cities, arguing that 'urban communities' and hence 'true cities' were only found in the West.  This course seeks does not seek to essentialize Western or non-Western cities.  Instead, it seeks to explore and tease out common themes that thread through the diverse geographical regions and cultures of Asia.

title: Visual Cultures of India
description: Topics in Architecture and Urbanism of Asia.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This lecture course concentrates on the images (art, advertisements, photography, television, and cinema), material culture (such as, clothing), and environments (architecture, urban planning, and public rituals) of India.  During the semester, we will examine Indian visual cultures from the ancient to the modern periods.  This historical trajectory will be complemented by a critical focus on selected thematic issues. During these moments we will compare and contrast cases studies from across India, spatially and temporally.  These historical ruptures, or time travels, will allow us to see the continuities and discontinuities between the past and present.  Thematic issues and ideas that will be examined in this class include sexuality, the representation of women, patronage, cultural encounter and cultural synthesis, iconoclasm, the relationship between landscape and architecture, rethinking the canon, ways of seeing, art and craft, the sacred and secular, colonialism, modernism, nationalism, and the pleasures of Indian cinema. No prior knowledge of India is necessary.

title: Asian American Women Writers
description: Major texts by Asian American women writers.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course examines contemporary Asian American women's literature in a discussion based, task-oriented classroom. How do women negotiate multiple affiliations, whether ethnic, familial, or national?  We will focus on issues such as coming of age, the policing of women's sexuality, and the formation of collective political consciousness. In addition to looking at works that engage issues of immigration and acculturation in the U.S., we will explore the legacies of colonialism in Asia and the literary portrayal of geopolitics. The course will investigate the ways in which literature can be a forum for interventionist critique of both domestic race relations and international politics.  How does literary form experimental and lyric poetry, realist memoir, or the graphic novel provide the vehicle of such critique?  We will situate literature not as a site for "learning  culture, but for understanding political movements, Cold War nationalism, racial segregation, and sexuality.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: This seminar-style course meets once a week, focusing on roughly a book, film, or text a week. We will cover 8 primary literary texts-poetry, novel, graphic novel memoir--and two films. Attendance is required given the once-a-week structure.
instructorProvidedContent.format: seminar, discussionRequirements: attendance and participation; 2 papers; in class presentation; 2 exams

title: Second Semester Classical Chinese for Chinese Speakers
description: Building on basic grammar and vocabulary learned in the first semester, this course improves comprehension of literary Chinese prose and poetry as well as the discipline of translation from and into Classical Chinese for students who are native or near- native speakers of modern Chinese. title: Elegant Revenge: Chinese Arts and Drama
description: Uses popular TV dramas like The Legend of Zhen Huan to explore how eighteenth-century Chinese court women's lives and material culture are reimagined today. Topics include the imperial palace's architecture, interior design, rituals, religion, idealized womanhood, women's objects, cross-cultural exchange, theater, festivals, and the full range of fine arts and crafts - from painting, calligraphy, and embroidery to textiles, glass, ceramics, furniture, jewelry, and costume design.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: AH118 ELEGANT REVENGE: CHINESE ARTS AND DRAMA Since it debuted in 2011, the Chinese television series The Legend of Zhen Huan / Empresses in the Palace (Ch. Zhenhuan zhuan) has been rated as one of the best TV productions on imperial women in Qing China (1644-1911). Based on the art historical and textual sources, the material life at the Qing court was restaged in this show. Such theatrical reimagination has generated heated discussion on the rich material practices in late imperial China in social media. The Qing empire, now often referred to as a material empire, has gained a second life in the popular culture. In these shows, imperial women's artistical talents were fancied as efficient means to facilitate their revenge and conspiracy to climb up to the imperial ladder. In this course, we will follow the episodes in The Legend of Zhen Huan and selections from several other harem dramas and explore the art forms and concepts that developed cross Qing period. Organized according to the growth of the main protagonist Zhen Huan from a lower rank imperial concubine to a powerful Empress Dowager, the course examines the  material, technique, subject and function of imperial palace from its architectural and interior design, ritual and religious practice, idealized womanhood and women's things, cultural exchange between China and the rest of the world, theater and festivals to the development of various fine arts and craft technologies such as paintings, calligraphy, prints, embroidery, woven tapestry, glass, paper objects, ceramics, furniture to costume and jewelry design.

title: Introduction to East Asian Civilizations
description: Multidisciplinary and historical perspectives on the East Asian civilizations of China, Japan, Korea, Tibet and Mongolia from prehistory to the present, including developments in philosophy, economy, governance, social structure, kinship, geography, etc.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is an introduction to the political, intellectual and cultural transformations in East Asia from ancient times to the present.  We will draw on resources from the disciplines of history, political science, anthropology and international relations to examine the changes taking place in this region, often referred to as East Asia.  Throughout the course, we will examine why and to what extent it makes sense to think of East Asia as having a single cultural, political and economic dynamic.  At different times, the area has been seen to be unified based on different characteristics, such as Confucianism and Chinese writing system, tribute system, trade, Buddhism and numerous other factors.  We will study each of these aspects and understand how people of the region themselves grasped their identity, as well as question the benefits and disadvantages of thinking about East Asia as a geographical entity today.  We will keep the above questions in mind as we tackle world historical themes such as the formation of the Chinese state, the emergence of writing and literature throughout the region and the rise of revolution and hopes for radical change that became a major. historical force especially during the twentieth century.

description: Introduction to a wide variety of ancient Tibetan cultural beliefs, practices and motifs that are practiced to this day. title: Social Change in Contemporary South Korea
description: An exploration of social continuity and change of contemporary South Korea. Covers different institutions of a society - political, economic, and societal/cultural spheres. Incorporates material from anthropology, sociology, political science, economics, and law. Focus on South Korea after the division of the 'two Koreas'.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: 1.Instructors and CommunicationsClassroom: TBDClass: Mondays 2:25PM-5PM* Instructor: Eunsil Oh (eunsil.oh@wisc.edu)  Office: Social Sciences Building Unit 8116BOffice Hours: Mondays (11:30AM -- 12:30PM) or by appointmentEmail Policy & Office HoursIf you have a logistic question, please first consult the syllabus and Canvas. The best way to communicate with me is via email (eunsil.oh@wisc.edu). Try writing your email with a proper title and greeting and make sure to write your name as you prefer to be called. Please show your respect by being professional through email and avoid being too casual (i.e. Hi there, Hey, Ms., etc). Email me with the course number (i.e. Soc 336) in the subject line to talk about accommodations or to schedule an appointment if my office hours do not work for you. I will respond to emails within 48 hours during the workday (9AM-5PM). If you have to miss a lecture, please contact the professor and contact a fellow student for notes. If you will be missing more than four lectures, email the professor. Also, if you have any questions or comments about course material, it is best to sign up and to visit me during my office hour.   2.Course Description and Lecture Overview Course Description Using theories and concepts from sociology, in particular, theories explaining social continuity and change, this course provides a social science perspective of contemporary South Korea. Course contents are divided based on different institutions of a society - political, economic, and societal/cultural spheres. This is a sociology course, but the nature and orientation of the course are interdisciplinary, incorporating readings in anthropology, sociology, political science, economics, and law. Timeframe wise, we focus on South Korea (hereafter, Korea) after the division or the 'two Koreas.'This course pays careful attention to the intersection of multiple structures of inequality such as gender, race/ethnicity, citizenship, class, and sexuality. Also, critically examining the modernization theory that assume linear progression of societies, idea that sex and gender are fixed biological realities, this course discusses what sociologists have contributed to our understanding of social change; continuity; and contemporary South Korea. Each class will consist of half lecture and half discussion. During lectures, the assigned readings are placed in a larger framework. During our discussion time, we are going to understand, apply, and creatively develop sociological concepts using the case of contemporary Korea. We will utilize various means including Canvas and zoom to maximize our learning process. In addition, we will do small group exercises (pairing to grouping) in class to facilitate discussions. This will allow you to better work through challenging concepts and theories, and to apply these theories to your own experiences. title: Love and Politics: The Tale of Genji
description: Explores the themes, structure, and reception history of Japan's The Tale of Genji (ca. 1008). Not open to students with credit for E ASIAN 361 prior to Fall 2019.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: I am so excited to teach this course again! The Tale of Genji is a great big soap opera that can also be read as political critique, religious teaching, and (more recently) tool for selling merchandise. In this course, everyone will read two translations of the tale: Royall Tyler's English version (which has ties to Madison!) and another in the language and/or genre (manga, anime, audiobook, etc.) of their choice. By discussing competing versions of the same chapters, while considering broader themes (politics, romance, religion, commerce, etc.) we will learn more about the book and ourselves that we ever could otherwise... and, judging from the experience of many other Badgers who've taken this course, we will have a ton of fun doing it. Genji, the hero, is someone whom Badgers love to hate!
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Please feel free to email me for a copy of the syllabus from the last time I taught the course (2025). Actual assignments will depend on the size of the class!
instructorProvidedContent.format: This class meets in two "power-lectures" but is mainly discussion based. Each session will start with a general discussion of the hero's latest actions, followed by a mini-lecture from me on a broader theme, then turn to small group activities connecting the day's assigned chapter(s) to that theme. We will also watch/view/listen to a lot of related media as we consider how reactions to the tale have changed over time. If there's student interest, we will also have a couple of (optional) pizza-movie nights to see some of the best and worst adaptations and related works.

title: Cities of Asia
description: Historical overview of the built environment of cities of Asia from antiquity to the present; architectural and urban legacy in its social and historical context; exploration of common themes that thread through the diverse geographical regions and cultures of Asia. Not open to students with credit for LCA 379 prior to Fall 2019.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This semester long survey course, presents a historical overview of the built environment of the cities of Asia from antiquity to the present.  Most surveys of the city focus on the West, even though the earliest neolithic settlements are found in western Asia, and the first true cities were constructed between the Tigris and Euphrates around 3500 B.C.  Max Weber's work on the City was influential in drawing a contrast between Western and non-Western cities, arguing that 'urban communities' and hence 'true cities' were only found in the West.  This course seeks does not seek to essentialize Western or non-Western cities.  Instead, it seeks to explore and tease out common themes that thread through the diverse geographical regions and cultures of Asia.

title: Southeast Asian Literature
description: An introduction to the societies, politics and cultures of Southeast Asia through modern literature. Fiction, testimony, poetry and ephemeral materials will be read alongside literary analysis to understand the roles of writing and art in social and political transformation. Topics will include revolution and uprising; violence and war; environment, migration and displacement; gender and sexuality; censorship and what cannot be written; and cities, the countryside and the spaces between them. Not open to students with credit for LCA 403 prior to Fall 2018

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Taking the end of the wars in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia in 1975 as a chronological point of departure and concluding with writing by political prisoners in the present, this course is an introduction to the contemporary literature of Southeast Asia.  This course begins from the starting premise that rather than standing apart from politics, society and the economy, literature and other forms of cultural production are both reflective of and deeply intertwined with both the daily life of citizens and the governance of the polity. What does life feel like in the countryside and the city? What different futures have authors imagined and dreamt up? How do individuals and communities cope with mass terror and the exile and displacement that often follow?  Together, we will examine these and other questions in short stories, novels, poetry, memoir, graphic novels, as well as the unexpected and innovative visual and internet forms that literature increasingly takes. Through paying close attention to the topics taken up by writers and the transformation of publishing in response to both censorship and financial constraints, the course examines the development of contemporary writing as well as the contexts in which it is produced and gathers meaning. We will pay particularly close attention to translation, including its modes and methods. The course includes both careful, focused readings of literature from individual countries as well as comparative themes which traverse the region. These themes will vary from year-to-year, but for Spring 2027 they will be 1) War, Home and Exile; 2) Migration and Movement; 3) Queer Lives/Living; 4) Dissent; and 5) Prison.

title: Visual Cultures of India
description: Concentrates on image complexes (art, photography, and cinema) and visual environments (architecture, urban planning, and public rituals) of India; examination of visual culture through thematic issues such as, sexuality, patronage, cultural encounter, transculturation, ways of viewing, modernism, and nationalism. instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This lecture course concentrates on the images (art, advertisements, photography, television, and cinema), material culture (such as, clothing), and environments (architecture, urban planning, and public rituals) of India.  During the semester, we will examine Indian visual cultures from the ancient to the modern periods.  This historical trajectory will be complemented by a critical focus on selected thematic issues. During these moments we will compare and contrast cases studies from across India, spatially and temporally.  These historical ruptures, or time travels, will allow us to see the continuities and discontinuities between the past and present.  Thematic issues and ideas that will be examined in this class include sexuality, the representation of women, patronage, cultural encounter and cultural synthesis, iconoclasm, the relationship between landscape and architecture, rethinking the canon, ways of seeing, art and craft, the sacred and secular, colonialism, modernism, nationalism, and the pleasures of Indian cinema. No prior knowledge of India is necessary.

topics.longDescription: Communism, Anarchism, and Other Asian Lefts

title: Communism, Anarchism, Other
description: Advanced topics in Asian studies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: To imagine the world anew. Throughout the twentieth century communists, anarchists and other leftists throughout Asia struggled to make new societies in contrast to existing monarchy, colonialism and authoritarianism. Some succeeded in securing state power, such as Mao and the Chinese Communist Party, whereas others were brutally repressed, such as the Communist Party of Indonesia and early Japanese anarchists.  Some succeeded in forging more just societies, whereas others reconsolidated repression. In this seminar, we will collectively think through and across the region, from the Philippines to Japan to Nepal and beyond, and query what different kinds of worlds leftists imagined, built, and were unable to build.   Roughly chronological, we begin in the late nineteenth century with the anticolonial and anarchist imaginings and writings of Vietnamese dissidents and, for now, conclude with reflecting on the growth of fascism globally. We will criss-cross the region by reading primary theoretical, party and movement texts; memoirs of those involved in left struggles; writings by outside supporters and critics; and academic analysis. Our emphasis itself is non-canonical: in its current iteration, Mao is not on the syllabus. As we read and think, we will pay attention to how struggles were imagined and lived, what roles were played by ideology [and which ideologies], and how the individual, movement, power, nation, and globe acquired meaning and were transformed. Who are the figures behind leftist ideas and movements? Why are states and other repressive powers so afraid of dissent, and what strategies have they used to suppress movements? What do success and failure mean, how might they be assessed, and do they change over time? Underlying our reading, conversations, and writing will also be a reflection on the very category of our analysis: left. Does it illuminate? Obscure? Do both? What forms of intellectual practice and writing are adequate to writing the histories and presents of the left?

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is a study of the way traditional Chinese xiaoshuo (unofficial narrative and fiction), from Six Dynasties tales to Qing novels, intersects with geography. title: Climate Change, Climate Action: The Social Dimensions of Climate Change
description: The planet's climate is changing, and humans are causing it. This means that climate change is not only a topic of study for the biophysical sciences, but also for the social sciences. Focuses on the social dimensions of climate change: the social, political, environmental, and economic factors that shape the drivers and impacts of climate change and the ability of different places and communities to respond. Examines both the social problems that arise from climate change and the social solutions to mitigate and adapt to the climate crisis. How do these social dimensions shape climate change, and how does climate change shape different social dimensions? What climate solutions are being proposed, what climate solutions are already being implemented, and how can we critically evaluate the uneven impacts of those solutions across society and space?

title: Water and People
description: Water is central to the functioning of planet Earth and is influential to shaping many historical and present-day cultures across the globe. As humans increase their impact on Earth's water cycle, our understanding of the multiple roles of water becomes critical to finding sustainable strategies for human and ecosystem health. Explore different perspectives around cultural significance of, engagement with, and access to water, with particular focus to case studies from the United States. Identify the human influence on water quality and quantity in a changing global climate, from local, regional, and global perspectives, and how different racial and ethnic communities in the United States are differentially impacted.
