title: Synthetic Biology Seminar
description: Synthetic biology is a burgeoning field encompassing understanding and designing biological systems spanning from biomolecules to ecosystems. It builds on advances in molecular and cellular technologies to revolutionize biological engineering in the same way that organic synthesis transformed chemistry and integrated circuit design transformed computing. Synthetic biology has the potential to address many of society's grand challenges including: understanding human disease, sustainable biomanufacturing, medical diagnostics and therapeutics, programming mammalian cell behaviors, engineering living materials, information storage, carbon sequestration, and energy generation. Latest advances in the field will be reviewed by covering literature including but not limited to biomolecular design, sequence-structure-function relationship, regulatory and signaling networks, metabolic engineering, interactions in microbial communities, cell-based therapeutics and genome design.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Agricultural and Life Sciences, College of

title: Membrane Protein Structure and Function
description: Membrane proteins comprise over a fourth of proteins encoded in any given genome, providing many vital functions to all cells. For example, ion channels and pumps modulate the membrane potential and help conduct information via nerves and other long distance conducting tissue. Transporters mediate the uptake and secretion of molecules. Receptors, such as G protein coupled receptors and receptor protein kinases, transfer information about the environment to the inside of the cell. Membrane proteins also contribute to the shape of the cell, the structure of the membrane and a myriad of other functions.  Structure/function relationships for this critical class of proteins are discussed, addressing questions such as "how do membrane proteins fold?", "how do certain important classes of membrane proteins work?", "what are the challenges in studying membrane proteins" and "what methods are available for studying their biophysical properties?"

title: Evaluating AI for Ag & Env Sys
description: Specialized subject matter of current interest to undergraduate students.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Course description: This course prepares students to evaluate whether Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are reliable, responsible, and appropriate for agricultural and environmental decisions. Reliability asks whether a system works as claimed under specified conditions and is supported by evidence about data quality, uncertainty, calibration, robustness, transferability, and scientific consistency. Responsibility asks whether and how the system should be used and is supported by evidence about fairness, privacy, security, accountability, human oversight, and social and environmental effects. Students learn and apply knowledge-guided machine learning (KGML) on the user-friendly PyKGML platform to integrate scientific, mechanistic, operational, or relational knowledge with data-driven models. A semester project brings the two anchors together in an evidence-based assurance case and recommendation for a real agricultural or environmental use.Overview:Reliability asks whether the AI system works as claimed under the conditions in which it will be used. It concerns data and measurement quality, uncertainty, calibration, robustness, transfer across farms, ecosystems, seasons, climates, sensors, and management practices, and consistency with scientific knowledge. Responsibility asks whether and how the system should be used. It concerns affected groups, fairness, privacy, security, accountability, human oversight, and social and environmental consequences. A system can satisfy one anchor and fail the other, so the course keeps the two questions distinct before bringing them together.Students work with realistic cases and datasets from crop, livestock, water, nutrient, food, ecosystem, and advisory settings. During the first two-thirds of the course, each week has one primary anchor so that students learn which evidence supports reliability and which judgments support responsibility. The final weeks integrate both anchors through generative AI evaluation, deployment planning, peer review, and the AI assurance dossier. The dossier explains what a system can do, where it can fail, who may be affected, how it should be governed, and whether its use is justified.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Two 75-minute meetings each week. Hands-on activities take place during regular class meetings. Additional time spent out of class for reading, case preparation, technical work, assignments, and the semester project.

input: Evaluating AI for Ag & Env Sys

title: Communicating Evolutionary Biology
description: Exposure to diverse topics in contemporary evolutionary biology and development of critical thinking and communication skills. Most weeks guest lecturers present their own primary research on a specialized topic in evolutionary biology. Seminars include perspectives from genetics, ecology, geoscience, zoology, botany, microbiology, systematics, molecular biology, and integrative research. Some weeks feature special topics and discussions on pedagogical, legal, outreach, or other issues in evolutionary biology. Includes thinking critically about methodology, experimental design and interpretation, and how conclusions are reached in evolutionary biology by reading primary and secondary literature, attending seminars, discussing topics with speakers and other students, and preparing a written report.  The 3-credit version of the course delves deeper into communication of evolutionary biology to researchers, undergraduates, K-12 students, and the general public.

title: The Physics of Medical Imaging with Ionizing Radiation
description: Concepts and principles on the physics of medical imaging systems that form images using high energy photons are presented. Such systems are divided into two categories: (1) those based on the transmission of x-rays through the human body, including radiography, mammography, fluoroscopy, and computed tomography (CT), and (2) those based on the emission of gamma rays or annihilation radiation following radioactive decay of an internal radiolabeled molecule, including the gamma camera, single photon emission tomography (SPECT), and positron emission tomography (PET) and PET hybrid imaging systems. Emphasis is placed on understanding how physics, system design, and imaging technique determine image performance metrics such as contrast, signal-to-noise ratio, and spatial resolution. Clinical applications and radiation safety concepts are detailed for the different types of imaging systems.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Topic Title: Data Science for Healthcare..........Description:  Data science algorithms are being increasingly used to improve healthcare delivery for patients These algorithms, when combined with large volumes of heterogeneous data collected from both within and outside hospitals, have the potential to improve human health This course will provide a foundation for applying data science methods to healthcare In particular, we will discuss several supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning algorithms focusing on working with healthcare data We will also dive into case studies and highlight issues that are particular to healthcare data science, such as unique evaluation metrics, imbalanced datasets, multi data types, model bias, usage, effectiveness, and interpretation..........Strong background: Basic knowledge of mathematical statistics through graduate coursework, experience with programming and data analysis in R or Python

title: Environmental Biogeography
description: Explores how physical and biological factors affect the distribution of terrestrial biomes, ecosystem types, and biodiversity, as well as the role of disturbance and recent human activities on differences in past and modern day species distributions.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course takes an ecosystems approach to understand how physical -- climate, geologic history, soils -- and biological -- physiology, evolution, extinction, dispersal, competition, predation -- variables and processes interact to affect the past, present and future distribution of terrestrial biomes and all levels of biodiversity: ecosystems, species and genes. A particular focus will be placed on the role of disturbance and to recent human-driven climatic and land-cover changes on differences in historical and current distributions of global biodiversity. Throughout the course, we will discuss how historical and current biases in the representation of practitioners and in the methods used affect interpretations of biogeographic research and its applications.COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES To learn patterns and mechanisms of local to global gene, species, ecosystem and biome distributions To learn how past, current and future environmental change affect biogeography To learn how humans affect geographic patterns of biodiversity To learn major paradigm changes in biogeography and how changes in conceptual frameworks and technology have altered interpretations of data and understanding of processes To learn how to apply concepts from biogeography to current environmental problems To learn how legacies of colonialism and scientific racism affect historical and current biases in the representation, methods, practice and applications of biogeography To learn how to read and interpret the primary literature, that is, scientific articles in peer-reviewed journals.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Lecture and in-class discussion

title: Ecosystem Simulation Modeling
description: Introduces process-based mathematical models of ecosystems that are simulated on the computer. Ecosystem simulation models describe the major pools and fluxes in an ecosystem and the factors that regulate those fluxes. Mathematical equations are used to represent the processes that control how major pools (state variables) of an ecosystem change over time. Mechanistically rich, process-based ecosystem models are increasingly seen as critical for anticipating ecosystem change in a no-analog world. Learn why and how ecosystem simulation models are used in ecology. Knowledge of general ecology such as (e.g. BOTANY/F&W ECOL/ZOOLOGY 460) is strongly encouraged.

title: Border and Migration Studies of Latinx America
description: Drawing from cultural studies, border studies, migration and race theory, explores through cultural and literary texts the social and political issues regarding migration, contact zones, transculturation, and/or diaspora. Considers the various meanings of the word "border" or "frontera". What is a border geographically speaking? What does it mean in political and legal terms? How do we conceive the border in cultural, literary, linguistic, political, judicial, and personal ways? What is like to live on the border or on the margins? It is said that the border is a contact zone, a meeting point, a way to transfer and share information, an invitation to (in)tolerance and ex/inclusion. Read texts from history, politics, cultural anthropology, literature, and theatre to grasp the vast understanding of what is life on the border. Focus on the humanities, paying close attention to how visual artists (theater, performance, documentaries) understand and confront life on the border.

input: Border and Migration Studies of Latinx America

description: Offers an introduction to the culture and history of the Mexican and Latin American origin people in the United States. title: Chicanx/e and Latinx/e Literatures
description: Historical, political, and aesthetic roots and directions of Latinx/e and Chicanx/e short stories, novels, poetry, music, plays, films, and essays.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: We will study Latinx literature from the early twentieth century to the present that feature characters confronting revolution, occupation, gentrification, displacement, genocide, extractive technologies, surveillance and policing, and neo-colonialism. We will consider who these texts speak to and why, what they reveal about situations and conditions of crisis, how they portray processes of social change, and what meaning we might take from them in the present. We will also examine the features of memoir/testimonio, realism and speculative fiction that characterize these texts. Finally, we will discuss the relevance of theories of decolonial, relational, and/or resistant literatures with respect to our readings. Assignments include discussion, quizzes, class journals, midterm and final exam. 3 credits. Sophomore standing. Fulfills Literature general education requirement.

description: Explores the philosophy of fundraising and development, its bearing on the nonprofit sector, as well as the practical strategies employed by nonprofits in their fundraising efforts to secure time, talent and treasure for sustaining their work. Nonprofit sector organizations (NPO) seek to thrive in their efforts to have a positive impact in bringing social change - to individuals, families, and communities and, indeed, the world. Development is a mindset - a way to frame the NPO's thinking and behaviors in providing a comprehensive approach to broad mission support.

title: Nature, Race, and Human Difference
description: What do we mean when we talk about nature? What does it mean to call something natural? Are humans part of nature, and is human difference a product of nature or culture? An introduction to the concepts of nature, culture, and race in both the ancient Mediterranean and contemporary US society with an emphasis on how ancient accounts of human difference have shaped-and continue to shape-modern discourse. Approaching the topics of race, nature, and the environment using critical resources afforded by the humanities, consider how the nature/culture binary is deployed in definitions for race and ethnicity, and show how the experiences of racially marginalized groups in the United States are impacted by ancient debates surrounding nature and human difference, as well as their re-articulation over the intervening millennia.

title: The Art and Archaeology of Ancient Rome
description: Explores the art and archaeology of ancient Italy, the Roman Republic, and the Roman Empire from the Iron Age to Late Antiquity.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: In the Art and Archaeology of Ancient Rome we explore the material culture of the ancient Roman Empire from the early Iron Age through the age of Constantine the Great. This course uses archaeology to shed light on how the ancient Romans understood and explained their universe, deities, religion, gender, warfare, codes of behavior and justice, and attitudes about life and death. The course focuses on the city of Rome and its monuments and archaeological discoveries, but also on findings from urban centers and sanctuaries beyond Rome, like Ostia, Pompeii, Athens, Ephesus, Leptis Magna, Palmyra, Zeugma, and Ilion (Troy). Students learn how to recognize, describe, discuss and interpret the art of the ancient Romans, and they also learn about archaeological methods, current excavations, ethics and archaeology, modern challenges of museums and collections of antiquities; and the legacy of ancient Roman material culture and technologies in the modern era.

title: The Romans
description: Latin literature in translation with emphasis on its social background.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course has two goals: first, providing a broad historical survey of Roman civilization, and second, delving into the aspects of Roman society that made it distinctive, influential, and often problematic. Using skills afforded by humanistic inquiry, we will examine the tensions inherent in a society that produced sensitive reflections on the virtue of mercy while subjecting the Mediterranean to their control through a brutal, imperialist process, that extolled the importance of freedom while being sustained by the labor of millions of enslaved people, and that developed an intricate system of representative democracy that nevertheless excluded broad swathes of the population and eventually coexisted (if only in name) with autocracy. Lectures will provide the historical, cultural, and literary background necessary to understand the readings, which will cover a variety of themes and methodologies relevant to studying the ancient Mediterranean. Students will further explore and analyze the material in discussion sections and written assignments, fulfilling the requirements for Communications B courses.

title: Athenian Democracy
description: Explores key issues in the ideology and practice of Athenian democracy. Examines democratic values, institutions, rhetoric, and sociology in order to provide the basic tools to understand democracy in its ancient context.  Engages with a variety of source material (literary, archaeological, epigraphic) in order to develop multiple skills of interpretation. Some questions examined include: What are the key features of Athenian democracy, how did it change over time, and how did it differ from modern democracy? How did the Athenians justify and critique this political system? How did they reconcile citizen egalitarianism with social inequalities of wealth, gender, and status? To what extent were women, foreigners, slaves, or the poor included or excluded from politics? Was Athenian democracy a robust political system or a system in crisis?

title: Cities and Sanctuaries of Ancient Greece
description: Topics include urbanism in ancient Greece in theory and practice; the forms, technologies, patronage and use of buildings; the creation and conception of urban space; and the organization of religious sites, dedications, and rituals.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course explores the secular and religious landscapes of ancient Greece, and the sites in which Greeks lived and worshipped: their cities and sanctuaries. We will start by studying the Greek polis in theory, examining theories of city planning and the creation of the polis as an ideal society, reading the works of philosophers including Plato and Aristotle, urban planners such as Hippodamus of Miletus, and the inscriptions on stone in which laws and decrees were recorded. We will consider the historical and social factors such as colonization which led to the foundation of new cities and constitutions, and the development of concepts of citizenship, equality, and democracy in these new cities. We will then turn to the process of building a city. We will look at both monumental and domestic architecture, and consider not only the forms of architecture but also the technologies of construction, patronage, use and reuse of buildings, and the finds which are associated with such buildings which help reconstruct their chronology and use. We will consider the ancient Greek house and household, the roles of men, women, and slaves, the organization of household space and how it relates to the organization of civic space, the household and the urban economies, and the agricultural countryside of the Greek polis. Finally, in the latter part of the course we will address the religious life of the ancient Greeks within this civic context. After a brief introduction to Greek religion and cult practice, we will look at various sanctuaries in the Greek world. We will consider how sanctuaries were organized, what sorts of activities went on in them, and how they were related to civic life. We will end with an examination of religious art in its sacred context.

title: Reboots, Remakes, & Retellings
description: Why do certain stories and characters persist and reappear through adaptation, reboots and retellings? What are the challenges and possibilities of adaptation, what do they tell us about media, literature, meaning, narrative, and creativity, and what is their cultural significance?  Learn to critically examine adaptations across multiple media, including film, television, literature, games, comics, apps, and online media. Gain a broader understanding of how popular narratives, myths, heroes, and villains work and a deeper awareness of artistic style.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Adaptations, remakes, sequels, prequels, reboots, and franchises are plentiful. Lazy media criticism often bemoans the lack of new ideas today, suggesting that adaptation is a new or increasing phenomenon, even though most literary traditions begin with retellings, and many of the most revered artists throughout history have been adaptors par excellence. This course will thus go beyond hot takes to instead critically examine what adaptation, reboots, and retellings are, why they are so plentiful, why they have always been so plentiful, what are the challenges and possibilities of adaptation, what they tell us about media, literature, meaning, narrative, and creativity, and what cultural work they do. We will consider adaptations across multiple media, including film, television, literature, games, comics, apps, and online media. Why have Batman, James Bond, Elizabeth Bennet, the Skywalkers, Spidey, and more kept coming back? A deep dive should help us find some answers.

title: Netflix's Streaming Revolution
description: Explore various topics in film and media studies, history, and theory.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: In 2007, when Netflix started making its media catalog available to view via Internet streaming, many saw the move as little more than a quirk for a company previously known for delivering DVDs by mail. But this move quickly ushered in an era of streaming television, which is now the predominant way that television is delivered in the US and many other countries. This course analyzes what the streaming era is and how it has disrupted business as usual and society in so many ways. Along the way, we'll explore what television is, could be, and what it's becoming. And we'll consider many issues surrounding streaming, including: bingeing, algorithmic recommendations, "the streaming wars,  how to regulate the Internet, impacts on storytelling and genre, what it means for creative products to be "data-driven,  what streaming is doing to the film industry, the end of "mass  media and the rise of "niche -broadcasting and filter bubbles, the ascendance of nostalgia and of "the rewatch,  how and why we use television, how television is globalizing at a rapid rate, and more. The course is open to anyone interested in how Netflix, Disney+, Apple, and peers "matter,  how they hold sway over us, and what media look like in 2027.

The Future of Creative Contracts, Residuals, and LicensingWeek 4 - 2000 Shows at Your Finger-Tips: Curating the Streaming Library + Murderer or Savior? title: Gender and Communication
description: Effective communication requires awareness of how gender influences communication and our capacity to build lasting and meaningful relationships. Learn about theories and concepts to understand how gender influences our interpersonal, professional, and social lives. Topics include terms and concepts relevant to the study of how we communicate about gender, sex and sexuality, including identity, language and nonverbal behavior, socialization, close personal relationships, education, work, violence, media and social movements.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Effective communication requires awareness of how gender influences communication and our capacity to build lasting and meaningful relationships. Learn about theories and concepts to understand how gender influences our interpersonal, professional, and social lives. Topics include terms and concepts relevant to the study of how we communicate about gender, sex and sexuality, including identity, language and nonverbal behavior, socialization, close personal relationships, education, work, violence, media and social movements.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: This course is about the relationship between gender and communication. Our method of study will be a combination of reading, discussion, online lecture, research, and analysis with a goal of coming to a broad definition of gender, as well as an examination of how this knowledge connects with our personal identity and experiences, and our position in society. More specifically, we will learn about gender and communication through four modules of study, and a final wrap-up.The first module is an introduction to terms, definitions, and concepts relating to gender and sex, and the placement of these definitions in the field of communication. This section will also be concerned with how gender reflects and is influenced by our lifelong construction of personal identities. We will study the influence of family on our definition of gender, the topics of femininity and masculinity, and transgender.The second module will focus on gender as it relates to communication behavior. We will examine gendered language and gendered nonverbal behavior, and how we are taught these things through schooling.The third module will examine the impact of gender on our social and personal relationships as well as in organizations. This will include a discussion of gendered violence in relational and societal contexts.The fourth module is a broader examination of how gender and communication exists within a societal framework. In this section we will study gender and communication within the topics of the media and social movements.

title: The Discourse of Dictators, Demagogues & Extremists
description: Analyze the persuasive communication of demagogues, dictators, and extremists, including speeches, manifestos, branding, imagery, music, films, conspiracy theories, and social media campaigns. Compare the charismatic and fear-based appeals of current leaders to public figures and groups of the past. Explore and critique recurring and distinctive elements of speech. Address core questions: When people lose confidence in existing political orders, how do demagogues, dictators, and extremists emerge to exploit these uncertainties and gain power? What makes their rhetoric and leadership styles so seductive? Why are so many people willing to become loyal, often fanatical followers? How do some leaders seize and sustain state power while others spiral slowly toward self-destruction? How does studying this discourse help us understand ways to critique and counter authoritarianism and extremism today?

input: The Discourse of Dictators, Demagogues & Extremists

description: Specialized subject matter of current interest in communication theory and research.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Maintaining good health is challenging: making decisions about treatments and other courses of action, managing uncertainty about their future or the trajectory of their illness, coping with large volumes of information containing potentially conflicting advice, and responding to changes in their identities and relationships as a consequence of illness. Managing those challenges can be helped or hindered by communicating with others (e.g., family, friends, and health care providers). In this course, we will explore the role of interpersonal communication in the management of physical and mental health. The class will draw on theories and research from communication and related social science disciplines. In examining this scholarship, we will continually apply these theoretical concepts to real-world situations and connect research findings to practical implications.

title: Seminar: Contemporary Rhetorical Theory
description: A review of recent and ongoing theoretical developments in rhetorical theory.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This graduate-level seminar is aimed at critically analyzing the role of digital media and technology in the constitution of social experience and public discourse. Together, we will be thinking about the topics including (but not limited to) the role of infrastructures, the centrality of digital cultural practices, and the politics and rhetorics of the digital. While "digital studies  could mean a range of things from digital production to digital humanities, and a range of methods including big data approaches, this seminar adopts an interdisciplinary, critical humanities approach. Which is to say that our objects and themes in this seminar are going to be based in the digital era, but our thinking about the digital might be thought of as remarkably analog. While the onset of the digital has often been thought of as a "revolution,  such terminology leads us to think in terms of total breaks. In contrast, our digital studies approach will make connections to non-digital pasts. This is especially true of more macro-level themes such as digital infrastructures and digital culture, in which we will have to employ a more longue-dur e lens to make sense of their current shape. In approaching digital studies this way, we will maintain a focus on questions of power and control at three levels: discourse what people think of and say about and through the digital; practice what people actually do with the digital; and design how power may be generated and expressed through the material and conceptual construction of digital technologies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Sp 2027 CES 499: Independent Study in Engaged Sociology"Supporting Farmers and Local Food Resources in Vernon and Crawford Counties, Wisconsin 45 hoursNote: We expect to accept two students for this 499 opportunity. This 499 supports a project that is underway in Vernon and Crawford Counties in southwestern WI. You can do this work remotely by email and zoom. By consent of instructors. This is a Sp 2027 opportunity only and will not be offered in the future. If interested, please email Nan Enstad nenstad@wisc.eduYour Instructors/ Research Team:Nan Enstad (she), Professor in Community and Environmental Sociology, nenstad@wisc.eduElena Bird (they/she), Researcher in Community and Environmental Sociology, ebird@wisc.eduTeam Meeting:We meet as a full team every other week for 30 minutes. You will also have one-on-one sessions with Elena or Nan as needed.Project Description:This ongoing project collaborates with the Vernon-Crawford chapter of the Wisconsin Farmers Union. In the heart of the Driftless region, rich with organic farms, a farm to table food scene in the Viroqua area, and many farmers markets, small and mid-sized farmers in Vernon and Crawford county still struggle to make local food accessible to their community and keep farming attainable for beginning farmers. This project supports their efforts to build a farmer-led, community food system model by developing decision making resources and supporting network building.499 students will contribute by compiling information from beginning farmers and creating public facing reports to support community decision-making. Depending on learning interests, they will assist lead researchers in one or two of the following:  Conducting 4-10 Beginning farmer interviews and analyzing data  Producing a public-facing PDF guide to grocery stores, farm stands, farmers markets, CSAs, food pantries, and other food access points in Vernon and Crawford Counties.  Producing an interactive map using ArcGIS online or Google Maps. Similar to MKE Food Councils Food Environment Map project: https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/4883a0957d124294aa236d9e9cc696a5/page/Page?views=Food-PantriesCourse Objectives:By the end of this semester, you will be able to:(1) Contribute research-quality work to an active Community Based Research Project: conduct interviews, transcribe and analyze qualitative data, prepare outreach materials(2) Apply community-based research ethics: Explain how research design, consent practices, and IRB governance shape how to ethically engage with rural communities.(3) Implement methods for soliciting, facilitating, and receiving community feedback for Community Based Research projects.Skills you will build:You do not need any particular skills beyond being a CES student to register for this opportunity. However, you will gain the following tangible skills:Interview track  Readings on qual methods and ethics  Human subjects training online, IRB training  NVivo trainingPublic-facing Report and Map Track  Qualitative methods and ethics readings  Canva and design trainings with Design Lab  ArcGIS online basic trainingBoth Tracks  working on collaborative research team,  analyzing qualitative research findings,  assessing outreach and outreach goalsEstimated Credit Hours:UW--Madison defines a credit hour as a minimum of 45 hours of learning activity. The 1-credit standard for this course is met by an expectation of a total of 45 hours of student engagement with the course learning activities. We will aim at a discussion that is informed by empirical research and by work done in ethical theory, political philosophy, and other relevant disciplines, and whose character is rigorous, clear, nuanced, and unbiased.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Professor Laura "Hobbes  LegaultCourse Title: Demystifying Artificial IntelligenceCourse Description: Demystifying AI is a course for students in non-technical fields who want to better understand how AI actually works. During this class you'll learn some of the basics of artificial intelligence functionality and explore the high-level mechanics of Large Language Models (LLMs) through reading, discussion, writing, and other interactive in-class activities.Typical Topics/Schedule: Each week we will focus on a different aspect of AI. Topics will range from the foundational Machine Learning concepts like supervised/unsupervised learning to the modern strategies of LLMs and other common algorithms, but the exact schedule is subject to change.Course Format: Students will be assigned weekly preparation activities (including reading or exploration of a tool) to complete outside of class. Lecture time will be screen-free, and include activities like handwritten reflections on the week's topic, discussions, and embodied computing activities where students simulate the actions of a computer. As AI is a rapidly changing field, some time each week will be reserved for discussing any late-breaking developments in the world of AI. There is no assigned textbook; readings will be provided.

title: Programming II
description: Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming using classes and objects to solve more complex problems. Introduces array-based and linked data structures: including lists, stacks, and queues. Programming assignments require writing and developing multi-class (file) programs using interfaces, generics, and exception handling to solve challenging real world problems. Topics reviewed include reading/writing data and objects from/to files and exception handling, and command line arguments. Topics introduced: object-oriented design; class vs. object; create and define interfaces and iterators; searching and sorting; abstract data types (List,Stack,Queue,PriorityQueue(Heap),Binary Search Tree); generic interfaces (parametric polymorphism); how to design and write test methods and classes; array based vs. linked node implementations; introduction to complexity analysis; recursion.

title: Machine Organization and Programming
description: An introduction to fundamental structures of computer systems and the C programming language with a focus on the low-level interrelationships and impacts on performance. Topics include the virtual address space and virtual memory, the heap and dynamic memory management, the memory hierarchy and caching, assembly language and the stack, communication and interrupts/signals, compiling and assemblers/linkers.

title: Programming III
description: The third course in our programming fundamentals sequence. Covers balanced search trees, graphs, graph traversal algorithms, hash tables and sets, and complexity analysis and about classes of problems that require each data type. Involves design and implementation using high quality professional code, a medium sized program, that demonstrates knowledge and use of latest language features, tools, and conventions. Additional topics may include inheritance and polymorphism; anonymous inner classes, lambda functions, performance analysis to discover and optimize critical code blocks. Introduces industry standards for writing high-quality, maintainable code.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Topic Title: AI-Assisted Software Development and Intelligent Applications Description: This course examines the dual role of artificial intelligence in modern software development: as a transformative tool for developer productivity and as a core architectural component of next-generation software. Students will master AI-assisted development workflows to optimize the entire software development life cycle, leveraging intelligent tools for requirements analysis, code generation, debugging, and automated testing. The course provides rigorous, hands-on experience in full-stack development, teaching students how to architect and integrate large language models (LLMs) and AI agents into scalable applications. By utilizing industry-standard tools for version control, CI/CD, and cloud deployment, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of building, managing, and maintaining AI-native software at every stage of its life cycle. Pre-Reqs: CS 400 Required for course: Students must purchase a subscription to Claude Code.  This will be the tool taught and used during the course.

title: Software Engineering
description: Ideas and techniques for designing, developing, and modifying large software systems. Topics include software engineering processes; requirements and specifications; project team organization and management; software architectures; design patterns; testing and debugging; and cost and quality metrics and estimation. Work in large teams on a substantial programming project.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: If you can write code, that's a skill. If you can build, ship, and maintain a complex software system in a team of six without breaking production that's Software Engineering.CS/ECE 506 is designed to simulate a professional software environment. You will move beyond structured, individual assignments to tackle open-ended challenges where requirements change, communication matters, and process is just as important as the code.Our focus is not just on writing code, but on the entire Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) from project idea to final deployment.1. Understanding the Focus: The "Mosaic" of Software EngineeringA common misconception is that CS 506 teaches new programming languages or low-level technical fundamentals from scratch. In fact, no new programming languages or fundamental coding concepts are taught in CS 506. Instead, think of CS 506 like assembling a mosaic or solving a complex puzzle: it is a practical, integrative course where you take the foundational technical skills you have acquired in other classes and piece them together into a complete, semester-long software project using modern engineering methodologies.CS 506 emphasizes process and teamwork. It focuses on modern software engineering paradigms and practical industry challenges.+ Emerging Trends & Responsibility: Exploring Ethics in Software Engineering and applying AI-driven software engineering techniques to modern workflows.+ Agile Philosophy & Scrum: Practicing iterative development, sprint planning, estimations, retrospectives, and backlog management.+ Architecture & Design Patterns: Structuring software systems using proven object-oriented and architectural design patterns.+ Testing & Quality Assurance: Writing automated unit, integration, and system tests, including strategies for maintaining code quality under project pressure.+ DevOps & Containerization: Building modern deployment pipelines and using tools like Docker for environment configuration and CI/CD integration.2. Realistic Industry Team Dynamics & Course Structure:- No Self-Selected Teams or Custom Ideas: Mimicking real-world corporate environments, CS/ECE 506 students do not choose their teammates or pitch their own project ideas. Teams are algorithmically formed based on complementary skill sets (e.g., balancing frontend and backend experience), shared project interest preferences, and compatible availability outside of class. Because CS/ECE 506 is a joint CS and ECE course, suggested project ideas can involve hardware development or software-hardware integration, making it a versatile option for both ECE and CS majors.- Required Interactive Workshops: Lecture attendance is required because most lecture sessions function as interactive workshops where project teams meet in-person in a collaborative style classroom to execute key Agile milestones, including sprint planning, architectural planning and reviews, sprint retrospectives, peer code reviews, and project evaluations.3.Where CS/ECE 506 Is Highly Beneficial?Taking CS 506 is particularly highly recommended if your target career path aligns with industry-standard software development and modern team workflows:+ Simulating Corporate Team Mechanics:Working with assigned teammates who have diverse skill sets prepares you directly for professional engineering teams, where you rarely choose your collaborators or projects.+ Navigating Contemporary SE Challenges:Exposure to topics like AI-assisted software engineering, software ethics, and maintaining code quality under project pressure prepares you for current industry realities that go beyond writing basic algorithms.+ Mastering Industry Tools & Methodologies:Hands-on experience with Docker, CI/CD, Scrum ceremonies, project estimation, and AI-assisted engineering gives you an immediate head start in internships and full-time roles.+ Strong Interview & Portfolio Material:Navigating real team dynamics, managing code reviews, and delivering a

Previous exposure to numerical computing (e.g. Matlab, Python, Julia, R) required.

title: Algorithmic Game Theory & Learning
description: Game theory is a mathematical lens for studying interactions among strategic agents, modeling these situations as games with the goal of understanding and influencing outcomes. Core topics include non-cooperative game theory, mechanism design, and cooperative game theory, examined via the lens of a computer scientist, drawing on tools from theoretical computer science, optimization, probability, and machine learning. Themes include the impact of self-interested behavior on others and on societal outcomes, the emergence of equilibria under such behavior, how such equilibria can be computed or approximated, designing mechanisms to ensure fair and efficient outcomes, and how cooperation can lead to fair value distribution. Particular emphasis is placed on studying, designing, and implementing algorithms.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Topic Title: AI-Assisted Software Development and Intelligent Applications Description: This course examines the dual role of artificial intelligence in modern software development: as a transformative tool for developer productivity and as a core architectural component of next-generation software. Students will master AI-assisted development workflows to optimize the entire software development life cycle, leveraging intelligent tools for requirements analysis, code generation, debugging, and automated testing. The course provides rigorous, hands-on experience in full-stack development, teaching students how to architect and integrate large language models (LLMs) and AI agents into scalable applications. By utilizing industry-standard tools for version control, CI/CD, and cloud deployment, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of building, managing, and maintaining AI-native software at every stage of its life cycle. Pre-Reqs: CS 400 Required for course: Students must purchase a subscription to Claude Code.  This will be the tool taught and used during the course.

title: Stochastic Programming
description: Stochastic programming is concerned with decision making in the presence of uncertainty, where the eventual outcome depends on a future random event. Knowledge of integer optimization (COMP SCI/I SY E/MATH 728) is helpful, but not required.

title: Integer Optimization
description: Introduces optimization problems over integers, and surveys the theory behind the algorithms used in state-of-the-art methods for solving such problems. Special attention is given to the polyhedral formulations of these problems, and to their algebraic and geometric properties. Applicability of Integer Optimization is highlighted with applications in combinatorial optimization. Key topics include: formulations, relaxations, polyhedral theory, cutting planes, decomposition, enumeration.  Students are strongly encouraged to have knowledge of Linear Programming  (e.g., COMP SCI/I SY E/MATH 525), including algorithms, duality and polyhedral theory.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: In Integer Optimization problems, our task is to find one integral point, in a given polyhedral region, that minimizes a given linear objective function. Integer Optimization is a thriving area of discrete mathematics, which is applied nowadays to a multitude of human endeavors, thanks to high quality software. It was developed over several decades and is still evolving rapidly. The goal of this course is to present the mathematical foundations of Integer Optimization. We will survey the theory behind the algorithms used in state-of-the-art solvers. Special attention is given to the polyhedral representations of these problems, and to their algebraic and geometric properties. The broad applicability of Integer Optimization is highlighted with applications in combinatorial optimization and number theory.This course is proof based. Prerequisites are linear algebra, and a certain mathematical maturity.This course is based on the book Integer Programming by Michele Conforti, Gerard Cornuejols, and Giacomo Zambelli.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Topics include: polyhedral theory, perfect formulations, relaxations, cutting planes, and enumeration.

title: Data Exploration, Cleaning, and Integration for Data Science
description: Big Data is often said to deal with four Vs: volume, velocity, variety, and veracity. The focus is on variety and veracity challenges, which often arise in data science projects. In many such projects, data is often incorrect, hard to understand, and come from a variety of sources. Data scientists often spend 80% of their effort to explore, clean, and integrate this data, before analysis can be carried out to extract insights. As a result, managing variety and veracity has received significant attention. Study these topics, understand their challenges, and discuss solutions. These solutions often require data management, machine learning, big data scaling, cloud, crowdsourcing, and user interaction techniques. Knowledge of machine learning/AI [COMP SCI 540], databases [COMP SCI 564] and Python [COMP SCI 320] recommended.

input: Data Exploration, Cleaning, and Integration for Data Science

title: Dichotomy for Counting
description: Advanced topics in algorithms, complexity, and cryptography. The exact topic varies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Topic Title:  Complexity Dichotomy for Counting......Breadth:  Band 3......Description:  There have been great advances in the complexity dichotomy theory for counting problems. If NP \not = P, then there are problems in NP that are of intermediate complexity, i.e., they neither in P nor being NP-hard. The same is true for counting problems, in terms of P versus #P. However, it is a fact that almost all problems at this level are found to be either in P or #P-hard. This led to the study of complexity theory. We will discuss the classification problem for broad classes of #P problems. We will study Graph Homomorphisms, Counting Constraint Satisfaction Problems, and Holant Problems. Students can get a glimpse of the topics in the book (available on UW Madison Library):  ...... https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/complexity-dichotomies-for-counting-problems/5DC3008A992DC40D3E94D97F8E76C12A   ......Prerequisites:  NONE......Strong Background:  Strong mathematical background expected.

title: Psychology of Mindfulness
description: An academic and experiential introduction to mindfulness meditation framed within the perspective of psychology is provided. Scientific research and modern meditation instructions that have formed the basis of a variety of secular mindfulness-based interventions are reviewed. Readings will adopt a variety of perspectives and methodologies, including conceptual/theoretical work, clinical trials, review articles including meta-analyses (i.e., aggregating findings across studies), and measurement-oriented studies. Key topics include: Buddhist and historical underpinnings of secular mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and similar interventions (e.g., lovingkindness and compassion-based meditation), and empirical literature pertaining to neuroscientific and clinical effects of mindfulness training and related interventions.

title: Clinical Mental Health Counseling: Diagnosis and Treatment Planning for Counselors
description: Examine the treatment and practice implications of different mental health diagnoses and adjustment disorders. Reviews advanced principles of mental health diagnoses based on DSM 5 and ICD 10 nomenclatures and contextualizes this review for the practice of counseling applied and adapted for a diversity of clients and communities. title: Game Design II
description: Explore the expressive, social, and cultural impact of games as a medium through focused creation of a single capstone project. Develop an analog or digital game depending on  interest and skill set. Designed to build skills in designing interactive games using an iterative approach that incorporates user testing and feedback. Focuses on design practices common to all games which can be applied by a game designer working in any medium, including sports, board games, computer games, and videogames. Opportunities to explore a wide variety of independent games as well as the platforms used to create them.

title: Comparative Animal Nutrition
description: Nutrients and their assimilation, function, and interactions that affect metabolism in mammals.  Differences among species will be used to emphasize unique digestive and physiological functions and how these differences affect metabolism of nutrients. Humans will be used in some comparisons. Follows physiological progression of nutrients, starting with an overview of the digestive tract followed by water and builds on specific roles of nutrients and substrates needed to provide basic processes required for maintenance, tissue accretion, and homeostatic regulation of nutrients.

Fosters appreciation for the translatability and universality of knowledge between human and animal health and disease.

title: Science of Cutaneous Disease
description: The practice of Dermatology encompasses diseases of the skin, mucosal surfaces, hair and nails. The scientific specialty integrates cellular and molecular biology, immunology, microbiology, and physiology to support patient care decisions. Learn basic science principles of normal and abnormal cutaneous functioning, building on the principles introduced in the MED SC-M 774. These core concepts will be applied though interactions with patients in the clinical setting, building foundational basic science knowledge to diagnose and treat dermatologic diseases.

title: Individualized Clinical Elective in Dermatology
description: Experience blends medical and procedural dermatology, dermatopathology and basic science topics. Advance patient care skills through exposure to a broad array of common and complex cutaneous diseases, formulation of basic differential diagnoses and treatment plans, and performance of common diagnostic procedures. Experience via rotations through general adult and pediatric dermatology clinics, as well as specialty clinics. Opportunities may arise for participation in inpatient dermatology consults. All clinical activities will be completed under the direct supervision of attending physicians and residents. Participate in additional educational activities, including faculty lectures, Grand Rounds conference, and reading or on-line assignments. Additional patient care related learning activities may be assigned by instructors (e.g., literature reviews, presentations on specific topics); these are dependent on the individual student, attending physician, and clinical site.

title: What is Design?
description: Design is a key component of our daily lives and can profoundly affect all people. But how? And to what end? What does design mean and what can it do for us? Interrogate those questions by looking broadly at the place of design in everyday life, and how design intersects with society, economics, politics, the environment, and culture. Study the form, function, and philosophy of design, from what we wear on our bodies to how we move through the world. Ground discussions in close observation and analysis of previous design solutions, leading to innovative approaches to the roles, and responsibilities, of design for the future.

title: Human-centered Design and Business
description: Design thinking is an iterative problem-solving process geared toward producing innovative solutions for complex and persistent problems in various fields and organizations. Its process, culture, and value system from both design and business point of views will be covered: Empathetic understanding of the end users, problem definition rooted in systems thinking, ideation with a strong emphasis on creativity, visualization and prototyping, testing rooted in a set of research methods, and finally, the importance of iteration in bringing about innovative solutions. The path from project to market will also be explored, with an understanding of how one might balance desirability, feasibility and viability.

title: Dimensions of Material Culture
description: This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of material culture studies. It is intended for students interested in any professional endeavor related to material culture, including careers in museums, galleries, historical societies, historic preservation organizations, and academic institutions. During the semester, students have varied opportunities to engage with and contemplate the material world to which people give meaning and which, in turn, influences their lives. Sessions combine in some way the following: presentations from faculty members and professionals who lecture on a phase of material culture related to his/her own scholarship or other professional work; discussion of foundational readings in the field; visits to collections and sites on campus and around Madison; discussion of readings assigned by visiting presenters or the professors; and exams and short papers that engage material culture topics.

title: Environmental Control Systems: Lighting, Acoustics, and Thermal Comfort in Buildings
description: The ways in which we design, construct, and operate has significant impacts on the building occupants and the environment. Architects, designers, and building engineers can work closely together to reduce depletion of critical resources, prevent environmental degradation, and create built environments that are livable, comfortable, safe, and productive. Offers the foundational knowledge on which such practice can be built on. Through a series of lectures, field measurements, and building simulations, understand how lighting, acoustics, and thermal properties behave in buildings and influence the building occupants. The proper application of building design as well as methods for designing and evaluating these features are discussed.

title: Research Methods in Design
description: Future designers need to have critical research knowledge and skillsets that include mastery of various research methods, related issues, and practical experiences in understanding and interpreting quantitative or qualitative research. Design research allows designers to be involved directly with objects, products, and environments they design through human-centered inquiry. The major concepts addressed include design research and its influence on the practice of design, generating research questions, critical literature review, research evaluation, data management and analysis, and various research strategies, all geared toward application to various design practices.

title: Dimensions of Material Culture
description: This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of material culture studies. It is intended for students interested in any professional endeavor related to material culture, including careers in museums, galleries, historical societies, historic preservation organizations, and academic institutions. During the semester, students have varied opportunities to engage with and contemplate the material world to which people give meaning and which, in turn, influences their lives. Sessions combine in some way the following: presentations from faculty members and professionals who lecture on a phase of material culture related to his/her own scholarship or other professional work; discussion of foundational readings in the field; visits to collections and sites on campus and around Madison; discussion of readings assigned by visiting presenters or the professors; and exams and short papers that engage material culture topics.

title: Economics of Race in the United States
description: Historical and contemporary sources and causes of, and potential policy responses to, racial and ethnic economic inequality in the United States. Topics covered include healthcare, education, labor markets, housing and neighborhoods, wealth, and criminal justice, with a focus on aspects of the economy where there are differences in economic outcomes for racial or racial minority groups. Questions include how these differences can result from disparities in how people, markets, or policies treat or impact different groups using economic theory as a foundation, and how economists have studied and measured these differences. In light of the history and range of economic opportunity and change in some communities, particular attention is given to the African American experience.

title: Markets and Models
description: An investigation into the various ways that markets determine the allocation of scarce resources: via a single market-clearing price, waiting in line or other forms of rationing, search, a centralized matching algorithm, an auction, or a contest.  We will examine real-world examples of each type of market, and introduce and solve a formal theoretical model of each to see what insights it leads to.

title: Machine Learning for Economists
description: Introduction to the use of Machine Learning (ML) in economic analysis. Covers basic techniques of ML, much attention will be devoted to evaluating the use of these tools in economics. Learn how economists are integrating the tools of ML with econometric techniques in current empirical research. Gain hands on experience in using these techniques to answer traditional questions of interest to economists. Topics include (i) an in-depth discussion of the differences and similarities in goals, empirical settings and tools between ML and econometrics, (ii) supervised learning methods for regression and classification, unsupervised learning methods, large data analysis and data mining, (iii) recent methods at the intersection of ML and econometrics, designed for causal inference, optimal policy estimation, estimation of counterfactual effects. The methods are taught with an emphasis on practical application.

title: Bayesian Statistics
description: Introduces the theory, methods, and computational procedures needed to perform advanced Bayesian data analyses. Predictive and decision-theoretic motivations including subjective probability, risk, admissibility, and exchangeability; highlights key components of Bayesian analysis (i.e., prior, likelihood, posterior, and predictive distributions) within standard parametric models and advanced hierarchical and multilevel models; demonstrates the iterative process of model specification, implementation, criticism, and revision with applied case studies; implements computational techniques (e.g., Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference) in modern probabilistic programming languages.

title: Decolonial Theory
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in African societies and cultures.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Course Title: Decolonial TheoryDecolonize this, decolonize that -- but what does this all mean? In the 2010s "decolonization  became an academic buzzword, sometimes leading to significant change, and sometimes merely indicating that one was following an intellectual trend. At times, one (honestly, "I ) wondered if anyone had actually done the reading. This course will take a chronological approach to decolonial theory, beginning with writers frequently cited by present-day decolonial theorists, and then turning to those theorists writing today. This structure is meant to help students see how ideas build on one another. The readings are Africa-focused -- due to the professor's specialization -- but include writers from outside the continent. Students with various geographical foci are welcome in this class, in the hopes that learning across continents can increase solidarities and strengthen students' own research and writing. In addition, this course can be taken as part of the Graduate Certificate in Visual Cultures. If you are pursuing that certificate, I expect your writing projects to address issues in visual and/or performance studies.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Preliminary Reading list:C saire, Discourse on Colonialism, 1950Fanon, Wretched of the Earth, 1961Thiong'o, Decolonising the Mind, 1986Mudimbe, The Invention of Africa, 1988Glissant, Poetics of Relation, 1990Mbembe, On The Postcolony, 2000 Smith, Decolonizing Methodologies, 1999Mignolo, The Darker Side of Western Modernity, 2011Ndlovu-Gatsheni. Empire, Global Coloniality and African Subjectivity (2022) Tamale, Decolonization and Afro-Feminism, 2020 Ferdinand, Decolonial Ecology: Thinking from the Caribbean World (2022)Taiwo, Against Decolonization: Taking African Agency Seriously (2022)

description: Addresses policies, trends, and debates in the evolution of the American community college from the beginning of the 20th century to the present, as well as current research on the community college and the diverse body of students it serves. instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This interdisciplinary graduate seminar prepares prospective leaders in academia, administration, and student affairs to understand, navigate, and lead the adaptation of Generative AI in higher education. Drawing on leadership theories and learning/behavioral theories, students will examine how higher education professionals make sense of AI's impact on their work, roles, and careers. The course focuses on both institutional and personal dimensions of AI adoption, including strategy, decision-making, communication, resistance, uncertainty, and emotion. Students can develop the leadership capacities and AI literacy needed for their future professional and academic endeavors.A core component of the course is a weekly hands-on AI workshop series that helps students build practical fluency with Generative AI. Through training modules on LLM and token fundamentals, basic and advanced-level prompt engineering, Claude Skills, image generation, and data visualization, students gain direct experience using Generative AI tools responsibly, ethically, and efficiently.

title: History of Race and Inequality in Urban America
description: Examine the historical relationships between metropolitan change, economic transformation, and the construction of race and how those processes have shaped mass incarceration, educational, housing, and income inequality, and the experiences of racial/ethnic minorities who have been marginalized or discriminated against. Key questions include: What is the historical nature of inequality and opportunity in metropolitan America? What policies and ideas have historically promoted inequality, and how have those policies and ideas shifted over time? How have marginalized people responded to inequality, and what impacts have various modes of resistance had? Lastly, what is "race," how has its meaning changed over time, and how has it historically shaped inequality and opportunity?

input: History of Race and Inequality in Urban America

title: Introduction to Education Policy
description: Introduction to K-12 education policy, policy processes, and school governance in the United States. title: Youth, Education, and Society
description: Explores the study of youth through theoretical, historical, social, and cultural perspectives with a focus on Minoritized Youth; interrogates the concept of "youth" as a socially constructed category; examines how "youth" have been positioned within educational, political, economic, and social contexts; analyzes how youth's racialized experiences intersect with other social identities: social class, gender, and sexuality. title: Human Rights and Education
description: Explores questions related to human rights and education, from the individual to the global level; from the abstract to the practical: What does it mean to be human? How do we learn to be human? What rights mark a human being? Do all human have rights? If they have a right to education, do they have a right to a particular kind of education? Can one global education and human rights model best meet the needs of our incredibly diverse global population? Can the global human rights framework improve current educational, national, social, and economic inequities? How so? How does education as a human right relate to human rights education? and who should decide the answers to these questions, and how? Investigates the tensions and boundaries of the human rights framework to reduce social inequality through methodological inquires in educational case studies, including: educational inequality; victims of the war on drugs; working children's rights; and climate change.

title: Globalization and Education
description: Discuss the ways education is inextricably linked to global political, economic, and social contexts. Reflect on both scholarly research and popular conceptions of market, society and schools in different geographic and cultural contexts. Approach globalization from a context-sensitive, place-based approach, rather than abstract, predictive method through interdisciplinary analysis. Explore the concept of globalization across disciplinary frameworks including anthropology, geography, and history. Provides critical analysis to understand the challenges facing education in a globalization era, to build stronger commitment to helping address those challenges, and a set of skills for researching and writing about them. Examine the following "problem-spaces": globalization and migration; globalization and race; global testing and assessment; marketization of education; global city development and higher education; youth culture and globalization.

title: History of American Education
description: Examines the history of education in America from the colonization of North America to the present to consider education in its broadest sense - as a process of individual development and cultural transmission. Explores such topics as the rise of common schools in the urban North; the education of Native Americans, immigrants, slaves, and free blacks; the evolution of teacher training (primarily for women); various philosophies of "progressive" school reform; the politics of desegregation, bilingual education, and special education; the articulation between high school and college work; and the evolving federal role in American education.

title: Health, Nutrition, and Education Policy
description: Explore the relationships between health, nutrition and education. Use theory and conceptual frameworks from a range of disciplines (e.g., public and population health, political science, economics, sociology, nutritional sciences, etc.) to understand complex factors that influence wellbeing in children. Highlight distinct views regarding food/nutrition insecurity as a public problem and explore the ways policy affects children's health in educational settings. Investigate the roles educational institutions and commercial actors play in defining and implementing food system and other policies that impact health. Practice communicating clearly about these complex issues.

title: Education in Emergencies
description: The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimates that more than 82.4 million individuals have been forcibly displaced from their homes. More than a third of them are refugees, and more than 13 million are under the age of 18. In contrast to the portrayals of children wandering among the iconic UNHCR white tents in refugee camps, new images of refugee boys and girls attending public schools raise questions about the role of humanitarianism and education across the world. What are the causes of forced migration? Who counts as a refugee today? What do camp refugees and urban refugees have in common? How do we guarantee access to school for these populations? What would a high-quality curriculum look like for these students?

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: SOC 955Advanced Qualitative Methods(Writing Papers and Dissertations with Qualitative Data)Eunsil OhPrerequisitesStudents must arrive with a collected qualitative data set (interviews, fieldnotes, or a document corpus) and must circulate a rough full draft, 20--40 pages, before Week 8. A master's thesis, comps paper, or dissertation chapter in progress qualifies. Co-authored work is permitted if co-authors are informed it will be discussed in class.Course DescriptionThis seminar teaches doctoral students to turn qualitative data (interviews, ethnographic fieldnotes, and texts for content, discourse, or archival analysis) into publishable articles and dissertation chapters. It runs in two parts. Part I (Weeks 1--7) treats the major qualitative traditions as ways of writing, not only ways of collecting data: each week pairs a tradition with a concrete writing move applied to the student's own data. Part II (Weeks 8--14) is a manuscript studio: students revise a full draft section by section toward submission, review one another's work, and practice the review-and-revision cycle.From the first week, the course is framed around one goal: making your work into a publication and finding its home in the discipline.Learning ObjectivesBy the end of the course, students will be able to: Distinguish how interactionist, interpretive, cultural-relational, extended-case, and feminist/Indigenous traditions build arguments from qualitative data. Position their own project within one tradition and anticipate how a rival tradition would read it. Code, select, and present qualitative evidence (quotes, scenes, documents) with stated prevalence and attention to variation. Write each section of a qualitative article: abstract, analytic introduction, methods, findings, and conclusion. Review qualitative manuscripts and respond to reviewers and editors. Plan the path from article or chapter to dissertation and book.

title: Embodied Cognition & Education
description: Theories of embodied cognition, and related theories of enacted, extended, and embedded cognition, have had increasing influence on general theories of cognition and philosophy of mind, and therefore have importance for education. Featuring interdisciplinary work, with readings and topics drawn from scholarly literature from several fields, including: neuroscience, psychology, philosophy, robotics and artificial intelligence, phenomenology, linguistics, and anthropology. Develop familiarity with the prevailing theories, empirical findings, and methodologies used to investigate ways that the body and body-based processes (such as perception) influence and constitute cognition, and the implications and applications of embodied cognition for education, including learning, assessment, and teaching practices. Apply these theories to research and design projects.

title: Item Response Theory Methods and Applications
description: An introduction to item response theory (IRT) as a theory of measurement in the social sciences. Examine in detail the quantitative foundations of this approach to measurement, and contrast it to related techniques (classical test theory, factor analysis) considered as alternative statistical theories for measurement. Thoroughly examine the fundamental dichotomous and polytomous IRT models as well as their multidimensional extensions. Review estimation techniques, focusing especially on EM/maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation methods. Discuss the many applications of IRT methodology, including test construction, development of short forms, appropriateness measurement, linking and equating methodologies, differential item functioning, and computerized adaptive/multi-stage testing. Covers contemporary innovations in IRT modeling, including the integration of process-related data (e.g., response times, action sequences) and models for novel item formats.

input: Item Response Theory Methods and Applications

title: Software Engineering
description: Ideas and techniques for designing, developing, and modifying large software systems. Topics include software engineering processes; requirements and specifications; project team organization and management; software architectures; design patterns; testing and debugging; and cost and quality metrics and estimation. Work in large teams on a substantial programming project.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: If you can write code, that's a skill. If you can build, ship, and maintain a complex software system in a team of six without breaking production that's Software Engineering.CS/ECE 506 is designed to simulate a professional software environment. You will move beyond structured, individual assignments to tackle open-ended challenges where requirements change, communication matters, and process is just as important as the code.Our focus is not just on writing code, but on the entire Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) from project idea to final deployment.1. Understanding the Focus: The "Mosaic" of Software EngineeringA common misconception is that CS 506 teaches new programming languages or low-level technical fundamentals from scratch. In fact, no new programming languages or fundamental coding concepts are taught in CS 506. Instead, think of CS 506 like assembling a mosaic or solving a complex puzzle: it is a practical, integrative course where you take the foundational technical skills you have acquired in other classes and piece them together into a complete, semester-long software project using modern engineering methodologies.CS 506 emphasizes process and teamwork. It focuses on modern software engineering paradigms and practical industry challenges.+ Emerging Trends & Responsibility: Exploring Ethics in Software Engineering and applying AI-driven software engineering techniques to modern workflows.+ Agile Philosophy & Scrum: Practicing iterative development, sprint planning, estimations, retrospectives, and backlog management.+ Architecture & Design Patterns: Structuring software systems using proven object-oriented and architectural design patterns.+ Testing & Quality Assurance: Writing automated unit, integration, and system tests, including strategies for maintaining code quality under project pressure.+ DevOps & Containerization: Building modern deployment pipelines and using tools like Docker for environment configuration and CI/CD integration.2. Realistic Industry Team Dynamics & Course Structure:- No Self-Selected Teams or Custom Ideas: Mimicking real-world corporate environments, CS/ECE 506 students do not choose their teammates or pitch their own project ideas. Teams are algorithmically formed based on complementary skill sets (e.g., balancing frontend and backend experience), shared project interest preferences, and compatible availability outside of class. Because CS/ECE 506 is a joint CS and ECE course, suggested project ideas can involve hardware development or software-hardware integration, making it a versatile option for both ECE and CS majors.- Required Interactive Workshops: Lecture attendance is required because most lecture sessions function as interactive workshops where project teams meet in-person in a collaborative style classroom to execute key Agile milestones, including sprint planning, architectural planning and reviews, sprint retrospectives, peer code reviews, and project evaluations.3.Where CS/ECE 506 Is Highly Beneficial?Taking CS 506 is particularly highly recommended if your target career path aligns with industry-standard software development and modern team workflows:+ Simulating Corporate Team Mechanics:Working with assigned teammates who have diverse skill sets prepares you directly for professional engineering teams, where you rarely choose your collaborators or projects.+ Navigating Contemporary SE Challenges:Exposure to topics like AI-assisted software engineering, software ethics, and maintaining code quality under project pressure prepares you for current industry realities that go beyond writing basic algorithms.+ Mastering Industry Tools & Methodologies:Hands-on experience with Docker, CI/CD, Scrum ceremonies, project estimation, and AI-assisted engineering gives you an immediate head start in internships and full-time roles.+ Strong Interview & Portfolio Material:Navigating real team dynamics, managing code reviews, and delivering a
