instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This seminar approaches Indigenous musics and musical practices through ethnomusicological and critical Indigenous studies frameworks. Our focus will be on Indigenous musics of the top two thirds of Turtle Island what I am resisting calling here "Canada  and "The United States,  especially since a lot of Indigenous communities and musics do not organize themselves according to these relatively new nation states. That said, we occasionally venture further afield. The goal here is not to master, taxonomize, pull apart, dissect, extract, or make knowable Indigenous musics. What, then, will we do instead? We will listen to music, sound, ideas, even to feelings and learn some skills of knowledge production born out of not knowing. These is a certain kind of rigor and discipline to "unmastery,  but it is often not noticed as such. We will work to notice it, often bringing to light settler colonial practices that might masquerade as "just listening.  As Dena'ina scholar Jessica Bissett Perea suggests, we will attempt to "move beyond colonial questions of containment 'who counts as Native' and 'who decides' and colonial questions of measurement 'what exactly is "Native  about Native music?'  considering instead Indigenous artists' practices of "self-determination and resurgent world-making  (2021, 6). Already in this description, you can see a methodology and an ethos emerging. With the help of guest artists, we will take up multiple genres of music including powwow, Inuit throat games, country music, round dance, and Indigenous Western art music. With the help of key writers like Philip Deloria, Jessica Bissett Perea, Dylan Robinson, Kim TallBear, Eve Tuck, and K. Wayne Yang, the majority of whom speak from embodied experience as Indigenous peoples themselves, we will also study how Indigenous musics have been taken up by music scholars from the nineteenth century to the present. Key concepts like sovereignty, resurgence, decolonization, indigenization, and settler colonialism will be anchor points throughout the course. Topics include the use of Indigenous songs in Western art music, music research in/with/for/by Indigenous communities, pretendianism, and Indigenous feminisms, to name a few. This class revolves around reading, listening, and discussing. It will be a challenge, and many of the readings require slow, careful attention. But I welcome anyone who is up for the challenge to join (including 1-2 undergraduates), even if you are not sure you yet have the skills. We will build them together.

title: Multivariate Analysis of Ecological and Community Data
description: Examines common methods of multivariate data analysis in ecology and environmental science. Covers methods for the analysis of complex, multidimensional datasets that are collected in the study of plant, invertebrate, fish, and bird communities. Addresses the concurrent analysis of the environmental factors that may drive community distributions. Provides the basis for predictive modeling of distributions across landscapes. General methods covered include ordination (PCA, DCA, NMDS, CCA), clustering (or classification), and other comparative analyses of data matrices (ANOSIM, Mantel tests).  Includes an applied, "hands-on" approach on how to use these tools, and the circumstances under which their uses are either appropriate or inappropriate.

description: Improve language proficiency and deepen your cultural understanding of the contemporary Francophone world through the study of French-language literature, film, advertising, journalism, and other forms of expression. instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How can studying society and culture in French help you speak that language better?  How does learning about traditions and identity, the arts, and social and environmental questions in French-speaking parts of the world make you a more efficient and creative language user? This course, given entirely in the French language and led by the longtime director of the UW-Madison Professional French Masters Program, will help you find concrete answers to these questions.  During the semester, we will focus on three broad themes: tradition, identity and ways of life (Module 1), leisure and the arts (Module 2), and major social issues (Module 3). In helping you explore each of these themes, the course uses a basic French grammar review and texts drawn from storytelling, advertising, film, journalism, graphic arts and other sources, to help you improve your ability to describe, analyze, defend and question ideas in French.  Students leaving this class will be prepared for advanced-level coursework in literary, history, culture and civilization more importantly, though, they will be more comfortable engaging with native-level French speakers in all kinds of situations.

title: Exploring Paris
description: Explore the city of Paris through the diverse, historical, creative, and anecdotal perspectives offered by writers, filmmakers, and other artists. Discuss how authors like Emile Zola, Ernest Hemingway, James Baldwin, and French Nobel Prize laureate Patrick Modiano introduce a range of voices and eras. Explore key neighborhoods, city maps, significant landmarks, and pivotal historical events, culminating in a nuanced appreciation of Paris's spatial, historical, and literary complexity.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is taught entirely in English, no knowledge of French language is required. It counts for literature and humanities credits. In this course we will explore the city of Paris through the diverse, historical, creative, and anecdotal perspectives offered by writers, filmmakers, and other artists. We will read classic novels and stories taking place in Paris by Emile Zola (The Belly of Paris), Ernest Hemingway (A Moveable Feast), and James Baldwin (Giovanni's Room), as well as a more recent works by French Nobel Prize-recipient Patrick Modiano (Dora Bruder). We will also explore Paris by examining maps, listening to songs, and viewing films about the city. Feel free to contact me if you have any questions: Joshua Armstrong, jtarmstrong@wisc.edu.

title: Exploring Montreal and Quebec
description: Examine Montreal and the province of Quebec through cinema, television, and literary texts. Explore historical and social themes central to Quebec identity, including evolving conceptions of French Canadian and Quebecois identity, particularly in intellectual and cultural life. Analyze how storytelling reflects and critiques cultural traditions rooted in France, as well as the impact of the Quiet Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s on national identity. Investigate cultural diversity in Quebec through the perspectives and voices of selected authors and filmmakers.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This introductory course invites students to discover the Canadian city of Montreal and its province, Quebec, through its cinema, television, and literary storytelling (including essays, novels, short fiction, and other genres), all in English translation. Throughout the semester, students encounter three unique historical and social themes in Quebec: "French Canadian" identity in the city and province,  the "Quiet Revolution" of the 1960s and 70s, and cultural diversity in the province, as shown through the voices of the authors we study here.Study of all three of these major themes will reveal how Quebecois culture and identity are shaped by both external forces (the rest of Canada, France, the United States, and the Global South) and internal cultural paradoxes (English and French in Montreal, the unique economies and subcultures of Quebec's major regions, urban versus suburban life, the experience of indigenous, Anglophone and immigrant minorities).  Ultimately, students completing this course will have a better understanding not only of what makes Quebec unique in North America, but also of cultural and historical diversity in this part of Canada today.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Hockey and identity; the Roman Catholic Church; Jewish immigrants in Montreal; Quebec nationalism; French language laws; the Indigenous novel; Vietnam war refugee literature; narratives of childhood; Canadian bilingualism; code-switching, North American-style.

title: Advanced Writing Workshop
description: Develop writing and oral expression at an advanced level through writing and discussion of internet journalism, translation, or creative genres. Taught in French.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Learning objectives Gain experience in presentational writing in French, including description, narration, and other creative genres like free verse, comic strip, word play, etc. Demonstrate understanding of relationships between form and content in French texts, i.e., how certain linguistic and stylistic techniques make meaning in particular genres Develop interpersonal speaking abilities in French (e.g., giving constructive criticism, complimenting, seeking additional details, hypothesizing, describing, and comparing)  Refine your French presentational speaking abilities, e.g., pronunciation, intonation, and other aspects of delivering texts orally to an audience Be an active participant in a writing community, giving and receiving feedback in the interest of improving everyone's texts  Gain awareness of the language-learning process and your own identity as a developing language learner through goal setting and reflectionThis course views reading, writing, and speaking as complementary ways to communicate ideas, feelings, and experiences. In other words, how we read influences how we write. Likewise, our discussions are an important part of the writing process. In French 312, we will explore how to make meaning in different communicative modes in French, and we will analyze different textual genres to better understand why certain techniques are used and what effects they have on meaning. After gaining familiarity with these techniques, you will use them to create your own texts. As a course participant, you will compile a portfolio of texts, set your own learning goals, and contribute actively to our writing community.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Creative writing topics include description/observation, playful poetry and prose, and digital storytelling in French.
instructorProvidedContent.format: In-person 50-minute class sessions. Workflow: During each module you will complete four types of homework assignments -- thematic analyses of texts (Analyse de textes), linguistic and stylistic analyses of texts (Outils linguistiques et stylistiques), discussion forums, and writing workshop preparation. For each module, you will complete part of a project portfolio. Projects are prepared using Google Docs. You will participate in peer review, 1-on-1 writing feedback conferences with the instructor, and revision of your texts.

description: Cultural study of contemporary Francophone Africa, focusing on issues in government, organizations and enterprise. Exploration of cultural and professional relations between Francophone Africa and France, the European Union, and the United States.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How do current issues in governance, business and international organizations operating in the French-speaking world intersect with French studies and your desire to use your French after graduation?  How are current social, political and professional realities in French-speaking Africa today reflected in the media, and how are they unique? How can French majors, double majors, and Certificate students use French to make themselves marketable for jobs in business, non-profits and government? description: Intensive grammar and reading for those with little or no experience in French. Readings from appropriate texts in the humanities, sciences, social sciences.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The goal of this course is to give students with no previous knowledge of French the ability to read texts that are necessary or useful for their research. The fundamental elements of French grammar are given over the course of the semester.  Basic exercises focus on translation from French to English.  A good deal of memorization will be required, but students will generally not be expected to reproduce forms in French, just to recognize them.  French pronunciation will NOT be studied extensively, and students will NOT learn to speak French or to understand spoken French, just to read texts written in French. No previous knowledge of French is required; those who have studied some French but cannot yet read texts in their field of research are welcome to take the course.  French 391 can be taken by graduate students in many departments as a means of fulfilling a foreign language reading requirement (please consult your home department regarding its particular policies). Undergraduates with sophomore standing are also eligible to take this course, which is appropriate if they plan to go on to graduate school in a field other than French.This is a lively course with plenty of student interaction, and lots of individual guidance from the instructor.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Le roman fran ais aux XXe et XXIe si cles:Dans ce cours, nous commencerons en lisant trois romans canoniques, repr sentant chacun un mouvement ou tendance important dans la litt rature au XXe si cle : Du c t  de chez Swann de Marcel Proust (1913, le modernisme), Nadja d'Andr  Breton (1928, le surr alisme), et Le ravissement de Lol V. title: Gender, Women, Bodies, and Health
description: Examines both physiological and social processes relating to gender and health across the lifespan among cisgender, transgender, and non-binary individuals. Examples of topics include hormonal processes, reproductive anatomy & physiology, sexuality, sexual pleasure, chronic illness, depression, and sexual violence. A primary course objective is for students to connect information about their bodies and personal health to larger social and political contexts. In particular, considers how health and health disparities are shaped by multiple kind of social inequalities, particularly inequalities based on gender.

title: Gender, Sexuality, and Global Health
description: Provides an introductory overview to critical global health studies, linking past trends to current research and health inequalities. Examines current trajectories in disaster relief and public health interventions through a gendered lens, with a solid grounding in the historical context. Explores social, demographic, political, economic, and ecological determinants of global health, and the ways that these factors interconnect with biomedicine to create and affect health outcomes, both within and across countries. Uses an intersectional approach to analyze how public health policies prioritize whose lives represent "save-able" or "salvageable" ones in the public, political, and corporate eye.

title: Women in Ethnic American Literature
description: American literature by and about women, written by authors from ethnic groups.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This asynchronous online course held during winter intersession explores the intersections among race, ethnicity, gender, class, nationality, and sexuality in fiction, poetry, memoir, and visual texts by, Asian American, American Indian, Latina, Black, and multiracial self-identified women in the U.S. The course is structured thematically around overlapping social issues within a cross-cultural framework, focusing on four themes in particular: racial authenticity and ethnic belonging; coming of age and externalizing the gender role; activism and radical consciousness; and disembodied racial meaning. One of our goals will be to understand the ways in which girls and women from diverse backgrounds negotiate competing affiliations and loyalties amid differing notions of home, place, and community.  We will pay particular attention to issues of childhood, narrative voice, and sexual awareness. The course reader includes work by Pat Parker, Cherrie Moraga, Alice Walker, Janice Gould, Toni Cade Bambara, Hisaye Yamamoto, In s Hernandez Tovar, Chrystos, and Toni Morrison among others, with secondary reading by Immanuel Wallerstein, Hazel Carby, Sunaina Maira, and bell hooks. NOTE: This is an intensive, online course to be completed during winter break with Spring course credit. However, it will be completed prior to the first day of Spring semester (see dates listed). Students should be prepared to complete all reading and course assignments on time each day; twice daily posts are required in lieu of in-person class meetings. Each of the 15 days (modules) represents a week of a traditional semester. Internet access for twice daily posting; one group Zoom meeting and one individual Zoom conference are required. Open to English and GWS majors.

title: Gender and Communication
description: Effective communication requires awareness of how gender influences communication and our capacity to build lasting and meaningful relationships. Learn about theories and concepts to understand how gender influences our interpersonal, professional, and social lives. Topics include terms and concepts relevant to the study of how we communicate about gender, sex and sexuality, including identity, language and nonverbal behavior, socialization, close personal relationships, education, work, violence, media and social movements.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Effective communication requires awareness of how gender influences communication and our capacity to build lasting and meaningful relationships. Learn about theories and concepts to understand how gender influences our interpersonal, professional, and social lives. Topics include terms and concepts relevant to the study of how we communicate about gender, sex and sexuality, including identity, language and nonverbal behavior, socialization, close personal relationships, education, work, violence, media and social movements.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: This course is about the relationship between gender and communication. Our method of study will be a combination of reading, discussion, online lecture, research, and analysis with a goal of coming to a broad definition of gender, as well as an examination of how this knowledge connects with our personal identity and experiences, and our position in society. More specifically, we will learn about gender and communication through four modules of study, and a final wrap-up.The first module is an introduction to terms, definitions, and concepts relating to gender and sex, and the placement of these definitions in the field of communication. This section will also be concerned with how gender reflects and is influenced by our lifelong construction of personal identities. We will study the influence of family on our definition of gender, the topics of femininity and masculinity, and transgender.The second module will focus on gender as it relates to communication behavior. We will examine gendered language and gendered nonverbal behavior, and how we are taught these things through schooling.The third module will examine the impact of gender on our social and personal relationships as well as in organizations. This will include a discussion of gendered violence in relational and societal contexts.The fourth module is a broader examination of how gender and communication exists within a societal framework. In this section we will study gender and communication within the topics of the media and social movements.

title: Race, Sex, and Texts (How to do things with writing)
description: Explore how race, gender, and sexuality intersect with language and inform textual experiences. Learn how written texts in various forms and genres impact and play major roles in enforcing, or challenging, expectations about race and sex in the United States. Engage with documentation, such as marriage licenses, passports, federal policies, anti-slavery petitions, letters to the editor, posters, and hashtag activism, to follow public debates and everyday individual actions where writing and talking about sex and race makes a difference. Focus on the power of words to break bones and heal wounds. Examine historical and contemporary interconnections among race, sexuality, gender, and texts in the United States.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: What does it mean to identify as a Midwesterner? A Badger? An American? Or none of those things? And how do narratives and language around race, gender, and sexuality affect how cultural identities are constructed and circulated? This course will explore the ways we create and curate ideas of place, identity, and belonging. We will particularly look at the role of narrative, archives, and museums in this constitutive rhetorical work. We will use rhetorical frameworks to examine the stories we tell about our campus, our city, our region, and our nation -- and ultimately ourselves. Students will complete a narrative analysis, a museum curation project, and a community-based narrative project, along with other research and multimodal work.

input: Race, Sex, and Texts (How to do things with writing)

title: Law, Sexuality, & Society
description: Examines the legal and social development and implications of laws governing sexual behavior, human reproduction, media, privacy, and topics related to sexuality, sex and gender. Includes historical analyses of laws connected to present day regulations of sexuality, demonstrating the origins of many of the world's most frequently debated civil rights issues. Chief focus on the United States legal system, with some content including examinations of institutions around the world. Investigates taken-for-granted knowledge and assumptions about sexuality and look at legal, cultural and social constructions of sex in society. Covers intersectional social implications, including race, (dis)ability, class, etc. Topics include: obscenity, pornography, sex work, sexual surrogacy, birth control, abortion, sex education, sexual violence, sex offenders, sexual citizenship rights, trans and intersex legal topics.

title: Gender and Politics in Comparative Perspective
description: Examines the gendered nature of political institutions around the world, including implications of women's exclusions from public life in a global context; the obstacles to women's greater participation; how women have gained greater voice in political leadership in some countries; and the differences women make in the political arena. Not open to students with credit for POLI SCI 643 prior to fall 2017

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Women of all races, ages, gender identities, and sexual orientations have become energized to run for political office in the United States in unprecedented numbers in recent years. Kamala Harris's electoral victory as the first woman of color vice president was an important achievement, as was Nancy Pelosi's ascent to Speaker of the House. Nevertheless, the United States still trails many countries in female representation, ranking 85th globally. Some of the poorest and most authoritarian countries in the world, like Rwanda, Nicaragua, and the United Arab Emirates, have some of the highest rates of female legislative representation in the world, in contrast to some of the wealthiest and most democratic countries.  We will be asking in this course what accounts for these differences.The course will examine the implications of women's exclusion from public life globally; the obstacles to greater participation; how women have gained a stronger voice in political leadership in some countries; and the different kinds of issues women bring to the political arena.  In this course, we will be asking:  How important is it to have equal political representation?  Do women make a difference once in office?  Would having more women in politics change the nature of public policy or even how politics is conducted?  Do women engage in politics differently from men?We will also consider in this course some of the obstacles for women as voters, candidates, and officeholders.  What particular constraints do women face when running for office?  How much do women's chances of being elected to office depend on the electoral system, cultural attitudes toward women in leadership, family obligations, the media, party support, and campaign financing?  The course will engage various debates regarding women's political participation, including controversies over critical mass, electoral quotas, and substantive representation.  We will ask the extent to which women influence politics once elected to office, given the existing political culture and institutional rules.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Shattering the Glass Ceiling, Global Struggles for Suffrage, Problems of Legislative Representation, Gender and Elections, Political Impact of Women's Movements, Women and Citizenship, Women and Conflict, Women in the Executive, Women, Politics and the Media, Women and Race

title: Asian American Women Writers
description: Major texts by Asian American women writers.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course examines contemporary Asian American women's literature in a discussion based, task-oriented classroom. How do women negotiate multiple affiliations, whether ethnic, familial, or national?  We will focus on issues such as coming of age, the policing of women's sexuality, and the formation of collective political consciousness. In addition to looking at works that engage issues of immigration and acculturation in the U.S., we will explore the legacies of colonialism in Asia and the literary portrayal of geopolitics. The course will investigate the ways in which literature can be a forum for interventionist critique of both domestic race relations and international politics.  How does literary form experimental and lyric poetry, realist memoir, or the graphic novel provide the vehicle of such critique?  We will situate literature not as a site for "learning  culture, but for understanding political movements, Cold War nationalism, racial segregation, and sexuality.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: This seminar-style course meets once a week, focusing on roughly a book, film, or text a week. We will cover 8 primary literary texts-poetry, novel, graphic novel memoir--and two films. Attendance is required given the once-a-week structure.

title: The Environment of the Womb: Epigenetics and Parent/Child Health
description: Concentrating social and ecological environments as well as that of the body, focuses on the toxic effects of late industrialism, epigenetics and maternal/fetal health as well as destabilizing ideas about "normal" reproduction. Examine how the possibilities for expanding the scope from maternal/fetal health to "parent/child" health - where kinship is not strictly about biologic belonging or coming "straight from the womb," but also about love and a safe home or chosen family. Undergirding our analysis is an "eco-social" approach, guided by questions of what constitutes "health," access to living a healthy life - in a body and on a planet that feels safe to inhabit.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: When did women in the United States start using birth control?  How does gender influence the experience of illness? The course also explores the diversity of expectations and experiences within the category of "woman.

title: Contemporary Theorizing in Gender and Women's Studies
description: Examines assumptions and debates in contemporary theorizing about gender and women including what constitutes "good" gender and women studies' theorizing, how to recognize gender-based oppression when we see it, how gender, race, sexuality, and other hierarchies of power intersect, as well as the merits of transnational theorizing about gender and women. Explores whether gender and women's studies' theorizing is a form of activism, how to teach theory in gender and women's studies' classrooms, the value of cultivating distinct gender and women studies' methods, and other dimensions of putting gender and women's studies' theorizing into practice.

title: Anthropology of Gender
description: Theoretical and ethnographic approaches to the anthropology of gender, focusing on current works. Topics include sexual inequality, research methods, gender and history, gender and ethnographic writing, cultural constructions of masculinity, sexuality, and gender studies and anthropological theory.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This seminar offers a close examination of gender and embodied identities in cultural and cross-cultural perspectives.  We will explore a range of ethnographically grounded works, both classic and recent, tracing the roots and efflorescence of a subdiscipline and its current discourses within and beyond anthropology. Topics include sex/gender, race, and indigeneity in early modernist ethnography; feminist anthropologies from second-wave feminism to the 2020s, gendered histories and political economies, masculinities, nonheteronormative genders and sexualities; lesbian, gay, and transgender as globalizing  cultural constructions; anthropologies of sexuality and the body; gender and religion; gender, environment, and ecofeminisms; migrations and gendered borderlands, and gender and globalization.   This cross-listed seminar may be taken either as Anthropology 920 or Gender and Women's Studies 920.  Please contact the instructor for further information.
instructorProvidedContent.format: This seminar will meet once a week for 2.5 hours.  Seminar members will contribute regularly in seminar as well as asynchronously to reading-based Canvas discussions of seminar themes and occasionally screen and comment on seminar-related videos . Each seminar member will write a 12-15 page term paper and will present on it in seminar during the last two weeks of the semester.

description: Research seminar on specific topics in gender and women's studies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This seminar delves into queer creative process as historical and transdisciplinary research method.  Together we will analyze visual and narrative methods by engaging a shared set of genre-expansive monographs, documentaries and graphic memoir concerning contested histories, genocide, war, fascism, censorship, and queer/trans lives. This is not an art methods course (I don't teach technique), the assignments analyze artistic narrative methods by using hands-on and hand-produced engagement of and through physical, hard-copy genre-expansive formats.

title: Human-centered Design and Business
description: Design thinking is an iterative problem-solving process geared toward producing innovative solutions for complex and persistent problems in various fields and organizations. Its process, culture, and value system from both design and business point of views will be covered: Empathetic understanding of the end users, problem definition rooted in systems thinking, ideation with a strong emphasis on creativity, visualization and prototyping, testing rooted in a set of research methods, and finally, the importance of iteration in bringing about innovative solutions. The path from project to market will also be explored, with an understanding of how one might balance desirability, feasibility and viability.

title: Business Analytics I
description: Development of quantitative intuition through practical applications and use of analysis tools. Specifically, emphasis will be on how to manage, summarize, explore, and visualize databases. The essentials of probability will be introduced and applied to decision problems where there is uncertainty. title: Communicating Evolutionary Biology
description: Exposure to diverse topics in contemporary evolutionary biology and development of critical thinking and communication skills. Most weeks guest lecturers present their own primary research on a specialized topic in evolutionary biology. Seminars include perspectives from genetics, ecology, geoscience, zoology, botany, microbiology, systematics, molecular biology, and integrative research. Some weeks feature special topics and discussions on pedagogical, legal, outreach, or other issues in evolutionary biology. Includes thinking critically about methodology, experimental design and interpretation, and how conclusions are reached in evolutionary biology by reading primary and secondary literature, attending seminars, discussing topics with speakers and other students, and preparing a written report.  The 3-credit version of the course delves deeper into communication of evolutionary biology to researchers, undergraduates, K-12 students, and the general public.

title: Developmental Genetics for Conservation and Regeneration
description: Human-induced factors such as changes in land use and global climate are causing rapid worldwide biodiversity loss. Can modern molecular genetics contribute to species preservation? In this course, we will first explore the challenges and potential of molecular genetic methods based on biobanking, gene editing and nuclear transfer for animal biodiversity preservation. Topics covered will include: i) maternal factors and early animal development, ii) interspecies somatic cell nuclear transfer (isSCNT) and oocyte-mediated reprogramming in animal cloning, iii) developmental, phylogenetic and ecological considerations for biobanking, iv) gene editing and synthetic biology as potential tools to recapture biodiversity. Use knowledge in animal population status, developmental genetics and phylogeny to address real-life problems involving the conservation of threatened animal populations.

title: Human Geography: Space, Place, Society, and Politics
description: We live in a world that is both interconnected and fragmented. Data, capital, cultural fads, and environmental issues span borders. At the same time, these movements do not mean borders have disappeared nor do they undermine the meaningfulness of place in people's lives. Human geography explores the economic, political, social, cultural, and technological dynamics that drive interrelationships across and divisions in space. Human geography is about the why of the where. It is about the experience of feeling connected and disconnected, stuck in place, out of place, included and excluded. We explore multiple meanings and experiences of space, which we encounter through watching or playing sport, following social media accounts of geopolitics, traveling to another country, or spending time in our hometowns.

input: Human Geography: Space, Place, Society, and Politics

title: Introduction to the Earth System
description: Introduction to how the Earth system works and what makes Earth livable. Gain appreciation for how the atmosphere, oceans, life, and earth's surface interact to shape our local, regional and global landscapes.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Welcome to the Earth System. The Earth is the place where we live, the water that we drink, the air that we breathe, and the home to all known life in the universe. The earth is a system, composed of many interacting subsystems: the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, lithosphere, and anthrosphere. The earth is dynamic. We live in a swiftly changing world, characterized by rapidly changing climates, shifting landscapes, and growing human populations. Now, more than ever, it's essential to understand how the Earth system works, how it affects our livelihoods, and how we are altering the physical environment of our planet.Geography/NIES 120 provides a critical foundation for students by introducing them to how the Earth system works and what makes Earth livable. Through this course you will gain a deeper appreciation for the diverse processes that shape our local, regional and global landscapes. Many students take this course to fulfill their physical science requirement. Others use it as a gateway to majors and careers in Geography, Environmental Studies, Environmental Science, and Sustainability.

title: Climate Change, Climate Action: The Social Dimensions of Climate Change
description: The planet's climate is changing, and humans are causing it. This means that climate change is not only a topic of study for the biophysical sciences, but also for the social sciences. Focuses on the social dimensions of climate change: the social, political, environmental, and economic factors that shape the drivers and impacts of climate change and the ability of different places and communities to respond. Examines both the social problems that arise from climate change and the social solutions to mitigate and adapt to the climate crisis. How do these social dimensions shape climate change, and how does climate change shape different social dimensions? What climate solutions are being proposed, what climate solutions are already being implemented, and how can we critically evaluate the uneven impacts of those solutions across society and space?

title: Making the American Landscape
description: Traces the history and evolution of the American cultural landscape from precolonial times to present. Explores how class, ethnic, and racial inequality have shaped the appearance of the American landscape over time, and how that landscape in turn has affected relationships between people and groups through the present day. Examines extraordinary things (civic structures (like our State Capitol), National Parks, War Memorials) and more ordinary kinds of places (mining towns, cotton plantations, sites of recreation and leisure, and suburban tract housing) to stimulate critical thinking about how these places have served people and groups unequally and disproportionately over time and across space. Considers complex meanings of American spaces and places to different people and groups, stimulating empathy and encouraging participation in a multicultural society.

title: Green Urbanism
description: Over half of the world's population now lives in urban areas, with an expected increase of 2.5 billion people in the next 30 years. As urbanization (broadly defined as the conversion of previously undeveloped lands into urbanized uses) continues and intensifies, we are faced with a number of environmental issues, for instance, fragmentation and destruction of habitats, and decreased air and water quality.  Explore how urbanization impacts ecological processes and resulting environmental outcomes, strategies for "designing with nature," and behavioral, planning, and policy responses to urban environmental problems.

title: Environmental Biogeography
description: Explores how physical and biological factors affect the distribution of terrestrial biomes, ecosystem types, and biodiversity, as well as the role of disturbance and recent human activities on differences in past and modern day species distributions.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course takes an ecosystems approach to understand how physical -- climate, geologic history, soils -- and biological -- physiology, evolution, extinction, dispersal, competition, predation -- variables and processes interact to affect the past, present and future distribution of terrestrial biomes and all levels of biodiversity: ecosystems, species and genes. A particular focus will be placed on the role of disturbance and to recent human-driven climatic and land-cover changes on differences in historical and current distributions of global biodiversity. Throughout the course, we will discuss how historical and current biases in the representation of practitioners and in the methods used affect interpretations of biogeographic research and its applications.COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES To learn patterns and mechanisms of local to global gene, species, ecosystem and biome distributions To learn how past, current and future environmental change affect biogeography To learn how humans affect geographic patterns of biodiversity To learn major paradigm changes in biogeography and how changes in conceptual frameworks and technology have altered interpretations of data and understanding of processes To learn how to apply concepts from biogeography to current environmental problems To learn how legacies of colonialism and scientific racism affect historical and current biases in the representation, methods, practice and applications of biogeography To learn how to read and interpret the primary literature, that is, scientific articles in peer-reviewed journals.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Lecture and in-class discussion

title: Changing Landscapes of the American West
description: Environmental change in the landscapes of the American West, in the recent past, present, and future, from the physical science background to human-environment interactions.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is an introduction to environmental change in the varied landscapes of the western United States. Visitors often see the mountains, deserts, and plains of the American West as pristine natural landscapes formed over geologic time. In fact they have been the setting of major environmental changes in the past century and will see even more dramatic change in the near future, because of both climate change and evolving human land use.The course will begin with a tour through the major regional landscapes of the American West, followed by a look at the region's varied climates, present and future. We will then take a detour into the history of the region from about 1800 to the early 1900s, starting with the land use practices of Indigenous people, which often had significant impacts on ecosystems and landscapes. We'll look at the dispossession of Native Americans by European settlers, focusing on the patterns of land ownership/management/use rights that developed through that process, and how they have influenced the viewpoints and practices of scientists, land managers, and policymakers since that time as they studied and responded to environmental change. Much of the rest of the semester is devoted to recent past, present, and future change in ecosystems, wildfire regime, hydrology, agriculture, and outdoor recreation, relating these changes to the many ways in which people have now altered the landscapes of the West, as well as the growing effects of climate change.There is no required textbook, but there will be required readings (and some videos), all available through topic modules in Canvas. Throughout the semester there will be weekly activities, usually requiring you to turn in a short response to class discussion or to your own exploration of online information sources.

input: Changing Landscapes of the American West

title: Human Geography of Southeast Asia
description: Introduction to the human geography and history of Southeast Asia, including important political and theoretical issues and policies and positionings of relevance for understanding the spatiality of the region, including the ways that ethnicity and indigeneity are playing out in Southeast Asia and among Southeast Asians in the United States.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Southeast Asia is a diverse region presently containing 11 nation states (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Myanmar (Burma), Malaysia, Philippines, Indonesia, Brunei, Singapore and Timor Leste), and arguably the southern-most part of China, especially Yunnan Province. Within those countries a large number of peoples self-identify as members of a wide variety of ethnic groups. Some of these are found across national borders, such as the Hmong, Akha and Brao, to name just a few, while a smaller number are found in only a single country, such as the Lua of Thailand and the Lavi from Laos. Religious and class differences are also important factors, as are livelihoods and politics. The human geography of Southeast Asia is dynamic and experiencing rapid change, thus making it a particularly interesting part of the world.This survey course is designed to introduce intermediary undergraduate students to the human geography of Southeast Asia, including the basic geography and history of the region, important political and theoretical issues, and policies and positionings of relevance for understanding the human spatiality of the region, including the ways that ethnicity and indigeneity are being evoked in Southeast Asia and amongst Southeast Asians in the United States.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: The first eight classes provide some general background about Southeast Asia and the key concepts being used in the course. Case studies of different countries in Southeast Asia are then presented. Finally, there are a few classes specifically related to Hmong and Lao ethnic politics in Asia and the United States.

title: Carto Production & Project Mgt
description: Explores emerging topics in Geography.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course combines the principles of cartography, wayfinding design, and project management, preparing students for real-world applications in spatial communication and design. Modeled after professional practice, students will learn to plan, scope, execute, monitor, and evaluate complex design projects while working collaboratively on a client-based initiative for the Department of Geography. Through a hands-on, team-oriented approach, students will design and develop a comprehensive wayfinding signage system to support the department's temporary relocation across multiple campus buildings, including Computer Sciences and Medical Sciences. The project will address real navigation and communication challenges faced by students, faculty, staff, and visitors while contributing to the department's public presence, branding, and visual identity strategy. Students will apply advanced cartographic design and production skills, including user-centered design, information hierarchy, typography, graphic communication, visual standards development, quality control, and production workflows using Adobe Illustrator, Photoshop, InDesign, and GIS. Agile project management methodologies and industry-standard collaboration tools, such as Microsoft Loop and Planner, will be integrated throughout the course. By combining service, design, and project management, students will gain practical experience while creating a lasting resource that supports the UW Geography community and advances the department's visual communication goals.GEOG 370 prerequisite required. GEOG 572 recommended. Junior, senior or graduate student standing recommended.

title: Human Transformations of Earth Surface Processes
description: Takes an earth systems approach to explore the role of human societies in shaping earth surface processes from local to global scales. We address how alterations to our landscapes and waterways affect biological, physical and chemical interactions among our biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere. We discuss methods used to distinguish the "human impact" from background variability.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: COURSE SYNOPSISThis course takes an earth systems approach to explore the role of human societies in shaping earth surface processes from local to global scales. We address how alterations to our landscapes and waterways affect biological, physical and chemical interactions among our biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere. We discuss methods used to distinguish the "human impact" from background variability.FULL COURSE DESCRIPTIONThe influence of human activities is now recognized to extend all over the globe, which has led some researchers to propose renaming our current geologic epoch the Anthropocene, for the "Age of Humans.  This course takes an earth systems approach to explore the role of human societies in shaping earth surface processes. We examine how alterations to earth's land surface and subsurface and waterways affect biological, physical and chemical interactions among our biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere. In particular, we focus on the methods used to distinguish the "human impact" from background variability. We also address historical and current barriers to equity in the practice of science. Topics covered include: approaches to understand earth system interactions, major alterations to biogeochemical cycles and geomorphic processes, biophysical consequences of changes in land cover and land use, urban biogeochemistry, geoengineering, diversity and equity in science. For each topic, we delve into the biophysical science behind each relevant process and discuss different approaches for characterizing and quantifying changes due to human activities. We explore the recent literature to evaluate how biogeochemical and earth system models incorporate human influences to better understand feedbacks between the earth surface, atmosphere and climate.At the end of the semester, students should be able to: Synthesize how major global biogeochemical cycles and earth surface processes are influenced by human activities at different spatial and temporal scales; Identify positive and negative feedbacks among the biosphere, geosphere and atmosphere at different temporal and spatial scales; Explain how different methods are used to characterize and quantify human effects on the earth system; Describe barriers to and strategies to advance equity in the practice of earth system science;  Interpret research findings in peer-reviewed literature; Summarize research for different audiences.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Discussion-based course. Assessments are based on assignments and projects.

input: Human Transformations of Earth Surface Processes

title: Decolonial Theory
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in African societies and cultures.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Course Title: Decolonial TheoryDecolonize this, decolonize that -- but what does this all mean? In the 2010s "decolonization  became an academic buzzword, sometimes leading to significant change, and sometimes merely indicating that one was following an intellectual trend. At times, one (honestly, "I ) wondered if anyone had actually done the reading. This course will take a chronological approach to decolonial theory, beginning with writers frequently cited by present-day decolonial theorists, and then turning to those theorists writing today. This structure is meant to help students see how ideas build on one another. The readings are Africa-focused -- due to the professor's specialization -- but include writers from outside the continent. Students with various geographical foci are welcome in this class, in the hopes that learning across continents can increase solidarities and strengthen students' own research and writing. In addition, this course can be taken as part of the Graduate Certificate in Visual Cultures. If you are pursuing that certificate, I expect your writing projects to address issues in visual and/or performance studies.

title: Geoscience Data Analysis
description: Introduction to the fundamentals of applied geoscience data analysis, focusing on solving practical problems using real real-world data.  Covers applied data analysis topics that are essential across a wide range of geoscience fields, including geophysics, geochemistry, hydrogeology, structural geology, sedimentology, geochronology, glacial geology, and geomorphology.  Covers the use of example geoscience data sets to display and describe data; calculate and propagate uncertainties; test hypotheses; fit functions to data with linear regression and multiple linear regression; account for artifactual and serial correlation; analyze time series and directional data; and design experiments to optimize collection of rock, soil, and water samples.

title: Global German Studies
description: Introduction to the multiple fields and methodologies for the study of language, culture, and texts of global German studies. Examines how German, Dutch, Turkish, and Yiddish, languages, peoples, ideas, and cultures have circulated across the world. Covers questions of migration, globalization, memory, and language.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: What is Global German studies? Throughout the semester, we will ask and answer this question together by learning about different methods for approaching and analyzing artifacts, practices, and perspectives of the German-speaking world within and across cultural and historical contexts (including in relation to Dutch-, Turkish-, and Yiddish-language cultures). Course themes include migration and diaspora, identity and belonging, religious conflict and pluralism, and change brought on by industrialization and globalization. Primary and secondary sources include texts by Tacitus, Martin Luther, Glikl, Immanuel Kant, Karl Marx, Walter Benjamin, May Ayim, Emine Sevgi  zdamar, Yoko Tawada, and more. Course assignments and requirements include written reflections, quizzes, a midterm, and a final project. This course is taught in English and no prior experience with German is required. This course fulfills the Humanities breadth requirement.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Fairytales, murder mysteries, sensational headlines, social media profiles ... Welcome to Intermediate German Writing! In this class, students will expand and enhance their writing skills in German by exploring a variety of different text types and genres reflecting the diversity of the German-speaking world. Daily course participation will involve active in-class discussion as well as collaborative and individual writing activities. Learners will work with authentic texts, music, and film, and they will also engage with synonyms, regional variations, and register to develop the skills to express themselves effectively and creatively in German. Materials and in-class discussions will be in German

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Climate Fiction is an emerging genre of literature, graphic novels, and other media as a sub-genre of science fiction describing and imagining scenarios of complex future ecological systems. The aim of this course is to explore the human experience of a changing climate as well as the consequences of pollution, waste, and resource extraction on communities on a global scale. We will analyze of works by German authors such as Lutz Seiler, Yoko Tawada, Ilija Trojanow, Christa Wolf, as well as writers from around the world, including Margaret Atwood, Octavia E. Butler, Amitav Ghosh, and others. While some works tell dystopian, and apocalyptic stories we will also encounter many stories that imagine a future of resilience.All readings, materials, and discussions will be in English. German language skills are welcome but not required. Text excerpts and other materials will be provided on Canvas.

title: Nachkriegsdeutschland
description: Selected topics in the culture of German-speaking countries.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: On May 8, 1945, the Wehrmacht unconditionally surrendered, marking the end of World War II (WWII) in Europe. The time following the capitulation is often referred to as Zero Hour (Stunde Null), during which Germany attempted to dissociate itself from the Nazi regime. While the term Stunde Null is contested in academic and political discourses today, it generally encapsulates the idea of a tabula rasa a radical break with the past and a sweeping new beginning. But what did Stunde Null actually look like in Germany? To what extent was 1945 really a new beginning, and in what ways did the past continue to shape the emerging postwar order? This course takes these questions as its starting point and examines life in Germany between May 1945 and 1949 through the analysis of different texts and media, including audiovisual material.The course will begin by equipping students with a foundation of historical knowledge regarding the social, political, and economic state of Germany between May 1945 and 1949. Next, students will examine different aspects of postwar life through a variety of literary and audiovisual texts that were published during or thematize this period, including radio plays, short stories, films, and graphic novels. Specifically, we will consider how WWII survivors of diverse identities experienced and came to terms with their new reality and how questions of guilt, responsibility, belonging, memory, and reconstruction were negotiated in the emerging postwar society. Toward the end of the semester, we will extend our examination beyond 1949 and consider how narratives that continue to shape political discourse in Germany today are, in part, rooted in the experiences, conflicts, and interpretations of the immediate postwar period. In doing so, the course builds a bridge between Germany's postwar past and the present and asks how the ways in which societies remember and interpret the past continue to shape political and social debates.The course is not only a historical content course, but also an introduction to how to read, analyze, and discuss various kinds of literary and audiovisual texts in German. It aims to equip students with historical and theoretical knowledge as well as language-learning and analytical strategies, while simultaneously building vocabulary and communicative competence in German. The course targets the development of all language skills (i.e., reading, writing, listening, and speaking), as well as critical thinking and interpretive skills. All course assignments and classroom discussions will be in German.Prerequisites: GER 249, 258, and 262 or GER 249 and 285

title: SLA Research in Practice
description: Selected issues in language acquisition and language teaching.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: SLA Research in Practice is an advanced, project-based seminar designed to support graduate students in moving an existing empirical second language acquisition (SLA) research project from proposal toward implementation, analysis, and/or dissemination. Unlike a traditional graduate seminar organized around a common set of readings, the course is structured around students' individual research projects and the concrete work required to advance them. Students enter the course with a substantially developed empirical project for example, a research proposal developed in a previous seminar, or another project for which significant conceptual and methodological groundwork has already been completed and identify a specific, feasible research goal to accomplish during the semester.The primary purpose of the seminar is to help students bridge the gap between designing an empirical SLA study and carrying it out. Depending on the stage of the project, semester milestones and goals might include developing and piloting research instruments; preparing an IRB application; recruiting participants and collecting (pilot) data; refining an analytic framework based on pilot findings; coding or analyzing data; interpreting findings; or producing a substantive written research report. Projects at more advanced stages may also be considered on an individual basis, including the preparation of a manuscript, dissertation chapter, or conference presentation when the proposed work would benefit from sustained collaborative feedback and is appropriate to the goals of the practicum.The seminar operates as a collaborative research workshop. Students will be divided into two groups, with each group presenting approximately every other week. Before their scheduled session, presenting students will regularly and independently circulate substantive work in progress, such as draft instruments, protocols, analytic materials, data excerpts, coding frameworks, manuscript sections, or presentation materials, to their peers. Class meetings will be devoted to discussing this work, identifying methodological or conceptual challenges, providing substantive feedback, and determining concrete next steps. At the conclusion of each workshop, students will establish specific goals to accomplish before their next presentation approximately two weeks later. Students are therefore expected not only to advance their own research independently between meetings, but also to engage seriously and constructively with their peers' projects throughout the semester.Because the course depends on sustained engagement with ongoing research, enrollment is limited and requires instructor permission. Prospective students will submit a project proposal before enrollment that describes the project's current status, work already completed, and a specific goal for the semester (including milestones to reach this semester goal). Admission is at the instructor's discretion and will be based on the project's readiness for sustained work, the feasibility of the proposed semester goal, and the student's ability to contribute to and benefit from the collaborative workshop format. Enrollment will be capped at six students, with the possibility of admitting up to eight students depending on project stage and fit.To be considered for enrollment:To be considered for the course, please send an email to julia.goetze@wisc.edu with a 1--2 page attachment covering: a 1 paragraph description of your project; your research questions; work completed to date; current project stage; specific semester goal/final deliverable; 3--5 anticipated milestones needed to accomplish the semester goal; and what kinds of feedback/support you expect to need from the group.

title: An Introduction to Fairytales
description: Introduces canonical and lesser-known works of the fairytale genre both within and outside of Europe. Explore tales as part of larger "circles," groups of adaptations over time, to trace how sociocultural values embedded in these stories change over time. In reading and viewing contemporary adaptations of these stories, consider how familiar formulas are reimagined across time, cultures, and media. Reflect on intersections of gender, race, disability, sexuality, religion, nature, and the family, and explore how these depictions are shaped by the national, cultural, and personal circumstance of their tellers and re-tellers.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: What do Disney, Shrek, the Nutcracker, and modern romantasy fiction all have in common? Regardless of audience and form, they all draw on and reimagine the elements, structures, and characters from fairy tales told around the world. From well-known storytellers and collectors like the Brothers Grimm and Hans Christian Andersen to the invisible women behind their work, we will explore the genre of the fairy tale from its unwritten beginnings to canonical and popular versions printed, translated, and filmed across the globe. In this class, we will consider how familiar formulas are reimagined across time, cultures, and media. We will explore tales as part of larger "circles,  groups of adaptations over time, to trace how sociocultural values embedded in these stories shift over the years. We will consider intersections of gender, race, disability, sexuality, religion, nature, and the family, and explore how these depictions are shaped by the national, cultural, and personal circumstance of their tellers and re-tellers. Moving beyond Europe, we will examine the genre as a richly transcultural aspect of world literature.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Week 1: What is a fairytale? Why do we tell stories?Week 2: The Cinderella Circle (1): Disneyfication, transformation, gender rolesWeek 3: The Cinderella Circle (2): historical contexts, ideology, the function of fairytalesWeek 4: The Snow White Circle (1): establishing the Disney FormulaWeek 5: The Snow White Circle (2): interpretations and re-interpretationsWeek 6: The Grimms save the fairytale? The Grimms and 19-century nationalismWeek 7: Women write the fairytale: the women behind the talesWeek 8: Hans Christian Andersen and the Little Mermaid: Disneyfying the literary fairytaleWeek 9: Andersen continued: the literary fairytale and the bourgeoisie homeWeek 10: The Beauty and the Beast circle (1): feminism and monstrosityWeek 11: The Beauty and the Beast circle (2): pop culture, fairtyales and eroticismWeek 12: The Aladdin circle (1): orientalism and exoticismWeek 13: The Aladdin circle (2): European variantsWeek 14: Fairytales of fairytalesWeek 15: Intersections of fantasy and romanticism

title: An Introduction to Central Asia: From the Silk Route to Afghanistan
description: Examination of human geography, ethnicity, nomadism and pastoralism, oases cultures, religion and international politics of the silk routes of central Asia. Not open to students with credit for LCA/HIST 265 prior to Fall 2018.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Central Asia has been a borderland region contested by the world's largest empires led by some of history's most infamous figures, from Chinggis Khan in the thirteenth century through Stalin in the twentieth. This course introduces students to the history of Central Asia through the lens of imperial enclosure to make sense of the region's staggering ethno-linguistic, racial, religious, political, and ecological diversity. During the semester, we will consider the following questions: How and with what consequences did imperial formations integrate territories, resources, and peoples into different political systems? How can we situate Central Asia in its regional and global contexts?

title: Foodways of Central Asia
description: Elementary topics in German, Nordic, and/or Slavic culture, folklore, linguistics, and/or language.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Dumplings, plov, and politics: how food tells the story of a whole regionWhat do a dumpling, a loaf of tandyr bread, and a bowl of tea have in common? In Central Asia, almost everything. Each one carries thousands of years of history from nomads moving across the steppe, caravans along the Silk Road, both Soviet Union and post-Soviet nation-building, famine and forced resettlement, migration and memory.In this course we treat food as evidence, a source as rich as any document or artifact. Why did plov become a symbol of the Uzbek nation, and beshbarmak of the Kazakh nation? How did plowing up the steppe for wheat permanently change what is served on the table today? Why do countries compete to "own" a dish on UNESCO's lists? And what lies behind the tired image of the "wild nomad" and other stereotypes? This course will teach you to see straight through them.We'll read anthropologists, historians, and archaeologists, watch films, and in a campus teaching kitchen, cook and taste dishes from the region ourselves, asking what they reveal about culture, hospitality, and identity. No prior knowledge of the region or its languages is required; just bring curiosity and a willingness to think.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Mondays & Wednesdays, 4:00 to 5:15 PM, open to all majors, a mixed lecture-discussion format, with an emphasis on discussion. Three hands-on food labs, held in a campus instructional kitchen, connect the course's themes to practice.

title: History of Race and Inequality in Urban America
description: Examine the historical relationships between metropolitan change, economic transformation, and the construction of race and how those processes have shaped mass incarceration, educational, housing, and income inequality, and the experiences of racial/ethnic minorities who have been marginalized or discriminated against. Key questions include: What is the historical nature of inequality and opportunity in metropolitan America? What policies and ideas have historically promoted inequality, and how have those policies and ideas shifted over time? How have marginalized people responded to inequality, and what impacts have various modes of resistance had? Lastly, what is "race," how has its meaning changed over time, and how has it historically shaped inequality and opportunity?

title: The Long Black Freedom Struggle from the Civil War to the Present
description: Explores the generations-long effort by African Americans and allied forces to achieve full citizenship in the U.S. and equitable footholds in American society. Forged in a history of enslavement and in many ways ongoing, this freedom struggle encompasses the history of abolitionism to the struggle for civil rights to the fight for Black Power to the effort to make Black Lives Matter. Introduces the history of African American people in the U.S. from the end of the era of slavery to the present day; explores how that history has been shaped directly by the actions and activism of Black people and their allies; considers how that history intersects with, shapes, and is shaped by other historical moments and movements; provides opportunities to think more actively about issues of belonging, citizenship, difference, and interpersonal and structural power; develops skills in historical analysis and argumentation.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Below are relevant portions of the syllabus from the last time I taught this class. Dates for meetings and deadlines will obviously change, and there will be minor tweaks, but this is by and large a fair representation of what the Spring 2027 syllabus will look like."The Long Black Freedom Struggle  refers to the generations-long effort by African Americans and allied forces to achieve full citizenship in the United States and equitable footholds in American society. Forged in a history of enslavement and in many ways ongoing, the Long Black Freedom Struggle encompasses the history of abolitionism to the struggle for civil rights to the fight for Black Power to the effort to make Black Lives Matter. "Freedom is a constant struggle,  as Angela Davis has written, is the guiding ethos for this class. This course explores the rhythms and rhymes of that constant struggle for Black Americans over the course of post-Civil War U.S. history.There are a whole range of aims and goals underlying a course such as this. If we were to whittle down to the five most sustained goals, however, they would be these: 1) to introduce students to the history of African American people in the United States from the end of the era of slavery to the present day; 2) to explore how that history has been shaped directly by the actions and activism of Black people and their allies; 3) to consider how that history intersects with, shapes, and is shaped by other historical moments and movements; 4) to give students from various backgrounds opportunities to think more actively about issues of belonging, citizenship, difference, and interpersonal and structural power, and 5) to invest students with the skills to analyze historical documents, secondary literature, and arguments about history in order to formulate forceful and coherent arguments based upon those analyses. While we will cover important names, dates, and events, our primary attentions will be paid to interpreting those pieces of data in the interests of assembling a more complete picture of African American and American history. In other words, we will be less concerned with memorizing minutiae than with better understanding history and the human experience. You've probably heard the adage about not seeing the forest for the trees. The trees matter. But so does the forest.This class meets twice weekly. It's designed as lecture-forward, but I also want us to engage collectively in discussions about the material we're studying. All readings in any given week must be completed by the Thursday in which they're assigned, as our structure will be such that the second half of those Thursday class sessions will be basically discussion sections. At the same time, students should be prepared and expect to be called upon at any point throughout the week to talk about relevant material.Course Aims and DescriptionBy the end of the semester, students will be able to:  Identify important events, movements, and people, in African-American history since 1865   Formulate arguments about change over time   Evaluate arguments about history   Determine what constitutes reliable and valid evidence   Interpret, compare, and contrast primary sources   Think critically about how the narratives about the past are constructed and told As a course that meets the University's Ethnic Studies Requirement, additional learning outcomes are as follows. By the end of the semester, students will  Have gained a better understanding of how racial conflict, inequality, and movements against the same in the past have shaped American society in the present   Have developed a better sense of their social position relative to history, and of how other people's pasts and experiences perhaps don't align with their own  Be better-equipped to operate in a pluralistic, multicultural society -- one in which their own experiences are not the assumed default
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Course Evaluation A couple of notes on attendance: 1) We're all adults. Whether or not you come to lectures is ultimately up to you. But unless you already have a very expansive knowledge of African American social, cultural and political history, or possess a preternatural ability to pull data and insights about Black history out of thin air, you are not going to do well in this class if you skip consistently. This is not a threat, but rather an experience-based promise from watching students try and fail to have their cake (not come to class) and eat it too (get a good grade). 2) Your health is important, in both the physical and mental senses. I will exercise grace should you need to miss class for any health issues, but please communicate with me about such needs as proactively as possible. You don't need to (indeed, should not) reveal private, confidential information to me about any health concerns you're dealing with, but please do let me know that you will be or recently were absent because of them.Papers: Due dates for the paper are listed on the course schedule below. These papers will be evaluated for content, coherence, argument, and style, working under the assumption that you will have plenty of time to write and revise them. Please note that you will also need to respond on the final exam to two of the assigned readings, but those will only be graded for content and argument since you will be writing them in the moment and won't have an opportunity to revise them.Exams: Specifics of the exam formats will be discussed closer to the time of the exams. Worth noting now is that a) they will be hand-written in class without notes available, and b) will focus far more on students interpreting and analyzing history (i.e. short essays) than in rote memorization (i.e. multiple choice). Exams are not graded for grammar, style, etc. The final exam is not cumulative.Final grades will be calculated on a percentage basis. Each component's piece of the pie is broken down as follows; you will note that none of them are skippable:Short paper: 20%Midterm exam (in-class): 25%Final exam (in-class): 25%Canvas posts: 20%Attendance: 10%Grading Scale:A: 92.5+AB: 87.5-92.49B: 82.5-87.49BC: 77.5-82.49C: 69.5-77.49D: 60-69.49F: <60I don't round up on grades, as that poses a slippery and potentially inequitable slope. You get what you earn, without room for negotiation. I will, however, do everything I can to offer extra credit opportunities throughout the course of the semester should there be things happening on campus that make sense to incorporate into our class.

title: US Labor and Working-Class History
description: An introductory survey of labor and working-class history. Describes processes of class formation and trajectories of labor movements. Interprets the contributions of diverse workers to American economy, culture, and politics. Maintains a central analytic focus on the intersections of race and gender with economic class in US History.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Who is a worker? Who decides the value of work? Why have some Americans been forced to labor, while others were deemed free to follow their work ethic? Why have employers and lawmakers sometimes invited workers to migrate to the US and at other times excluded them? How has economic polarization contributed to political polarization? What is working-class culture, and what does it have to do with the history of culture wars? This survey explores the lives and impact of diverse working peoples from the seventeenth century to the present. Lectures and readings center on interactions between three key historical processes: class formation, racialization, and movement-building.

title: Japan After 1945
description: Introduction to historical studies at the research university. Emphasis on interpretation and critical thinking. Topics vary.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: World War Two represents a transformational event for the twentieth century world.  The dramatic stories of the war and its aftermath include the momentary triumph of fascism as a global movement and its military defeat; the redrawing of geopolitical maps as hot wars resolved themselves into cold wars; the rise and fall of empires; decolonization and the emergence of a "third world  of new nations.  In what ways did World War Two and its aftermath reshape Asia? This course explores this question by looking at the case of Japan. How do the stories of Japan's defeat, the US occupation, and the creation of the regional cold war order complicate our understanding of the twentieth century world?History 201 is a course in the "historian's craft,  which means we learn basic skills in the practice of history through our study of post-imperial Japan. I have divided the course into four thematic sections, each exploring the World War Two transformation and its impact on postwar Japan. Part One opens with the experience of total war and total defeat. Part 2 focuses on the atomic bombing of Japan and compares "a-bomb cultures  in the US and Japan. Part 3 looks at the transition of the US-Japan relationship from war to peace and the impact of Japan's integration into the American cold war imperium. Part 4 examines the question of war crimes, war crimes trials, and the long afterlife of World War Two in public memory in Asia.
