title: Human Rights and Education
description: Explores questions related to human rights and education, from the individual to the global level; from the abstract to the practical: What does it mean to be human? How do we learn to be human? What rights mark a human being? Do all human have rights? If they have a right to education, do they have a right to a particular kind of education? Can one global education and human rights model best meet the needs of our incredibly diverse global population? Can the global human rights framework improve current educational, national, social, and economic inequities? How so? How does education as a human right relate to human rights education? and who should decide the answers to these questions, and how? Investigates the tensions and boundaries of the human rights framework to reduce social inequality through methodological inquires in educational case studies, including: educational inequality; victims of the war on drugs; working children's rights; and climate change.

title: Modern Latin America
description: A broad overview of Latin American history in the modern period, since independence but with a primary focus on the twentieth century. Particular emphasis will be placed on the socioeconomic, cultural, and political structures and processes that shaped and continue to influence life in Latin America. Key issues such as colonialism, nationalism, democracy, and revolution will be examined critically in light of broad comparative themes in Latin American and world history. Among the topics to be explored in detail will be the Mexican and Cuban revolutions, populism and dictatorship, socialism and neoliberalism, and drugs and migration.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How do you gain a democracy? Or lose one? Or get one back? The history of modern Latin America provides plenty of evidence, and this semester we're going to focus on that set of questions. We'll be covering what we can from Latin America from 1810-present, while really using class time to zoom in on key questions about democracy, its meanings, its challenges, in the past and today.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: We will learn about revolutions, like those of Mexico and CubaWe will learn about foreign intervention and its effect on democracyWe will learn about populist governments, like Per n in ArgentinaWe will learn about socialism, democratic and otherwiseWe will learn about dictatorships, like Brazil and Chile in the 1970sWe will examine the history and political science of fragile democraciesWe will explore the reasons that people fought for greater and more responsive democraciesWe will learn about the limitations of democratic inclusionWe will end by looking at the current state of Latin America and the democratic challenges that it faces
instructorProvidedContent.format: It's a lecture format, but I will be using class time to facilitate discussion about these key issues once per week. The exact format for doing so will depend on the size of the class. There will be a couple of in-class exams and a final assignment in which students will study a pro-democracy movement and describe its history

title: Globalization and Education
description: Discuss the ways education is inextricably linked to global political, economic, and social contexts. Reflect on both scholarly research and popular conceptions of market, society and schools in different geographic and cultural contexts. Approach globalization from a context-sensitive, place-based approach, rather than abstract, predictive method through interdisciplinary analysis. Explore the concept of globalization across disciplinary frameworks including anthropology, geography, and history. Provides critical analysis to understand the challenges facing education in a globalization era, to build stronger commitment to helping address those challenges, and a set of skills for researching and writing about them. Examine the following "problem-spaces": globalization and migration; globalization and race; global testing and assessment; marketization of education; global city development and higher education; youth culture and globalization.

title: From Fascism to Today: Social Movements and Politics in Europe
description: Investigates how everyday people shaped European history and politics, from World War I through today. Takes a comparative and interdisciplinary approach to analyze a range of major social movements in Europe, thinking in detail about what constitutes a social movement in the first place, and what determines its effectiveness. Key topics include the rise and fall of Fascism; the fate of the Communist and Socialist Left in Europe; the role of youth movements as drivers of change; and the constraints imposed on political organizing by both democratic and authoritarian societies. Drawing on a range of texts, songs, and films, investigates how people power has shaped the European state, and vice-versa, from 1922 through today.

title: The Cold War - From World War II to End of Soviet Empire
description: The Cold War was the first event to impact virtually all of humanity and left a lasting legacy that still shapes the current world order. Exploration of its conduct on five continents entails both a diversity of sources (film, fiction, documents, and memoir) and a range of topics (geopolitics, ideology, internationalism, empire, revolution, counterinsurgency, and covert operations). Its half-century history was marked by nuclear-armed stalemate and ideological competition in Europe, cultural politics of repression and generational revolt in America, interplay of anti-colonial nationalism and counterinsurgency in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, and a succession of major wars worldwide in Korea, Vietnam, Angola, and Afghanistan. By adopting an international perspective that carries us beyond the narrow ambit of the Moscow-Washington rivalry, integrate diverse global forces and particular national histories for a fuller understanding of an ever-changing world system.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The course probes the global dynamics of the Cold War, from its origins during World War II through the end of the Soviet empire in 1991. This transformative era in international history emerged as the Cold War coincided with the rapid decolonization of European empires to produce a world divided between two rival superpowers the United States and the Soviet Union. Not only did the Cold War split most of the world into rival communist and capitalist blocs, but it also penetrated deep inside many societies, shaping culture, electoral politics, and mass consciousness.  After exploring the Cold War's key aspects such as nuclear warfare, espionage, and mind control, the course tracks its history through three main phases. First, after the fall of the Iron Curtain across Europe in the late 1940s, the rival superpowers competed for dominion over this divided continent through espionage, cultural display, and deployment of nuclear weapons. As the conflict spread around the globe, it was marked by conventional warfare (Korea), communist revolutions (China, Vietnam), counterinsurgency campaigns (Greece, Malaya), and CIA-sponsored coups (Iran, Guatemala). After the Cuban missile crisis of 1962 brought the superpowers to the brink of nuclear war, the Cold War's superpower rivalry shifted to the Third World, marked by a massive surrogate war in Vietnam, violent CIA regime changes in Indonesia and Chile, and Soviet intervention to end the Prague Spring. In the Cold War's final phase after 1975, superpower surrogate warfare coincided with local struggles to produce devastating conflicts on three continents--in southern Africa, Central America, and Central Asia. In its concluding lecture the course will analyze how this past is shaping a contemporary superpower rivalry called "the New Cold War.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: As a global survey of the Cold War, the course moves to a different continent every week. During the Cold War's first phase (1947-1962), the course will examine conventional warfare (Korea), communist revolutions (China, Vietnam), counterinsurgency campaigns (Greece, Malaya), and CIA-sponsored coups (Iran, Guatemala). In the Cold War's second phase, the course will study the massive surrogate war in Vietnam, violent CIA regime changes in Indonesia and Chile, and Soviet intervention to end the Prague Spring. In the Cold War's final phase after 1975, superpower rivalry produced devastating conflicts on three continents--in southern Africa (Angola), Central America (Guatemala, El Salvador), and Central Asia (Afghanistan).

Drawing upon those lectures and parallel readings available on Canvas, students will participate in weekly in discussion sections. In addition to their participation grade from the discussion section, there will a midterm, a final exam, and an essay.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Analyzes the relationships between culture, strategy, and security through historical, structural, and critical perspectives to help interpret the global security environment. Examines cultural influences, broadly defined, on state and non-state security strategies, decisions, and behaviors through historical experiences and contemporary events. Cultural factors contextualize security strategies at the ideational and material levels, leaving their imprint on how groups and individuals act to achieve desired outcomes. Analyzes strategic behavior as culturally derived and appraises the advantages and limitations of this methodology for better understanding the security environment. Illustrates the relationships between cultural influences and their outcomes. Focuses on individual and small-group application and analysis.

title: Race, Ethnicity, and the Italian Americans
description: What does it mean to be Italian American? Must those who identify as such choose one identity over the other? How are they viewed by society? As Italian, American, or some undefinable other? Explore the history of Italian immigration to the United States and its effects on both the ethnic group and the hosting country, as recounted in literature and film both by those who experienced it firsthand and their descendants. Italians fleeing from racism and poverty in Italy found racial, religious, and cultural discrimination. Working toward "whiteness," Italian Americans traded off their own "Italian-ness" while clinging to aspects of it in the hope to preserve parts of their identity. They forged strong bonds with African American, Jewish, and other marginalized communities, in a relationship of understanding but also of tension and rivalry. Focuses on specific literary texts paired with textbook readings that provide their historical and social background.

title: Rome: Lust for Glory
description: Examines the development of Rome, "the Eternal City," and its continuing presence as both a metaphoric and physical focal point of Italian artistic and cultural sensibilities. Outline the development of Rome's authoritative or "mythical" status in literature, art, architecture and film, beginning in the Augustan era and arriving to today, focusing on significant moments in the creation and expansion of the actual city and its cultural influence in the late-Middle Ages, the Renaissance, the era of the Risorgimento (Unification of Italy), and the rise of Fascism. Develop ability to think critically about how the diverse material productions of writers (historians, playwrights, poets), painters, sculptors, architects, philosophical thinkers, and later filmmakers of the periods covered reflect one another and reflect the ideas and ideologies of their age.

description: Survey of Italian literature from Mid-Modernity to the 21st century. Topics vary. Taught in Italian.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: IT632, "Making Boccaccio: Writing, Editing, and Interpretation"This course explores Giovanni Boccaccio as both a literary author and an active participant in the material production, transmission, and interpretation of texts, chiefly as the "inventor  of the literary canon of the tre corone. A central component of the first part of the course will be Boccaccio's scribal activity and his engagement with the written book. Through the study of manuscripts, scribal practices, and authorial revision, we will investigate how Boccaccio's work as a copyist, editor, and compiler of texts informs our understanding of his literary production. The second part of the course will focus chiefly on the Decameron and will examine how Boccaccio's narrative art took shape through processes of composition, revision, compilation, and circulation. We will read the Decameron closely, focusing on its narrative structures, framing devices, generic experimentation, and representations of social and cultural life, while also considering how its meanings are shaped by the material forms in which it survives.

title: The Sabbath
description: What is the "Sabbath"? What does it mean "to rest"? Offers a broad, comparative introduction to the history of the Sabbath, from the Bible to the present day. Explore a range of textual sources from the Jewish and Christian traditions. Topics include the major theological, ritual, and cultural practices that have developed around the Sabbath. Analysis places emphasis on literary representations of the Sabbath across genres. Discuss contemporary political iterations of the Sabbath in modern, secular contexts.

title: Kosher Controversies
description: Elementary topics in Jewish philosophy and the arts.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Why did some people claim that Jack the Ripper was a kosher slaughterer? Why were Jews accused of stealing Christian children in order to make matzah for Passover? Why did Jewish women riot in the streets in New York City over the price of kosher meat? This course explores these and many other kosher controversies. In doing, so we will discover how in public discussions of kosher foods and laws there is a use of common imagery and concepts to depict Jews and Judaism through the foods they do and do not eat.Throughout, we will explore how kosher controversies were not just about the food, but about a variety of associated practices related (sometimes quite loosely) to food preparation: from ritual animal slaughter to the business of food distribution and preparation. From pork to artichokes, from chicken to oysters, we will follow the curious and indeed sometimes scandalous history of kosher food controversies.

title: Classical Rabbinic Literature in Translation
description: Introduction to the literature of the Classical Rabbinic or Talmudic period of Judaism (2nd to 7th centuries CE). Historical and intellectual background; the interrelation of liturgy, legal and non-legal literature.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Examine the literary corpus of the classical rabbinic period (70-640 C.E.) to understand how this group shaped the religion now known as Judaism. Interact closely with primary texts in translation to learn the operating principles of rabbinic logic, as well as how scholars (re)construct history based upon this corpus. Apply arguments made on the macro level (i.e., about rabbinic literature in general) to the micro level using drinks and drinking as a test case.

title: What Is Jewish Studies?
description: Introduces Jewish studies as an interdisciplinary field and examines Jewish history, culture, and thought through the major questions that guide the field, including: What is Jewish practice? What is a Jewish text? What is diaspora? What is antisemitism? And, who are the Jews? Explores a variety of responses offered by scholars, writers, theologians, and artists. Develop the ability to think transhistorically, bringing together biblical, medieval, modern, and contemporary perspectives. Anchor inquiries into the field of Jewish studies through the completion of a substantial research project.

title: Introduction to Sports Communication
description: Explore the central activities and concepts related to various communication professions involved in the realm of sports. These activities include sports journalism, sports broadcasting, sports marketing communications, and sports public relations. Consider major social issues that impinge upon these professions including how sports and media intersect with concerns associated with race and gender. Explore strategies to build careers in sports communications and beyond.

title: Mass Media in Multicultural America
description: An introduction to the roles and functions of print, film, electronic and digital media in multicultural America.  International comparisons highlight differences and commonalities in the social and cultural position of mass media in societies with racially and ethnically diverse populations.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: An introduction to the roles and functions of print, film, electronic and digital media in multicultural America. International comparisons highlight differences and commonalities in the social and cultural position of mass media in societies with racially and ethnically diverse populations. Counts towards the Sports Communication Certificate and Ethnic Studies degree requirement.

title: Gender and Sexuality in Mass Communication
description: Exploration of the role that gender and sexuality both play in media representation, production, reception, and activism.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This class focuses on issues of gender and sexuality, specifically in the news and entertainment media. We will look at women's roles in producing media content, how women are represented in writing and images, and how women are mobilizing via social media. We will also look at the representation of masculinity in the mass media, remembering the important point that masculinity is also gendered and sexualized. Finally, we will look at the representation of queer-identified and transgender subjects both on and off-screen, as well as tracing the intersections between race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality.

input: Gender and Sexuality in Mass Communication

title: Media Fluency for the Digital Age
description: An introduction to digital media and how it influences - and is impacted by - society, culture, politics, and the economy. Create on-trend digital media content and critically examine digital mediums, messages, and audiences.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The digital media landscape is rapidly evolving, and it has major ramifications on how we view and interact with political, social and economic landscapes. Become more fluent in digital media by examining current and emerging media and the issues and opportunities surrounding it, while producing and consuming digital media content. Being "digitally fluent" is considered a key 21st Century skill. So, what does it mean to be fluent in digital media? It goes way beyond putting a "snap" on your Story or posting to Facebook. It's a matter of knowing which medium is best given what you want to say - and who you want to converse with! Critically examine andengage with this media landscape. Analyze how digital media content is created and digested by various audiences across social, political, and economic environments. Counts towards the Digital Media Analytics Certificate.

input: Media Fluency for the Digital Age

enrollmentPrerequisites: Freshman, sophomore, or junior standing only
title: Introduction to Mass Communication
description: How the mass media are organized and how they function in modern society; their technological basis, economic and political foundations, and social implications.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This is an introduction to how the mass media are organized and how they function in modern society, their technological bases, economic and political foundations, and social implications. This combined lecture/discussion course introduces students to the interlinked entertainment, strategic communication, and journalism aspects of our mass media, and to the broad theoretical, historical, and critical perspectives that mass communication scholars use to understand and analyze these media processes. This course also fulfills the campus Communications-B requirement for refining your communication skills through written assignments, peer review, and revision. For those students considering careers in the media, this course should help you make informed decisions about your professional life and will serve as the prerequisite to entering the School of Journalism and Mass Communication. Required to apply to the School of Journalism & Mass Communication

enrollmentPrerequisites: Declared in a Journalism undergraduate program and JOURN 201 and concurrent enrollment in JOURN 203
title: Mass Communication Practices
description: Build increasingly sophisticated communication skills, including writing, editing, gathering information, working with data, and presenting stories through varying media forms. Develop an appreciation of how different media influence message design by communicators and reception by audiences. Develop a complex toolkit of conceptual and practical skills for media work in journalism, strategic communication, and hybrids. Build writing skills and critical thinking abilities, two elements common to success in any field.

title: Information for Communication
description: Develop information skills - information collection, information verification, information analysis, and information presentation (the CVAP approach) - that are used by professionals in journalism and strategic communication. Includes practical techniques that enhance basic skills related to the collection, evaluation, analysis and presentation of information. These skills will provide a foundation for the major and in journalism and mass communication careers.

title: Media & Politics
description: An introduction to the study of media and politics, examining the interactions between political actors, media institutions, and mass publics in a changing information environment, with a primary (but not exclusive) focus on the United States. Examines the critical functions that media institutions serve in political and democratic processes, shaping the nature and flow of information that citizens, public officials, and civil society need to make decisions in both public and private affairs. Explores the implications of evolving communication technologies for the nature of news and its consumption, attention and information processing, public opinion and the political agenda, political communication in campaigns and elections, and mass engagement in public affairs.

title: Principles and Practices of Reporting
description: Basic reporting for print and electronic media. Bring together technical and conceptual skills by creating a variety of print, audio, and web-based news stories on a current public issue.

description: Introduction to strategic communication for students interested in advertising, public relations, health communications, and political campaigns.

title: Sports Marketing Communications
description: Explore various activities related to the promotion domain of sports marketing including marketing research, sports branding, image management, advertising promotion, event promotion, sports sponsorships, and public relations. Examine each of these activities, and focus on the marketing communications associated with each of these activities.

title: Investigative Reporting
description: Techniques of investigative and long-form enterprise reporting. Includes extensive reporting in the field and a final project.

title: Creative Campaign Messages
description: Introduction to the creative aspects of message development for advertising, public relations, and other strategic communications.

title: Sports Reporting and Writing
description: Core skills and issues of communicating about sports to a mass audience in a changing media landscape, as well as advice and support in starting a sports communication career including access to professionals in the field. Utilizes professional, historical and theoretical perspectives in helping participants gain proficiency in disseminating information about sports-related events and topics for informative and strategic purposes, while developing a sense of the role of sport in contemporary society.

title: Long Form Video
description: Develop skills needed to conduct professional-level journalism and strategic communication in long-form video. Produce documentary pieces of covering a contemporary topic of local or regional interest and complete other exercises in video analysis, composition and production.

title: Storytelling Through Sound
description: Audio storytelling as an art form, with a focus on creating a series of episodic long-form audio storytelling segments. Develop interview and writing skills, as well as field recording and editing techniques. Develop personal style and voice, while learning practical skills necessary to write and produce audio content for over the air or online.

enrollmentPrerequisites: Declared in a Journalism undergraduate program and JOURN 345
title: Digital Media Strategies
description: Provides an overview of digital media from an objective, strategy, and tactical planning perspective within strategic communication media and promotion campaigns.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course takes the strategic communication foundations from JOURN 345 and focuses them on digital channels social media, content, SEO, SEM, email, and emerging platforms. You will work with a real client through a complete digital media planning process: research and situation analysis, tactical strategy development, and a final casebook and presentation. This is applied work designed to produce a portfolio piece that demonstrates your ability to think strategically about digital while executing across multiple channels and platforms.What you will learn:  Digital media strategy development: how to set objectives and craft strategies that integrate with overall communication goals  Audience research and analysis using professional tools: social listening, consumer databases, and search trends  Content strategy and message strategy: how to develop and distribute content across channels  Technical and tactical digital skills: SEO, SEM, social media management, and platform-specific strategies  How to evaluate, recommend, and optimize digital channels in an integrated campaign  Crisis communications in a digital context speed, stakeholder management, and cross-platform coordination  How to build, present, and defend strategic recommendations to client

title: Public Relations Strategies
description: Provides an overview of public relations from an objective, strategy, and tactical planning perspective within strategic communication campaigns. Investigates one core element of a strategic communications campaign and provides an in-depth study into the topic area of public relations.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course takes strategic communication deeper, focusing on public relations. You will develop a comprehensive PR campaign for a real client, moving from research and strategy through tactical execution. PR shapes how organizations are understood by the people who matter most: media, employees, customers, communities, regulators. You will learn how to build and protect reputation, navigate complex stakeholder relationships, respond to issues before they escalate, and produce the communications that drive action. This is applied work designed as a portfolio piece that demonstrates both strategic thinking and tactical execution in PR. This course counts towards the Digital Studies Certificate.What you will learn:  Strategic public relations planning: how to research, set objectives, and craft strategies aligned with organizational goals  Media relations and earned media strategy in traditional and digital channels  Stakeholder analysis and relationship management across multiple audiences  Content strategy and message development for PR audiences and channels  Issue management and crisis preparation: frameworks for anticipating problems and responding decisively  The range of PR specialties: corporate communications, employee communications, purpose-driven PR, brand and consumer PR, and more  Professional PR tools and databases for research, media relations, and monitoring  How to build, present, and defend strategic PR recommendations to clients

title: Mass Communication and Society
description: Relationships between mass communications and society; analysis and evaluation of media performance and of suggestions for change.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Considers the changing role of mass communication today through the lens of major historical shifts in the media system: the written alphabet, the print revolution, telegraph and radio, the Internet, and social media. How do new media technologies shape   and how are they shaped by   our social and cultural worlds? How has the quality of democratic life been altered by various media "revolutions ? These are the questions and themes we will explore over the course of a semester that begins with fables and folklore and ends with a look at the future of the digital networks that are so basic to our lives today

title: Mass Media and Racial Diversity
description: Delves deeply into the concepts and theories related to the subject of mass media and racial diversity. Key concepts such as race, ethnicity, stereotypes, and white privilege are examined and analyzed in the news, advertising, digital media and social media and their intersection with African Americans, Native Americans, Asian Americans, Latinx Americans, and Arab Americans. Different social and cultural roles assumed by mainstream media and alternative media are also explored.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course delves deeply into the concepts and theories related to mass media and racial diversity. It provides analysis of race, ethnicity, stereotypes, and white privilege in the news, digital media, and social media. This course examines mainstream news along with African American, Native American, Asian American, Latinx Americans, and Arab American media outlets

title: Law of Mass Communication
description: Freedom of speech and press with particular emphasis on major legal issues confronting media practitioners; introduction to such areas of law as censorship, libel, invasion of privacy, access to information, regulation of electronic media and commercial speech.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: JOURN 563 introduces students to legal principles and doctrines used to resolve conflicts involving freedom of expression generally and freedom of the press specifically. It is also designed to give students a fundamental working knowledge of how to solve common legal problems in media and public communication and how to use the law. Topics covered include First Amendment theory, censorship, compelled speech, regulation of political expression, telecommunication regulation, new technologies and regulation, libel, invasion of privacy, access to information, regulation of commercial speech, intellectual property, and journalist's privilege

title: Colloquium in Professional Communication Careers
description: Explores a wide variety of post-undergraduate communication career options available in Journalism. Topics related to job hunting, resume writing, and networking are also covered. Focuses on opportunities and challenges in a wide variety of communication fields, from advertising and public relations to radio, newspapers and TV broadcasting. Guest speakers or panelists will span different sectors (agencies, corporations, nonprofits, higher education, government, etc.).

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This is a weekly, one-credit graduate undergraduate colloquium series, sponsored by the School of Journalism and Mass Communication. Students enrolled in the class get tips to improve key 'first job search' tools (LinkedIn profile, Badger Bridge, resume, interviews, etc.) and explore a wide variety of post-undergraduate communication career options. We will focus on opportunities and challenges in a wide variety of communication fields, from digital /social media, advertising and public relations to podcasting, online news and TV broadcasting. Each week, we'll hear from a different guest lecture or a panel discussion, focused on a particular communications career

title: Mass Communication and Political Behavior
description: Interrelationships of news media, political campaigning, and the electorate. Impact of media coverage and persuasive appeals on image and issue voting, political participation and socialization.

title: The Impact of Emerging Media
description: Provides an introduction to the literature and research on emerging communication technologies (e.g., blogs, social media, massively multiplayer games, mobile devices) and the effects of these technologies on the individual and societal levels. Illuminates the psychological, social, political, industrial, and policy implications of the use of emerging communication technologies. Become equipped with a basic social and scientific understanding of the interplay between technology, individuals, and society, and recurring issues concerning the adoption and usage of new communication technologies. Emphasizes empirical approaches to understanding these relationships, delving into contexts such as journalism, strategic communication, and the place of digital media in politics and society.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course provides an introduction to research on emerging communication technologies -like social media, smartphones, videogames, personalized algorithms, and AI chatbots - on individual and societal well-being. Drawing on classical communication theory and recent research, we will examine questions about the interplay between technology, individuals, and society like 1) "How does smartphone use affect psychological well-being?", 2) "What is the relationship between dating app use and self-esteem?", 3) "How does social media use relate to people's belief in misinformation?", 4) "How does using AI chatbots affect individual creativity and critical thinking?", and 5) "How do algorithms shape our political behavior?" This course emphasizes empirical approaches to understanding these relationships and strengthening awareness of the different methods used to study emerging media. Throughout, we will discuss the real-world stakes of emerging media effects. Students will gain research-based approaches to develop healthier relationships to their own technology use, and learn about the interventions that can be implemented by families, journalists, policymakers, and technologists to reduce online harms

Illuminates the foundational concepts, frameworks, and tools brand management professionals use to drive awareness, consideration, trial and repeat of their offerings to increase market share and establish long-lasting brand equity with target consumer groups. Engages leadership and positioning principles to cultivate and communicate one's professional and personal brand in any career or life path.

description: Focuses on the application of biological, cultural and social theory and research to lifestyle change. There will be lectures by experts, experiential learning, and the application of course knowledge to student's lives through class assignments and activities. The transition to college requires students to construct a new lifestyle, take on new and greater personal responsibilities while at the same time meet rigorous academic challenges. This transition includes a loss of structured daily schedules, decreased family support for the day to day living, and greater responsibility for their finances and life choices. Students may have difficulty managing their time, exercise less, eat less healthy foods, engage in increased drinking of alcohol, and experience greater stress and depression when adjusting to college life. This life transition provides an opportunity for reexamination and an opportunity to make thoughtful choices about lifestyle.

title: Making the American Landscape
description: Traces the history and evolution of the American cultural landscape from precolonial times to present. Explores how class, ethnic, and racial inequality have shaped the appearance of the American landscape over time, and how that landscape in turn has affected relationships between people and groups through the present day. Examines extraordinary things (civic structures (like our State Capitol), National Parks, War Memorials) and more ordinary kinds of places (mining towns, cotton plantations, sites of recreation and leisure, and suburban tract housing) to stimulate critical thinking about how these places have served people and groups unequally and disproportionately over time and across space. Considers complex meanings of American spaces and places to different people and groups, stimulating empathy and encouraging participation in a multicultural society.

title: Dimensions of Material Culture
description: This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of material culture studies. It is intended for students interested in any professional endeavor related to material culture, including careers in museums, galleries, historical societies, historic preservation organizations, and academic institutions. During the semester, students have varied opportunities to engage with and contemplate the material world to which people give meaning and which, in turn, influences their lives. Sessions combine in some way the following: presentations from faculty members and professionals who lecture on a phase of material culture related to his/her own scholarship or other professional work; discussion of foundational readings in the field; visits to collections and sites on campus and around Madison; discussion of readings assigned by visiting presenters or the professors; and exams and short papers that engage material culture topics.

title: Dimensions of Material Culture
description: This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of material culture studies. It is intended for students interested in any professional endeavor related to material culture, including careers in museums, galleries, historical societies, historic preservation organizations, and academic institutions. During the semester, students have varied opportunities to engage with and contemplate the material world to which people give meaning and which, in turn, influences their lives. Sessions combine in some way the following: presentations from faculty members and professionals who lecture on a phase of material culture related to his/her own scholarship or other professional work; discussion of foundational readings in the field; visits to collections and sites on campus and around Madison; discussion of readings assigned by visiting presenters or the professors; and exams and short papers that engage material culture topics.

title: Fourth Semester Latin
description: Close literary analysis of the structure, style, and language of several Roman poets and prose writers. A critical rather than a purely historical approach to these authors.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: A Journey through "STEAM-themed Latin Prose from the 1st to the 17th Century CELatin 306 is an introduction to Latin literature in prose through selections from several authors who used the Latin language to provide invaluable information and different perspectives on "STEAM-themed  subjects like the art of writing, natural disaster, animals, the human body etc., through the centuries. The focus will be on the letters of Pliny the Younger (1st/2nd century CE) that offer insight into the world of the Roman elite in the High Empire and touch on a wide variety of subjects, including the eruption of Mount Vesuvius. Then we will move on to reading selections from the following authors: Pliny the Elder's Inventorum Natura (1st century CE), a first-century manuscript, identified as the journal of a scientific expedition conducted by Pliny the Elder in search of material for his Natural History, and his Naturalis Historia itself; Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae (6th/7th century CE), an etymological encyclopedia that summarized and organized a wealth of knowledge from hundreds of classical sources (e.g. Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia); and an educational classic of prime importance: Johann Amos Comenius' Orbis Sensualium Pictus (17th century CE), the first widely used children's textbook with pictures, designed to be a child's first Latin textbook, published first in Latin and German, subsequently republished in many European languages and used throughout the world for over two hundred years. This Spring, I'm looking forward to making the exciting transition from authentic Latin poetry (in Latin 305) to authentic Latin prose from different time periods with you. Join me for this journey!

title: Modern Latin America
description: A broad overview of Latin American history in the modern period, since independence but with a primary focus on the twentieth century. Particular emphasis will be placed on the socioeconomic, cultural, and political structures and processes that shaped and continue to influence life in Latin America. Key issues such as colonialism, nationalism, democracy, and revolution will be examined critically in light of broad comparative themes in Latin American and world history. Among the topics to be explored in detail will be the Mexican and Cuban revolutions, populism and dictatorship, socialism and neoliberalism, and drugs and migration.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How do you gain a democracy? Or lose one? Or get one back? The history of modern Latin America provides plenty of evidence, and this semester we're going to focus on that set of questions. We'll be covering what we can from Latin America from 1810-present, while really using class time to zoom in on key questions about democracy, its meanings, its challenges, in the past and today.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: We will learn about revolutions, like those of Mexico and CubaWe will learn about foreign intervention and its effect on democracyWe will learn about populist governments, like Per n in ArgentinaWe will learn about socialism, democratic and otherwiseWe will learn about dictatorships, like Brazil and Chile in the 1970sWe will examine the history and political science of fragile democraciesWe will explore the reasons that people fought for greater and more responsive democraciesWe will learn about the limitations of democratic inclusionWe will end by looking at the current state of Latin America and the democratic challenges that it faces
instructorProvidedContent.format: It's a lecture format, but I will be using class time to facilitate discussion about these key issues once per week. The exact format for doing so will depend on the size of the class. There will be a couple of in-class exams and a final assignment in which students will study a pro-democracy movement and describe its history

description: Foundation for advanced courses. description: An examination of the basic doctrines of constitutional criminal procedure, including constitutional rules governing searches, seizures, interrogations, and key stages of the adjudicative process. Designed to help students understand the key legal decision points in a criminal case, from the commission of a crime through the imposition of sentence, as well as the context in which these decisions are made. Develop professional judgment in the face of ambiguity: analyze critically, reason clearly, think creatively, exercise legal discretion, and make thoughtful, independent judgments.

title: Constitutional Law
description: An introduction to the constitutional law of the United States covering the basic structure of government in the United States, with emphasis on the federal government. Includes the role of the federal courts and the doctrine of judicial review; the rise of federal power, as reflected particularly in shifting definitions of "interstate commerce," the doctrine of separation of powers, with emphasis on current issues of legislative and executive branch authority; and judicial and other limitations on the exercise of authority by the states as well as selected rights protected in the Amendments to the Constitution.

title: Trusts and Estates
description: Examination of legal and real-world aspects of transmission of property, usually at death. In addition to legal fundamentals, strong focus on legal practice-i.e., on how the law plays out on the ground.

title: Introduction to Law and Humanities
description: Introduction to the dynamic relationship between law and the humanities, examining how legal systems both shape and are shaped by cultural, historical, and philosophical contexts. Through the study of literature, philosophy, history, pop culture, religious studies, and the arts, critically engage with the fundamental question of what law is and reframe legal concepts such as justice, rights, authority, and morality. Engage in the discussion of representative works of the discipline, different methodologies, and the ideas of key thinkers to highlight the humanistic dimensions of law. By analyzing court cases, historical sources, fiction, films, and philosophical writings, develop a deeper understanding of how law functions, how it tells stories, and how law is not only as a set of rules but a cultural and moral artifact.

title: Transitional Justice in World Politics
description: Provides an introduction to the study of transitional justice (TJ), or how institutions - local, domestic, and international - address the legacies of human rights abuses. Explore several key questions motivating the study of transitional justice: Why do societies pursue accountability for past repression in general? How do transitioning societies go about these pursuits? What effects might TJ policies have on prospects for democracy, rule of law, and future human rights abuses? Special attention to how local and global politics interact to influence both the development and the effects of different transitional justice policies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is an introduction to the study of transitional justice (TJ), or how institutions -- local, domestic, and international -- address the legacies of human rights abuses. In this course, students will be invited to explore several key questions motivating the study of transitional justice. Why do societies pursue accountability for past repression in general? How do transitioning societies go about these pursuits? What effects might TJ policies have on prospects for democracy, rule of law, and future human rights abuses? Throughout the course, special attention will be paid to how local and global politics interact to influence both the development and the effects of different transitional justice policies. As part of thecourse, students will also be exposed to the variety of research methods used to study TJ, including both qualitative and quantitative approaches at the sub- and cross-national levels of analysis.

title: Law, Sexuality, & Society
description: Examines the legal and social development and implications of laws governing sexual behavior, human reproduction, media, privacy, and topics related to sexuality, sex and gender. Includes historical analyses of laws connected to present day regulations of sexuality, demonstrating the origins of many of the world's most frequently debated civil rights issues. Chief focus on the United States legal system, with some content including examinations of institutions around the world. Investigates taken-for-granted knowledge and assumptions about sexuality and look at legal, cultural and social constructions of sex in society. Covers intersectional social implications, including race, (dis)ability, class, etc. Topics include: obscenity, pornography, sex work, sexual surrogacy, birth control, abortion, sex education, sexual violence, sex offenders, sexual citizenship rights, trans and intersex legal topics.

title: Crime, Gender and Justice
description: Focuses on the intersection between gender, crime and justice from a cross-cultural perspective. The gendered nature of the criminal justice system, female experiences of crime, prosecution and incarceration as well as the extent to which women are victims, offenders, and participants in the criminal justice system will be explored. Special emphasis will be placed on the theoretical implications of offending behavior and the intersection of gender with sexuality, race, ethnicity and class. The goal of this course is to provide a foundation for critically assessing the often controversial issues surrounding race, gender, crime, and criminal justice in society.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Information science is a field that focuses on the human element at the intersection of information, people, and technology. Learn what information is; explore existing and emerging technologies and social structures for creating, organizing, and disseminating it; and reflect on our broader personal or professional roles and responsibilities for managing it. Covers such topics as library science, cultural heritage practices, informatics, privacy, cybersecurity, user experience, human-centered AI, and information policy and ethics.

footnotes: You may contact us at enrollment@ischool.wisc.edu or by phone at (608) 263-2900.

title: History and Future of Books
description: Framed by a question about what books are, what books have been, and what books might be: past, present, and future. It assumes that "book" is a placeholder term for an object that becomes the site of questions and debates about a variety of media, expressions, and recording practices. A goal of the class is to understand the book as an active technology that shapes peoples, perceptions, and cultures rather than serving as a passive receptacle of them. This course will approach the book from a number of perspectives including book history, digital humanities, media studies, and human computer interaction, as well as examining industry-oriented interests such as e-reader manufacturing, book retail, and publishing.

title: Human-Centered AI (HCAI)
description: Current issues in library and information studies that are not addressed in sufficient depth in existing courses or that combine facets of several existing courses.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping how people work, make decisions, access information, and interact with technology. This course introduces students to Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HCAI), an approach to designing, developing, and evaluating AI systems that prioritizes human needs, values, and capabilities. Students will explore foundational concepts in artificial intelligence and machine learning, examine opportunities and risks associated with AI adoption across different domains, and investigate the social, ethical, and organizational implications of these technologies. Topics include human-AI collaboration, automation and augmentation, algorithmic bias and fairness, AI safety, transparency, trust, and governance. Through lectures, case studies, and hands-on design and evaluation activities, students will develop practical skills for critically assessing AI systems, identifying potential harms, and proposing human-centered alternatives.

title: Sound, Data, and Society
description: Current issues in library and information studies that are not addressed in sufficient depth in existing courses or that combine facets of several existing courses.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Sound is a tangible but also ephemeral force. How do data scientists and creators understand and deal with sound? This course uses a multi-faceted approach to the field of 'sound studies', exploring music and audio practice through sociocultural media studies, the arts, computation, acoustics and coding. Students will learn the basics of audio digitalization and examine how sound is transformed into data. Students will learn how to critically examine the way sound shapes the social environment and the techniques that designers and engineers use to shape sound. We will ask what counts as noise? We will also explore the role AI is playing in the sound engineering today, by examining the processes such as voice HCI, platforms such as Spotify and Suno, and through music programming tools such as Tidal Cycles. Cultural Studies and historical texts will provide context for our technical inquiries. No background in coding needed, Junior standing and Graduate. Final exams will include projects such as design of audio software apps, sound-art installations, and music suites, guided soundwalks, podcast/audio-documentary production, etc.

title: Things You Can't Say
description: Introduction to sociolinguistics through study of a particular topic. Focuses on how language is shaped by social factors such as gender, ethnicity, education, social status, and geographic location.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Things You Can't Say is a class about bad words what they are, and what processes all languages share with respect to them. This is a class on how a word becomes inappropriate, about the ways naughty words operate in the brain. This is a class on what it means to stipulate what people can or cannot say, and how that control extends through spoken, written, and signed language and across the lifetime. Indeed, some of the language considered offensive in our society mere decades ago is now considered utterly mundane and vice versa. We will investigate what kinds of topics or words are typically considered to be taboo or of -limits and how bans on blue language are enforced. In so doing, we'll discover that what is considered profane is determined by social and cultural norms, situational expectations, and individual preferences, habits, & identities; we will consider the similarity of linguistic operation beneath that dynamism. We will also discuss the cognitive paths of obscenity, and the psychological and physiological consequences of processing harmful language. The goal of this class is to take the unmentionable and illicit as an inherently interesting lens through which we may learn about human linguistic capability and creativity. Swearing is, scientifically and socially, cool. We will approach Things You Can't Say from the viewpoint of multiple disciplines that concern themselves with the study of Language and its use, including Linguistics, Neurobiology, Anthropology, Psychology, Literature, Rhetoric, and The Law. Students will have the opportunity to engage in self-directed research on a pejorative word of their choosing, and will have the space to present that research to our classroom community.

title: Language Emergence
description: Introduction to sociolinguistics through study of a particular topic. Focuses on how language is shaped by social factors such as gender, ethnicity, education, social status, and geographic location.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: For a long time, scientists thought that the origins of human language were inaccessible because we lacked records of the earliest spoken languages. But there actually are new languages around the world because sign languages emerge when deaf people come together in signing communities. We also have methods for studying language emergence in laboratory settings and through computer simulations. These developments allow us to explore the following questions: What uniquely human capacities lead to the creation of natural languages? How do languages change as they are transmitted across generations of users? What role do children play in this process - as they acquire languages do they change them? In this class we will explore a series of case studies of new and emerging sign languages and compare different methods for studying language emergence. We will also discuss the social and historical factors that lead to the emergence of new human languages.

description: Study of a particular topic in linguistics.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: We live in an era where we talk to our devices, and they talk back. But how does a computer actually "understand" a sentence? This course introduces the tools and techniques used to make computers process human language. We will explore how computer programs translate between languages, create text from speech, and categorize billions of data points. We will cover a broad range of methods not just generative AI to give you a complete overview of the field. No previous knowledge of programming is required for this interdisciplinary course.

title: Historical Sociolinguistics
description: Study of a particular topic in linguistics.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Still a young field, historical sociolinguistics is the application and development of sociolinguistic theories, models, and methods for the study of historical language variation and change over time (NARNiHS.org). Historical written documents don't just provide us with linguistic data, like verb forms and word order, but also tell us about the writers and how they positioned themselves in their social networks, how their writing varied according to who they were corresponding with, language attitudes and ideologies, and much more.  In this course, you'll do hands-on work with historical documents to learn what they can tell us about sociolinguistics, language variation and language change in the communities they come from.

title: Acquisition of Polysynthesis
description: Critical examination of selected issues in linguistics.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Many Indigenous languages of the Americas are known for polysynthesis, where single words may be morphologically complex and express the equivalent of a multi-word sentence in English. But despite their importance to the study of morphology and syntax, polysynthetic languages remain under-represented in the field of child language acquisition. This seminar explores academic literature on the acquisition of polysynthesis, surveying studies from the Arctic to the Amazon, and drawing comparisons to research on more-studied languages.

title: Slavic Science Fiction through Literature and Film
description: Explore the rich tradition of Slavic contributions to Science Fiction (SF). Survey early and contemporary works in the Czech, Polish, and Russian contexts, most of which are little known in the US but are nonetheless fundamental to SF as a world genre. Alongside reading these works, discuss and analyze film adaptations that have, in some cases, become more famous than written texts themselves.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: In the United States, science fiction (SF) is typically thought of as a quintessentially American (or American-British) genre. This course explores the rich tradition of Slavic contributions to SF. We will survey major writers and their works in the Czech, Polish, and Russian contexts, most of which are little known in the US but are nonetheless, as we will see, fundamental to the genre. We will read these works as both anchored in their particular cultural-historical circumstances and also for their contribution to the development of SF as a world genre. In this regard, SF is perhaps the dominant contemporary genre for sociocultural commentary and critique aimed at reimagining the world in which we live, and Slavic SF texts have played a defining role in establishing SF as such. Since the rise of film coincides with the rise of modern SF and since the intertextual dimension in SF literature is particularly strong, we will also compare and contrast the literary works with, where available, their film adaptations.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Authors and texts we will be reading include: Karel Capek (RUR, War with the Newts); Mikhail Bulgakov (Heart of a Dog); Evgenii Zamyatin (We); Stanislaw Lem (The Star Diaries, The Futurological Congress, Robot Fables); the Strugatsky brothers (Roadside Picnic)Films that we will watch and analyze include: Aelita, Queen of Mars; Ivan Vasilievich: Back to the Future; Solaris; Ikarie XB-1; The Congress; Stalker
instructorProvidedContent.format: Lecture with ample opportunities for small-group and full-class discussion

title: Soviet Life and Culture Through Literature and Art (from 1917)
description: Postrevolutionary Russian and Soviet visual arts, architecture, music and cinema; provides an inside view of life under socialism with the help of selected readings in Soviet literature.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Russian and Soviet Culture, 1917-1991What was it like to live, work, create, and dream in the Soviet Union? This course explores the cultural history of the Soviet era from the Russian Revolution to the collapse of the USSR. Through literature, film, visual art, music, memoirs, and historical documents, students examine how writers, artists, filmmakers, and ordinary citizens navigated a rapidly changing society shaped by revolution, war, ideology, censorship, and social transformation. Topics include the revolutionary avant-garde, Stalinism, World War II, everyday life under socialism, dissent and conformity, popular culture, and the Soviet Union's lasting cultural legacy. No prior knowledge of Russian language, history, or culture is required.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Week 1: Introduction to Soviet Culture and the Russian RevolutionWeek 2: Revolutionary Dreams and Early Soviet Literature, Poetry, and IdeologyWeek 3: The NEP Era, Popular Culture, and Everyday Life in the 1920sWeek 4: The Soviet Avant-Garde and the Socialist ExperimentWeek 5: Gender, Family, Propaganda, and the Rise of StalinismWeek 6: Socialist Realism, Film, and the Construction of the "New Soviet Person"Week 7: Mass Culture, Popular Music, and the Great TerrorWeek 8: World War II in Soviet Literature, Poetry, and MemoryWeek 9: Late Stalinism, Cultural Control, and Postwar SocietyWeek 10: The Death of Stalin, the Khrushchev Thaw, and the Gulag in LiteratureWeek 11: Dissent, Intellectual Life, and the Russian BardsWeek 12: Everyday Life, Consumer Culture, and Late SocialismWeek 13: Nonconformist Art, Film, and Underground CultureWeek 14: Perestroika, Glasnost, and the End of the Soviet Union
instructorProvidedContent.format: Interactive lecture and discussion course. Students analyze literature, film, music, visual art, and historical sources while exploring major themes in Soviet culture and society. No background in Russian language or culture is required.

title: Black Death and Medieval Life Through Boccaccio's Decameron
description: Have you ever wondered what it was like to live during the Black Death? Were our medieval and early-modern ancestors different from us, or are we challenged with similar problems? What can we learn from their lives? And, if we could, what could we teach each other? Discuss these topics while reading one of the world's greatest literary classics, Giovanni Boccaccio's Decameron, a text that will make us both laugh and cry. Through reading the Decameron, investigate medicine, art, culture, music, politics, religion, interpersonal and transcultural relations, warfare, fashion, gender and gender roles, as well as everyday life in the Middle Ages and early modernity. Also examines medieval written documents, twentieth-century feminist responses to the Decameron and filmic renditions of it, medieval frescoes, historical descriptions of the plague, and modern descriptions of, and reactions to, the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Climate Fiction
description: Exploration of diverse world literary traditions with an emphasis on German and German speaking cultures.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Climate Fiction is an emerging genre of literature, graphic novels, and other media as a sub-genre of science fiction describing and imagining scenarios of complex future ecological systems. The aim of this course is to explore the human experience of a changing climate as well as the consequences of pollution, waste, and resource extraction on communities on a global scale. We will analyze of works by German authors such as Lutz Seiler, Yoko Tawada, Ilija Trojanow, Christa Wolf, as well as writers from around the world, including Margaret Atwood, Octavia E. Butler, Amitav Ghosh, and others. While some works tell dystopian, and apocalyptic stories we will also encounter many stories that imagine a future of resilience.All readings, materials, and discussions will be in English. German language skills are welcome but not required. Text excerpts and other materials will be provided on Canvas.

Apply arguments made on the macro level (i.e., about rabbinic literature in general) to the micro level using drinks and drinking as a test case.

title: In Translation: The Drama of Henrik Ibsen
description: Often considered "the father of modern drama," the Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen (1828-1906) is a major figure of world literature whose dramatic works remain fascinating and globally influential, both as texts and through performance and adaptation. Read and discuss Ibsen in English translation, with a focus on Ibsen's historical contexts, dramatic techniques, social and political thought, and the reception and adaptation of his work in modern culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Often considered "the father of modern drama,  the Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen (1828-1906) is a major figure of world literature whose dramatic works remain fascinating and globally influential, both as texts and through performance and adaptation. In this course, students read and discuss Ibsen in English translation, with a focus on Ibsen's historical contexts, dramatic techniques, social and political thought, and the reception and interpretation of his work in modern cultures around the world. We will discuss Ibsen's famously progressive and provocative portrayals of women in plays such as Hedda Gabler, Ghosts, Rosmersholm, and A Doll's House.Please make sure to purchase the Penguin classics editions only.

topics.longDescription: Love and Politics: The Tale of Genji

title: Love & Politics: Tale of Genji
description: Focuses on a specific theme in Japanese literary history for in-depth study, such as Contemporary Japanese Novels or Japanese Women Writers.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: I am so excited to teach this course again! The Tale of Genji is a great big soap opera that can also be read as political critique, religious teaching, and (more recently) tool for selling merchandise. In this course, everyone will read two translations of the tale: Royall Tyler's English version (which has ties to Madison!) and another in the language and/or genre (manga, anime, audiobook, etc.) of their choice. By discussing competing versions of the same chapters, while considering broader themes (politics, romance, religion, commerce, etc.) we will learn more about the book and ourselves that we ever could otherwise... and, judging from the experience of many other Badgers who've taken this course, we will have a ton of fun doing it. Genji, the hero, is someone whom Badgers love to hate!
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Please feel free to email me for a copy of the syllabus from the last time I taught the course (2025). Actual assignments will depend on the size of the class!
instructorProvidedContent.format: This class meets in two "power-lectures" but is mainly discussion based. Each session will start with a general discussion of the hero's latest actions, followed by a mini-lecture from me on a broader theme, then turn to small group activities connecting the day's assigned chapter(s) to that theme. We will also watch/view/listen to a lot of related media as we consider how reactions to the tale have changed over time. If there's student interest, we will also have a couple of (optional) pizza-movie nights to see some of the best and worst adaptations and related works.

topics.longDescription: The Grand Tour and the Romantic Myth of Italy

title: Secrets & Legends of Florence
description: Treatment of a specific perific period, genre, theme or movement in Italian literature.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: What secrets lie behind Florence's magnificent palaces and famous works of art? Who were the powerful Medici, what intrigues marked their rise to power, and which legends about them still capture the imagination today? In this course, we will look beyond Florence's familiar reputation as the birthplace of the Renaissance to uncover the lesser-known stories that make the city so unique. From its Roman origins to the dramatic flood of the Arno River in 1966, Florence's past offers a wealth of fascinating stories, political intrigues, and enduring mysteries, where history and legend often intertwine.
keywords: Florence UnveiledEchoes of the Roman LegacyLiterary and Artistic TreasuresWhispers of Untold Stories

title: Diversity in Organizations
description: Provides a thorough understanding of the advantages and challenges presented by workplace diversity, suggesting techniques to manage effectively and maximize the benefits of diversity. Includes a comprehensive survey of demographic groups and an analysis of their history to foster a thorough understanding of the dimensions of diversity. Discussions will include effectively managing diversity on the basis of race, sex, LGBTQIA, religion, age, ability, national origin, and intersectionality in organizations and about issues various groups face, including discrimination. Provides practical insight into subconscious/implicit bias, team diversity, and diversity management in the United States and abroad.  Goal is to learn to work with diverse groups to create a productive organization in which everyone feels included.

title: Materials of the Modern World
description: The properties and structure of everyday materials. A non-mathematical exploration of the relation between structure and resulting properties of metals, plastics, ceramics, glasses, and composite materials. Case studies of important materials in the modern and historical context.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: An excellent course for Non-STEM majors.Do you ever wonder what common, everyday objects are made of and why?Come take our class where we explore the properties and structure of what things are made of! A non-mathematical exploration of the relation between structure and resulting properties of metals, plastics, ceramics, glasses, and composite materials. Together, we'll explore case studies of important materials in the modern and historical context with hands-on demos and field trips!No exams, no math, just lots of hands-on activities.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Steel - The material of skyscrapers and bridges. So strong!Concrete - Along with steel, concrete is the material of building.Paper - Extra, extra, read all about it. Paper has been a medium to record, store, and share information for millennia.Chocolate - A tasty treat. Or is it something more?Ceramics - More than just your high school pottery class.Plastic - Plastics are a relatively new invention. So light, so bendy, so forever.Glass - How does it come in all shapes and sizes? And why does it crack?Silicon - How did we put lightning into a rock, force it to do math?
instructorProvidedContent.format: In-person.Both lecture and hands on activites.

title: Linear Optimization

title: Probability Theory
description: A rigorous introduction to probability theory at an advanced undergraduate level. Only a minimal amount of measure theory is used, in particular, the theory of Lebesgue integrals is not needed. It is aimed at math majors and Master's degree students, or students in other fields who will need probability in their future careers. Gives an introduction to the basics (Kolmogorov axioms, conditional probability and independence, random variables, expectation) and discusses some classical results with proofs (DeMoivre-Laplace limit theorems, the study of simple random walk on the one dimensional lattice, applications of generating functions).

title: Modern Algebra 1
description: Groups, normal subgroups, Cayley's theorem, rings, ideals, homomorphisms, polynomial rings, abstract vector spaces.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Groups are fundamental objects appearing throughout much of higher level math, and are nearly ubiquitous in pure mathematics. They are objects defined by very simple axioms, but the overall theory ends up being quite rich. We will begin by giving the definition and developing some important properties groups may have. The theory truly begins to shine once we start seeing how groups relate to each other, including subgroups, homomorphisms, and quotient groups. We will see how all of these relate in the context of the so-called Isomorphism Theorems. Finally, we will close the class by introducing a closely related concept called a ring. The course will (tentatively) cover material in Sections 1.1-1.7, 2.1-2.5, 3.1-3.3, 3.5, 4.1-4.4, 4.6, 5.1-5.2, 7.1-7.6. The Preliminaries in Sections 0.1-0.3 will also be assumed, and will be reviewed in class if needed.

enrollmentPrerequisites: Graduate/professional standing or declared in Mathematics VISP (graduate or dissertator)
title: Randomized Linear Algebra and Applications
description: Random solvers have been playing increasingly crucial roles in the modern computational tasks. The recent breakthroughs in applied and computational linear algebra that incorporate techniques of randomization have proven to be of great importance in modern applied math, computational sciences and data science, such as inverse problems, machine learning and scientific computing. The guiding principle is that one may greatly reduce computational and storage expenses at the cost of a small probability of failure. Systematic study of these modern methods of randomized linear algebra solvers will be provided, presenting mathematical backgrounds, algorithms, and concrete applications. Core theoretical topics include randomized Kaczmarz and its generalization to stochastic gradient descent, randomized singular value decomposition, random sketching, matrix completion, and compressive sensing, and corresponding applications.

title: Integer Optimization
description: Introduces optimization problems over integers, and surveys the theory behind the algorithms used in state-of-the-art methods for solving such problems. Special attention is given to the polyhedral formulations of these problems, and to their algebraic and geometric properties. Applicability of Integer Optimization is highlighted with applications in combinatorial optimization. Key topics include: formulations, relaxations, polyhedral theory, cutting planes, decomposition, enumeration.  Students are strongly encouraged to have knowledge of Linear Programming  (e.g., COMP SCI/I SY E/MATH 525), including algorithms, duality and polyhedral theory.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: In Integer Optimization problems, our task is to find one integral point, in a given polyhedral region, that minimizes a given linear objective function. Integer Optimization is a thriving area of discrete mathematics, which is applied nowadays to a multitude of human endeavors, thanks to high quality software. It was developed over several decades and is still evolving rapidly. The goal of this course is to present the mathematical foundations of Integer Optimization. We will survey the theory behind the algorithms used in state-of-the-art solvers. Special attention is given to the polyhedral representations of these problems, and to their algebraic and geometric properties. The broad applicability of Integer Optimization is highlighted with applications in combinatorial optimization and number theory.This course is proof based. Prerequisites are linear algebra, and a certain mathematical maturity.This course is based on the book Integer Programming by Michele Conforti, Gerard Cornuejols, and Giacomo Zambelli.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is an introduction to Lie algebras,with a focus on finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebras over the complex numbers.Topics will include: solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras,Cartan subalgebras, the Cartan decomposition, the semisimple case,the Killing form, the root system, the Weyl group, Dynkin diagrams, and Cartan matrices.Our main goal is to classify up to isomorphism the finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebras over the complex numbers.The lectures will be self contained, and no prior knowledge ofthe subject is assumed. The textbook isRoger Carter. Lie Algebras of Finite and Affine Type. Cambridge U. Press 2005I will follow the Carter text more or less,covering roughly Chapters 1--8. This course should be valuableto anyone interested in Lie theory, quantum groups,algebraic combinatorics, number theory, and special functions.The only prerequisite is a good understanding of linear algebra, such aseigenvalues, eigenspaces, bilinear forms, and tensor products.

The emphasis of the course is on becoming proficient with the software and capable of operating an FE package at a high level, including benchmarking and verifying the FE model using simple analytical checks. title: Women and Health in American History
description: Women as patients and as health professionals in America from the colonial period to the present.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: When did women in the United States start using birth control?  How does gender influence the experience of illness?  Were nineteenth-century women expected to enjoy sex?  How have women served their communities as healthcare providers and activists?  These questions and others guide our exploration of women and health in American history.  In particular, it explores the personal experiences and the medical views of women's life-cycle events, the role of women as health care providers and activists, and the effect of gender on the perception and experiences of illness.  The course also explores the diversity of expectations and experiences within the category of "woman.

input: Women and Health in American History
