instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Title: Psychological Effects of AIDive into the cutting-edge intersection of human behavior and technology in this hands-on, highly interactive online course! Across 14 dynamic units, you will directly engage with and evaluate the psychological effects of state-of-the-art AI tools from LLMs to therapy bots making active AI use an integral part of your learning experience (so if you are opposed to using AI, this course is likely not for you). Driven by proven active-learning principles rather than traditional lectures, exams, and textbooks, the curriculum is designed to help you build real-world skills and consistency through daily engagement; you will be expected to actively interact with course content and collaborate with your peers via online discussions and synchronous, text-based chat throughout the entire term. You will benefit from a built-in Flexibility Accommodation, no quizzes, tests, or exams, and open-access materials, giving you the opportunity to work ahead and manage your own success. To learn more, view the full Course Syllabus at https://go.wisc.edu/914ct5 and review the Course Contract at https://go.wisc.edu/sxzyw3 to ensure you are ready to hit the ground running.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course explores the neural mechanisms underlying learning processes and decision-making behaviors. Students will examine how the brain acquires, processes, and utilizes information to guide adaptive behavior in complex environments. The curriculum integrates perspectives from cognitive neuroscience, computational modeling, and behavioral economics to provide a comprehensive understanding of the biological basis of learning and choice. Key topics include:  Neural circuitry of reinforcement learning and reward processing Neuroplasticity mechanisms supporting memory formation Neuromodulatory systems in motivation and exploration Brain networks involved in value-based decision-making Computational models of learning and decision processes Neuroimaging and electrophysiological approaches to studying choice behavior  Through literature reviews, critical discussions, and experimental design projects, students will gain advanced knowledge of how neural systems support the acquisition of new information and its application to adaptive decision-making. The course will emphasize both fundamental principles and cutting-edge research in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Psych of Human-Animal Interact
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: In this capstone course, we will take an in-depth look at the diversity of human-animal relationships. We will examine the types of species that humans most often interact with, and why humans form bonds with some species and not others. We will also look at the specific nature of these relationships, such as how we interact differently with companion animals, wildlife, and animals in agricultural and research settings. We'll consider how we can better understand our connections with animals by examining these relationships from both human and animal perspectives. We'll also address how an understanding of communication across species can improve relationships for both sides. Finally, by investigating some hotly-debated topics (e.g., Is it ethical to eat meat? Use animals for biomedical research? Breed animals for extreme characteristics for sporting competitions?), we'll develop an appreciation for the fact that human-animal relationships are complex, and that a variety of strong opinions exist regarding many of these relationships.

title: Neural basis - cogn control
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Cognitive control refers to the flexible adaptation of behavior in response to changes in the environment. The recent tragedy at an airport in Miami, in which the pilots of the landing airplane first released the brakes and increased the throttle--as though to abort the landing and to take off again--then "changed their mind  a second time and reapplied the brakes and re-released the throttle, demonstrates a failure of cognitive control (with fatal consequences).  Impairments of cognitive control are often salient characteristics of psychopathology, including schizophrenia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), major depressive disorder (MDD), and addiction. Although decades of behavioral neurology and neuropsychology have implicated a critical role for the prefrontal cortex (PFC), new breakthroughs from systems- and computational neuroscience focused on nonhuman animals, from brain imaging studies of humans, and from AI are steadily enriching our understanding of, AND raising new questions about, cognitive control.  In this course, we will critically evaluate recent evidence from these literatures to gain a better understanding of cognitive control across multiple levels of analysis, including cellular- and circuit-level mechanisms, population-level dynamics, and computational principles. PSYCH 414 Cognitive Psychology and PSYCH 454 Behavioral Neuroscience are not required prerequisites for this course. However, completing either course beforehand may provide helpful background and preparation for the material covered in this course.

title: Intelligence: Cells,Brains&LMs
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: What do bacteria, beehives, brains, and chatbots have in common? In this seminar we will explore the idea that they are all doing versions of the same thing: building internal models to predict what will happen next. On this view, intelligence is not unique to animals or even life, but is a more general property of physical systems. We will discuss the evolution of intelligence and the major transitions that occurred when simpler systems joined forces to predict the world in more powerful ways. Drawing on cognitive science, biology, and machine learning, we will examine surprising parallels between brains and AI that help explain why AI got so good so fast, and how language models can serve as "model organisms  for studying human cognition.

title: Trust&SocialLearning-Childhood
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How do we come to know things we have never directly observed, such as that germs cause illness, that historical events occurred, or that certain actions are morally wrong? In this seminar, we will examine how children acquire knowledge and beliefs from other people, and how they decide whom and what to trust. Drawing on developmental psychology, we will ask how children evaluate the reliability of different sources of information; how children respond when what others say conflicts with their own observations or intuitions; and how social and cultural environments shape what children come to trust. The course will be discussion-based and will pair an accessible book with contemporary empirical articles. Students will be assessed through seminar participation, discussion leading, short papers, and a final presentation.

title: Legal Psych:Crim&Civil Issues
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The topic of Legal Psychology: Criminal & Civil Issues brings together two distinct disciplines -- that of empirical and clinical methods found in the area of psychology; and that of substantive and procedural methods found in the legal system when social problems call for decisions and dispositions.  The melding of social science and the legal system does not come easily.   The course is intended to assist students in learning more about how one system which is founded on empirical results can assist another system rooted in pragmatics and rules.  The course also focuses on problematic social issues where we see the combination of psychiatric systems, or psychological processes, working within overarching structures organized within the legal system and driven by the rule of law.

title: Cognition, Dvlpmnt&Instruction
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Cognition, Development, and InstructionIn this course, we will consider fundamental issues about learning from the perspectives of cognitive and developmental psychology, and we will consider implications for how we design and implement instruction. We will address the following questions: How do cognitive and developmental processes enable and influence learning and teaching? How can we use knowledge of cognition and cognitive development to promote and enhance learning? How can knowledge of cognition and cognitive development inform efforts to ensure equity in educational practices?  We will also consider connections between research and practice. How do practitioners learn about research findings in cognition and cognitive development? How can research in cognition and cognitive development lead to changes in instruction and in teaching practices? How can we ensure that researchers in cognition and cognitive development address questions that practitioners would like to have answered?

title: Current Topics:Schizophrenia
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course provides an advanced, in-depth study of schizophrenia. Readings will cover the nature of schizophrenia from personal, theoretical, and research perspectives. Assigned readings will provide insights regarding how schizophrenia is viewed by individuals affected with the disorder and their significant others as well as how it is viewed by mental health professionals. Theories regarding the etiology of the disorder will be discussed at length. The diagnostic ambiguity of the disorder will be discussed, spanning from a historical perspective (such as Kraepelin & Bleuler) to present controversies. Various research strategies (genetic, psychophysiological, biological approaches) for examining schizophrenia will be explored.

title: HowWeSee:MaterialPerception
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How We See: Vision Science Through the Lens of Material Perception"Is it cake?" The viral trend where hyperrealistic cakes fool viewers into thinking they're looking at a shoe, a handbag, or a roll of toilet paper works because our visual system is normally so good at telling materials apart that a single convincing fake can stop us in our tracks. This capstone course asks how vision pulls that off: how the brain turns patterns of light into knowledge of the physical world that guides thought and action. Using material perception as a lens onto vision science as a whole, we trace this ability from image cues and the earliest stages of visual processing through high-level physical reasoning, its neural underpinnings, and its development. Finally, we explore applications by examining how artists, graphics researchers, and designers each engineer what we see materials to be.

title: Clinical Supervision, Consultation, & Community Psychology
description: Introduction to supervision and consultation as unique practices. Focuses on purposes of clinical supervision and consultation, theoretical frameworks and models of supervision and consultation, the roles and relationships related to clinical supervision and consultation, and legal, ethical and multicultural issues associated with clinical supervision and consultation. Also includes skill development in building a working alliance with a supervisee; providing developmentally appropriate performance feedback; planning and communicating strategies to develop rapport and motivation to solve problems in clients; negotiation and mediation to reach consensus and move past barriers; understanding and appreciating the diverse cognitive, behavioral, and effective characteristics of supervisees; applying theoretical material to case presentations and related experiential activities.

description: Offers an introduction to health policy in the United States. Examines the ways in which government plays a role in the provision and regulation of health care. Explores key aspects of health policy including the economics of health care (e.g., paying for and access to health care; the health care workforce; the role of markets and consequences of market/government failures, public policy that supports or promotes health; health care outcomes, quality, and disparities; and tools for evaluation) and special topics of interest such as policy addressing risky health behaviors, aging, mental health, and the Affordable Care Act. title: Advancing Public Policy in a Divided America
description: America is divided: at home, at work, and even in the media. This is true politically, as well. Given this, public policy conflict is all around us. Seek to understand and contextualize the partisan conflict present in modern American politics and policymaking today and explore individual-level tactics that public policy leaders, practitioners, and advocates may use that acknowledge conflict and attempt to move public policymaking forward. Explore ways in which policy conflict can be understood, managed, and channeled for the betterment of public policy decision-making in a divided America.

title: Evidence-Based Policy Making
description: Facilitates skill-building to answer questions such as how policymakers use research and evidence in their jobs, how researchers can make their work useful to policymakers, and how legislative support staff and other stakeholders use research and evidence to shape policy. Explore the definition of "evidence-based", learn about different kinds of evidence and how it is used, and learn strategies for judging the rigor of research evidence. Also explore the difference between an education-based approach to working with policymakers versus an advocacy-based approach, learn strategies for communicating research to policy makers (including written and oral presentations and data visualizations), research examples of successful evidence-based policymaking efforts, and understand the limits of using research in policymaking.

title: Discovering What Works in Health Policy
description: Introduces the key conceptual and methodological tools used in public program evaluation, with an emphasis on understanding the forces that shape health and disease as well as various policy solutions. Introduces the Potential Outcomes Framework, also known as the Rubin Causal Model. Establishes the distinction between causation from correlation using counterfactual thinking. Explores a wide variety of experimental and quasi-experimental research methods used to estimate causal effects, including randomized experiments, regression, matching, instrumental variables, fixed effects, regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences, and synthetic control. Many of the causal inference methods that we discuss require statistical and computational training in order to implement. Focuses on the nontechnical conceptual, theoretical, and intuitive underpinnings of these methods that are most salient to policymakers.

title: Women, Gender, and Public Policy
description: Examine women, gender, and sex and their interactions with public policy. Learn about equality, liberty, feminism, and intersectionality, whether these concepts should be incorporated into policymaking, and if so, how that can be accomplished through gender mainstreaming and gender policy analysis. Examine specific policy areas focused on women's social, economic, and political citizenship to understand the causes and consequences of gender discrimination. These specific policy areas include poverty, women's labor market participation, immigration, reproductive rights, sexuality, gender-based violence, climate change, transportation, and peace and security. Understand how gender is embedded in the politics of policymaking, and what strategies have been successful in achieving more gender-equitable policies across the globe.

description: The diagnosis and management of congenital abnormality requires an understanding of the basic principles of embryology, imaging, and genetics. Replicating how patients enter the medical system, the didactic path begins with ultrasound diagnosis of fetal abnormality. The embryological basis of the fetal malformations will be examined. From this center, exposure to advanced diagnostics, such as fetal echocardiography, fetal MRI, and genetic testing and counseling. Topics extend to early postnatal care (pediatric genetics and pediatric radiology). Participate in the Meriter Perinatal Conference, learn about genetic approaches to the diagnosis of fetal malformation syndromes, and learn the rudiments of an obstetrical sonogram.

input: Imaging and Embryology: The Basic Science of Fetal Dysmorphogenesis

title: Intensive Training in Clinical Ultrasound: Physics, Anatomy, Skills, Translation to Practice
description: Intensive training in clinical ultrasound scanning, including the physical basis of the image generation, the resulting opportunities and limitations of this technique, and ultrasound anatomy and physiology. footnotes: Thomas Grist, MD, Chair (608) 263-8821

title: Physician Financial Wellness
description: Graduating medical students are faced with a wide array of financial planning and wellness challenges. The median medical student debt has continued to increase, and there is a corresponding proliferation of federal repayment and forgiveness options. Other financial planning needs, such as budgeting and insurance, also arise during this time of transition. A unique opportunity to learn key concepts around budgeting, investing, insurance, and negotiation through independent and group learning experiences. This format allows for better analysis on financial decisions and to understand the impact of these decisions on both current and future financial health and wellness.

title: Clinical Nuclear Medicine Elective

description: High-level procedural experience on a clinical interventional radiology service. title: Real Estate Investment Analysis and Presentation
description: Real-world capstone experience of the real estate investment process from project conception to asset disposition with particular focus on analysis and presentation. Provides exposure to best known methods and practices that private equity and development firms use to conduct market research, project selection, financial feasibility, regulatory review, design considerations, construction management, debt financing, equity placements, equity waterfalls, property management, asset management and disposition. title: Disability and the Criminal Justice System
description: Explores the interaction between the criminal justice system and disability. Explores common experiences of persons with disability such as limited access to community services, poverty, and homelessness and the connection of these experiences to mass incarceration. Explores federal disability rights laws and the implementation of these laws in education, legal, and incarceration settings. Introduction to criminal justice reform to address the experiences of persons with disabilities in this system.

title: Individuals with Disabilities
description: Designed to expand the knowledge base of future educators, clinicians, and society members to better understand and serve the diverse needs and interests of individuals with disabilities. Introduces the concept of disability as well as the field of special education. The history, etiology, and characteristics of specific categories of disability are examined, as are educational and other federally mandated programs designed to address the needs of both children and adults with disabilities. Topics germane to the study of disability and the field of special education are explored.

title: Positive Psychology and Well Being
description: Introduction to positive psychology, or the science of human strengths, mental health, and well-being. Covers theory and current research on positive psychology including concepts of optimism, flow, gratitude, and purpose in life. Positive psychology concepts are discussed within the context of health promotion, with an emphasis on minimizing the impact of illness and disability. Learn to apply positive psychology concepts in personal and professional contexts to cultivate fulfilling, healthy, and meaningful lives.

title: Religion and Popular Culture-Local and Global
description: Introduces religious studies through the lens of popular culture. In recent decades, many have predicted the demise of religion and the "death of God." Indeed, many seem to embrace science and rationality over faith and the supernatural, yet religion, religious language, religious themes permeate popular culture. This raises many questions: What is popular culture? What role is religion playing in it? How can we better understand popular culture using religious studies theory? Explores these questions through theme parks in the U.S. and Japan, Sports, Music, and tattoos.

input: Religion and Popular Culture-Local and Global

title: A History of the World in 20 Buildings
description: Why were the ancient Egyptians obsessed with building elaborate tombs? Was the Taj Mahal really a monument to love? Why do the Greeks want the Parthenon marbles returned? Was Frank Lloyd Wright "modern?" How have buildings reflected and shaped the historical forces of the modern age, from colonialism, to industrialization, to globalization? Take a journey through space and time and explore the history of the world through its great buildings. Learn to recognize, analyze, and question the dynamic interaction between culture, politics, religion, and architectural form. Perhaps more than any other visual art, architecture is alive. Buildings shapeshift over decades, centuries, millennia. They stand as both witnesses to and agents of historical change. Unpack our buildings' histories to reveal their role in our shared human story.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Why were the ancient Egyptians obsessed with building elaborate tombs? Was the Taj Mahal really a monument to love? How did building with iron change . . . well, everything!? Why did architects embrace Brutalism, and why have so many people come to hate it? How have buildings reflected and shaped the historical forces of the modern age, including colonialism, industrialization, and globalization? Take a journey through time and space as we explore the history of the world through monumental buildings. Learn to recognize, analyze, and question the dynamic interaction between culture, politics, religion, and architectural form. Perhaps more than any other visual art, architecture is alive. Buildings shapeshift over decades, centuries, millennia. They stand among us as both witness to and agents of historical change. Together, we will unpack our buildings' histories to reveal their role in our shared human story.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Lecture, discussions, short writing assignments, comparative analysis, reading

input: A History of the World in 20 Buildings

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Examine the literary corpus of the classical rabbinic period (70-640 C.E.) to understand how this group shaped the religion now known as Judaism. Interact closely with primary texts in translation to learn the operating principles of rabbinic logic, as well as how scholars (re)construct history based upon this corpus. Apply arguments made on the macro level (i.e., about rabbinic literature in general) to the micro level using drinks and drinking as a test case.

title: Early Christian Literature: Matthew-Revelation
description: An exploration of Christianity's charter documents in the light of what modern scholarship has discovered about the New Testament's sociohistorical context, composition, theologies, and presentations of Jesus.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This Fall, consider taking a course that builds transferable skills and teaches you how to continue learning beyond the course about a topic of historical, cultural and personal interest for millions of people. First-year students are welcome in this course (just email instructor for permission) as well as those with more college experience.This course introduces the historical study of the origins of Christianity, primarily through examination of selected writings of the New Testament. It focuses on how these sources reflect what happened and what people believed and did in early Christian communities. Its first goal is acquainting students with what these sources actually say. Its second is challenging students to develop their understanding of what these sources might have meant to the first-century communities for which they were written. We will not cover every New Testament text, but we will focus on several key texts and on developing skills you can use for further study of the New Testament beyond this class.No prior background in the academic study of the New Testament is required for this course. I recognize that students come with a range of familiarity with the New Testament and am eager to help students who may be worried about their lack of it. For everyone regardless of prior knowledge, regular preparation and active participation are the surest ways to achieve success in the course.This course focuses on developing skills that students can use for further study in variety of fields while developing an understanding of early Christian communities and literature. It is based in conversational lectures and discussions supported with technology and a clear, engaging textbook.Graded exercises encourage development and improvement over the course and should be low-anxiety vehicles if students prepare as instructed and participate consistently. Students with a range of career and field interests and a range of preparation have taken this course successfully. Meets LIT requirement.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Unit 1 introduces historical, cultural and religious contexts important for understanding the New Testament and early Christianity. It covers the development of the New Testament and types of NT texts.Unit 2 covers the GospelsUnit 3 covers the Letters of PaulUnit 4 covers other writings, including Revelation and 1 early Christian text that is not in the NT.

Some exercises and discussion will be built into the class time.Exams consist of multiple choice, fill-in and short answer items. They are take-home, open-book and not timed. You will have a range of time to work on them before the submission deadline.Excellent participation can improve the grade; unexcused absences and lack of engagement can lower it.

title: Early Christian Literature: Pauline Christianity
description: By conventional reckoning, Paul was a major contributor to the development of Christianity. Analyzes both Paul's and other contemporary writings to assess the extent to which he contributed to the development of the early church.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Sophomore standing pre-req can be waived --- please contact the instructor for permission.HUM and LIT credit. This course is an introduction to the life and thought of Paul and the religious communities which he belonged to, formed or encountered, primarily via a thorough examination of "Pauline  literature of the 1st and early 2nd centuries. Secondarily, we will examine some later interpretations of Paul as they help our understanding of Paul and other first-century Jesus followers in their historical context and some aspects of Paul's legacy. No prior background in the academic study of early Christianity is required for this course. It is, however, a 300-level course and thus requires that demonstration of engagement with the course and development of critical thinking about the material exceed what might be expected in a lower-level course. I recognize that students come with a range of familiarity with the New Testament and am eager to help students who may be worried about their lack of it. For everyone regardless of prior knowledge, regular preparation and review and active participation are the surest ways to achieve success in the course.The course grade is based on open book quizzes, participation, and open book take-home exams.  Quizzes and exams are not timed; students must submit them by a set submission time. They usually have at least 24 hours for quizzes and longer for exams. The final exam is due at the end of the designated exam period for this course, but students may access it the last week of class and fit it into their own schedules up to the submission time.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: First, we'll explore the Jewish and Greco-Roman contexts of early Christianity. Second, we'll learn how to read a first-century letter-- very important for understanding what Paul says. Third, most of the course will focus on Paul's own writings in the New Testament. We will also discuss some early writings about or attributed to Paul and in a few cases we will discuss the diversity of interpretation over time of Paul's writing. In small discussion groups several times in the term (within the allotted 75-minute session times) student will consider Pauline passages of significance over time and employ short scholarly sources to help understand these in early Christian contexts.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Lecture with some classes based in small group discussion that counts toward participation. The course grade is based on open book quizzes, participation, and open book take-home exams.  Quizzes and exams are not timed; students must submit them by a set submission time. They usually have at least 24 hours for quizzes and longer for exams. The final exam is due at the end of the designated exam period for this course, but students may access it the last week of class and fit it into their own schedules up to the submission time.

title: Religion and Politics
description: Explores the relationships and interactions between religion and politics from a comparative perspective. Explores how religious institutions, elites, states, and societies interact, and how these relationships shape political behavior and outcomes across contexts. Analyze questions such as: Why does religion remain politically salient in an increasingly secular world? What drives religious nationalism and extremism? How do democratic and authoritarian states engage with religion? How does religion influence voting behavior? How do religious movements inform the global rise in populism? Integrate theoretical frameworks for religion and policies and cutting-edge research on American and global cases.

title: Risk Analytics and Behavioral Science
description: Learning to effectively navigate uncertainty is a key issue for all areas of business and especially for those engaged in explicit risk-management activities.  The skills for success in these environments include knowing how to formulate the right questions to ask, how to identify the information that is valuable for answering those questions, understanding how to process incoming information to distinguish signal from noise, and how to use that information to put structure to uncertain environments so that one can take good calculated risks.  This collective set of skills are at the heart of "decision analysis", which is a structured rational approach to making decisions under uncertainty.

title: Catastrophe Risk and Reinsurance
description: Examines market and public policy approaches for managing catastrophe risks. Describes how catastrophes such as hurricanes, wildfires, severe convective storms, terrorist attacks, cyberattacks, environmental disasters (e.g., oil spills), and epidemics create societal challenges by affecting many households and firms concurrently. Covers catastrophe models, which are used to estimate the potential losses from these events by simulating thousands of possible disaster scenarios. Describes the markets for reinsurance and insurance linked securities, how these products work, and the types of risks they cover. Compares public-private partnership models across countries for managing severe risks such as public terrorism reinsurance and cyclone risk pools to glean insights from these varying approaches.

title: Humans and Other Animals in Nordic Literature and Film
description: Engage with major questions in the field of animal studies while studying a variety of Nordic texts that center the animal, including novels, tales, and feature and documentary films. Through fiction, film, and theory, tackle questions such as: What distinguishes humans from animals? Can humans speak for animals, and should they try? And, what can Nordic literature and film teach us about humans and other animals in the Anthropocene?

title: Methods of Social Work Research
description: Examine foundational principles and processes involved in social work research to promote critical consumption of research that informs generalist social work knowledge base and practice. Evaluate empirical research to apply concepts and grasp strengths and limitations of various research designs. Gain foundational skills to engage in research activities that support evidence-based social-work practice. Address how questions are transformed into basic and applied researchable questions and the various considerations pertaining to conceptualization, measurement, sampling, and implementation of various qualitative and quantitative research designs, with particular attention to evaluation of social work practice and programs. Review social science research paradigms that shape researchers' worldview and methods, ethics and professional conduct in social work research, and the use of research as a tool to promote social work values and achieve social justice aims.

title: Reproductive Justice
description: Topics will vary, reflecting current issues and trends in social justice, social welfare, and social work.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This special topics elective course offers a holistic overview of the politics of reproductive health, rights, and justice through an anti-oppressive lens. It integrates perspectives from diverse scholars and activists to examine a wide range of topics including, but not limited to, access to abortion and contraception; the criminalization of pregnancy; forced sterilizations; and maternal mortality. To do so, we will critically analyze how systems of oppression including racism, colonization, mass incarceration, ableism, and environmental destruction, among others are used to govern bodies and reproduction. Importantly, we will also explore past and ongoing efforts to resist systems of oppression and fight for a more just world, including the role of social workers in supporting or constraining access to reproductive justice.

title: Social Change in Contemporary South Korea
description: An exploration of social continuity and change of contemporary South Korea. Covers different institutions of a society - political, economic, and societal/cultural spheres. Incorporates material from anthropology, sociology, political science, economics, and law. Focus on South Korea after the division of the 'two Koreas'.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: 1.Instructors and CommunicationsClassroom: TBDClass: Mondays 2:25PM-5PM* Instructor: Eunsil Oh (eunsil.oh@wisc.edu)  Office: Social Sciences Building Unit 8116BOffice Hours: Mondays (11:30AM -- 12:30PM) or by appointmentEmail Policy & Office HoursIf you have a logistic question, please first consult the syllabus and Canvas. The best way to communicate with me is via email (eunsil.oh@wisc.edu). Try writing your email with a proper title and greeting and make sure to write your name as you prefer to be called. Please show your respect by being professional through email and avoid being too casual (i.e. Hi there, Hey, Ms., etc). Email me with the course number (i.e. Soc 336) in the subject line to talk about accommodations or to schedule an appointment if my office hours do not work for you. I will respond to emails within 48 hours during the workday (9AM-5PM). If you have to miss a lecture, please contact the professor and contact a fellow student for notes. If you will be missing more than four lectures, email the professor. Also, if you have any questions or comments about course material, it is best to sign up and to visit me during my office hour.   2.Course Description and Lecture Overview Course Description Using theories and concepts from sociology, in particular, theories explaining social continuity and change, this course provides a social science perspective of contemporary South Korea. Course contents are divided based on different institutions of a society - political, economic, and societal/cultural spheres. This is a sociology course, but the nature and orientation of the course are interdisciplinary, incorporating readings in anthropology, sociology, political science, economics, and law. Timeframe wise, we focus on South Korea (hereafter, Korea) after the division or the 'two Koreas.'This course pays careful attention to the intersection of multiple structures of inequality such as gender, race/ethnicity, citizenship, class, and sexuality. Also, critically examining the modernization theory that assume linear progression of societies, idea that sex and gender are fixed biological realities, this course discusses what sociologists have contributed to our understanding of social change; continuity; and contemporary South Korea. Each class will consist of half lecture and half discussion. During lectures, the assigned readings are placed in a larger framework. During our discussion time, we are going to understand, apply, and creatively develop sociological concepts using the case of contemporary Korea. We will utilize various means including Canvas and zoom to maximize our learning process. In addition, we will do small group exercises (pairing to grouping) in class to facilitate discussions. This will allow you to better work through challenging concepts and theories, and to apply these theories to your own experiences. Come prepared to participate and to share your thoughts and questions with the rest of the class.Lecture OverviewIntroduction W1:  IntroductionSociological Toolkits to Understand Social Change Postcolonial Lens and Going Beyond the Western EyePart1: Political Organization and Social Change W2:  Gender Politics in Post-war S. instructorProvidedContent.format: 4.Course Workload and Assignments/ExamsCourse WorkloadThis is a 3-credit course. In accordance with the UW-Madison credit hour policy standards, this credit load is equivalent to the following: o150 minutes of classroom instruction (lecture and discussions)oA minimum of 6 hours of out of class student work each week (on average). oYour readings and assessment tasks have been selected accordingly.Assignments and ExamsPointsWeekly Memo and Participation200Weekly Quiz200Field Statement -Graded progress report (1) -Graded progress report (2) -Field Statement30050100150Discussion Leading Project-Graded progress report (1) - revision-Graded progress report (2) -- slides/outlines-Final presentation 300100100100Total 1000Attendance (Impact on the Final Grade). Attendance is mandatory and there will be free two passes, meaning you can feel free to use your free passes. More than two absences will result in your final grade falling by one-half of a grade (e.g. from A to AB, B to BC, etc.). Weekly Memo and Participation (200). All students -- regardless of the anticipated attendance - have to upload a weekly memo. In the memo, include 1) a synthesis (limiting to 250 words per reading) of all the readings for the upcoming week and 2) two topics (each with a question and a rationale behind your question, limiting to 250 words per topic) to discuss further in class. The memos are due by 5pm Friday (before the upcoming class). Please check specific prompt for each week before submitting. The weekly posting starts from Week 1 (due January 24th). Based on the questions uploaded by the students, the instructor will formulate a discussion flow for the last 30-40 mins of the class. Your participation grade will include overall participation in class as well as how you engage in the discussion. Also, persistent tardiness will have a negative effect on your evaluation. Your active participation is essential for the success of a course of this kind. Please refer to Canvas for the guidelines to have productive discussion. Weekly Quiz (200). There will be weekly quizzes composed of 6 questions. These quizzes will mainly be on the course readings, and lectures. These quizzes will take place every Monday at 2:30pm in class (if you cannot attend the class, you can still take the quiz online from home) via Canvas. Our first quiz will take place on our Week 2 (February 3rd). Field Statement (300). Write a 8-10 pages-long (double-spaced) field statement that synthesizes (not summarizes) past, present, and future studies on a specific topic of your choice. This is an exercise to understand the landscape of the literature on a topic and to systematically synthesize the knowledge that has been accumulated. There will be two graded-progress reports that will be due before submitting the final version. Detailed guidelines are uploaded in the Canvas (Under Files). Final product due 5pm on March 21st.K-Project Final Presentation: (300). Students will continue to work on their field statement starting with revising their statement based on the instructor's comments. Then, you will prepare to present the contents of your field statement to your classmates on the last week of our class (on April 28th). title: Law, Sexuality, & Society
description: Examines the legal and social development and implications of laws governing sexual behavior, human reproduction, media, privacy, and topics related to sexuality, sex and gender. Includes historical analyses of laws connected to present day regulations of sexuality, demonstrating the origins of many of the world's most frequently debated civil rights issues. Chief focus on the United States legal system, with some content including examinations of institutions around the world. Investigates taken-for-granted knowledge and assumptions about sexuality and look at legal, cultural and social constructions of sex in society. Covers intersectional social implications, including race, (dis)ability, class, etc. Topics include: obscenity, pornography, sex work, sexual surrogacy, birth control, abortion, sex education, sexual violence, sex offenders, sexual citizenship rights, trans and intersex legal topics.

title: Crime, Gender and Justice
description: Focuses on the intersection between gender, crime and justice from a cross-cultural perspective. The gendered nature of the criminal justice system, female experiences of crime, prosecution and incarceration as well as the extent to which women are victims, offenders, and participants in the criminal justice system will be explored. Special emphasis will be placed on the theoretical implications of offending behavior and the intersection of gender with sexuality, race, ethnicity and class. The goal of this course is to provide a foundation for critically assessing the often controversial issues surrounding race, gender, crime, and criminal justice in society.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: SOC 955Advanced Qualitative Methods(Writing Papers and Dissertations with Qualitative Data)Eunsil OhPrerequisitesStudents must arrive with a collected qualitative data set (interviews, fieldnotes, or a document corpus) and must circulate a rough full draft, 20--40 pages, before Week 8. A master's thesis, comps paper, or dissertation chapter in progress qualifies. Co-authored work is permitted if co-authors are informed it will be discussed in class.Course DescriptionThis seminar teaches doctoral students to turn qualitative data (interviews, ethnographic fieldnotes, and texts for content, discourse, or archival analysis) into publishable articles and dissertation chapters. It runs in two parts. Part I (Weeks 1--7) treats the major qualitative traditions as ways of writing, not only ways of collecting data: each week pairs a tradition with a concrete writing move applied to the student's own data. Part II (Weeks 8--14) is a manuscript studio: students revise a full draft section by section toward submission, review one another's work, and practice the review-and-revision cycle.From the first week, the course is framed around one goal: making your work into a publication and finding its home in the discipline.Learning ObjectivesBy the end of the course, students will be able to: Distinguish how interactionist, interpretive, cultural-relational, extended-case, and feminist/Indigenous traditions build arguments from qualitative data. Position their own project within one tradition and anticipate how a rival tradition would read it. Code, select, and present qualitative evidence (quotes, scenes, documents) with stated prevalence and attention to variation. Write each section of a qualitative article: abstract, analytic introduction, methods, findings, and conclusion. Review qualitative manuscripts and respond to reviewers and editors. Plan the path from article or chapter to dissertation and book.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Course FormatPart I meetings split in two: a seminar on the week's tradition (first half), then a writing lab where students apply its writing move to their own data (second half). Part II meetings open with a short lecture or journal-editor visit, then workshop two manuscripts per session. title: Water and People
description: Water is central to the functioning of planet Earth and is influential to shaping many historical and present-day cultures across the globe. As humans increase their impact on Earth's water cycle, our understanding of the multiple roles of water becomes critical to finding sustainable strategies for human and ecosystem health. Explore different perspectives around cultural significance of, engagement with, and access to water, with particular focus to case studies from the United States. Identify the human influence on water quality and quantity in a changing global climate, from local, regional, and global perspectives, and how different racial and ethnic communities in the United States are differentially impacted.

title: Human Transformations of Earth Surface Processes
description: Takes an earth systems approach to explore the role of human societies in shaping earth surface processes from local to global scales. We address how alterations to our landscapes and waterways affect biological, physical and chemical interactions among our biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere. We discuss methods used to distinguish the "human impact" from background variability.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: COURSE SYNOPSISThis course takes an earth systems approach to explore the role of human societies in shaping earth surface processes from local to global scales. We address how alterations to our landscapes and waterways affect biological, physical and chemical interactions among our biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere. We discuss methods used to distinguish the "human impact" from background variability.FULL COURSE DESCRIPTIONThe influence of human activities is now recognized to extend all over the globe, which has led some researchers to propose renaming our current geologic epoch the Anthropocene, for the "Age of Humans.  This course takes an earth systems approach to explore the role of human societies in shaping earth surface processes. We examine how alterations to earth's land surface and subsurface and waterways affect biological, physical and chemical interactions among our biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere. In particular, we focus on the methods used to distinguish the "human impact" from background variability. We also address historical and current barriers to equity in the practice of science. Topics covered include: approaches to understand earth system interactions, major alterations to biogeochemical cycles and geomorphic processes, biophysical consequences of changes in land cover and land use, urban biogeochemistry, geoengineering, diversity and equity in science. For each topic, we delve into the biophysical science behind each relevant process and discuss different approaches for characterizing and quantifying changes due to human activities. We explore the recent literature to evaluate how biogeochemical and earth system models incorporate human influences to better understand feedbacks between the earth surface, atmosphere and climate.At the end of the semester, students should be able to: Synthesize how major global biogeochemical cycles and earth surface processes are influenced by human activities at different spatial and temporal scales; Identify positive and negative feedbacks among the biosphere, geosphere and atmosphere at different temporal and spatial scales; Explain how different methods are used to characterize and quantify human effects on the earth system; Describe barriers to and strategies to advance equity in the practice of earth system science;  Interpret research findings in peer-reviewed literature; Summarize research for different audiences.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Discussion-based course. Assessments are based on assignments and projects.

input: Human Transformations of Earth Surface Processes

title: Border and Migration Studies of Latinx America
description: Drawing from cultural studies, border studies, migration and race theory, explores through cultural and literary texts the social and political issues regarding migration, contact zones, transculturation, and/or diaspora. Considers the various meanings of the word "border" or "frontera". What is a border geographically speaking? What does it mean in political and legal terms? How do we conceive the border in cultural, literary, linguistic, political, judicial, and personal ways? What is like to live on the border or on the margins? It is said that the border is a contact zone, a meeting point, a way to transfer and share information, an invitation to (in)tolerance and ex/inclusion. Read texts from history, politics, cultural anthropology, literature, and theatre to grasp the vast understanding of what is life on the border. Focus on the humanities, paying close attention to how visual artists (theater, performance, documentaries) understand and confront life on the border.

input: Border and Migration Studies of Latinx America

title: The Beautiful Game: Cultural Politics of Soccer
description: In the last three decades, soccer has been transformed from being a very popular game in certain regions of the world to what is now considered a multicultural phenomenon. Soccer has caught the attention of not only the international media but also of disciplines such as sociology, psychology and cultural studies, as well as art forms like photography and filmmaking, digital art and comics. However, more than just a form of entertainment soccer is considered a national sport in most of Latin America. How is it that a game that originated in 19th Century England was adopted by a large and varied culture as a matter of national identity and pride? Focuses on the history of soccer and on soccer as a cultural phenomenon intimately linked to nation building and to notions of progress and national self-image.

title: Spanish Phonetics
description: Practice course for improvement of pronunciation, and introduction to transcription and phonetic and phonemic analysis.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Spanish 320 is an advanced practice course that emphasizes improvement of pronunciation through a clear and concise introduction to phonetic and phonemic analysis in Spanish. We see how to produce the sounds of Spanish, their logical groupings/classifications and the way in which they change according to their phonetic environment. We also concentrate on applied pronunciation practice in the form of a variety of exercises and activities, and we are introduced to the phonetic transcription of Spanish language texts. We will explore the phonetic contrasts between English and Spanish in order to increase our awareness of their major articulatory differences and to improve our Spanish pronunciation. Summary analyses of some of the pronunciation differences across various Spanish dialects are explored as we work our way through the Spanish sound system.This 3-credit, "C  type, elementary level class meets in-person for a 50-minute class period Monday, Wednesday and Friday weekly during the semester and carries the expectation that students will work on course learning activities (reading, homework, oral activities, studying, etc.) for a minimum of 2 hours out of the classroom for every class period (for a minimum of 6 hours outside of class per week).IMPORTANT NOTE: Attendance is required.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Each week we will study approximately one chapter from the textbook. Chapter content will be summarized and explained with examples and additional pertinent information. Afterwards, we will utilize various in-class practice exercises to better understand and apply the acquired knowledge. Homework is comprised primarily of the phonetic transcription of a specific text and of oral practice of said text both in class and via recordings submitted in Canvas. There are several short, written and oral quizzes throughout the course, in addition to a final comprehensive exam.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Small class with intensive class participation. Written and oral exams. Written homework. Textbook and some additional readings.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Words and Images in Modern SpainIn this interdisciplinary course, students will explore a variety of contexts in which the interaction between words and images is essential to produce meaning. We will examine texts about images, texts within images, images as illustrations alongside texts, and texts and images that appear in different contexts but share a historical moment. Students will: 1) study the differences and similarities between literary and visual forms of communication, 2) discuss the relations between them with respect to specific case studies (periodicals, poetry, narratives, paintings, comics, films, and video games), and 3) present their research about topics of their own interest. The course will combine critical readings with a collaborative, workshop-oriented approach throughout the semester. Although modern and contemporary Spain is the main focus of the course, students are welcome to explore Latin American contexts and organize projects around them. Tangential topics within education, economics, pedagogy, psychology, sociology, marketing, STEM, or the arts are welcome! Come and have fun!   NOTE: All readings and materials will be available online through Canvas.

title: Race, Religion and Ethnicity in the Age of Empire
description: Drawing mainly from early modern Spanish and Colonial texts, covers encounters and relations with different forms of "otherness". Move from America to Spain and across the Mediterranean world to Istanbul, from the late 15th century to the 17th. Discuss issues of race, ethnicity, and religious affiliation. Spain's long history of relations between Muslims, Jews and Christians will form a backdrop to interactions with Amerindians, sub-Saharan Africans, Jews, Moriscos, Gypsies, North African Muslims and Turks. One of the millions of slaves during this period was Miguel de Cervantes, author of Don Quixote. He and many other writers would reflect profoundly on questions of "otherness" in works that would have universal implications and continue to connect with our concerns in the 21st century.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Networks and graph-structured data describe relationships between entities, such as peer-peer friendships among individuals in a social network, country-country trade relations in economics, or brain region-region co-activation in neuroimaging studies. In recent years, advances in data acquisition technologies and interest in the study of complex, interdependent systems have led to the proliferation of network datasets throughout the natural sciences, physical sciences, and engineering. This course provides an introduction to statistical methods, theory, and applications for network data analysis. Topics include network summary statistics and visualization, random graphs and latent variable models, clustering and dimensionality reduction, methods of estimation and hypothesis testing, spectral techniques, and computation in R. This course emphasizes real-world examples and applications.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
description: Special topics of interest in undergraduate students.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Develops the practice and theory of interpretable machine learning, with an emphasis on statistical problem solving through case studies. Topics include competing criteria for interpretability; linear and logistic regression as interpretable baselines; intrinsically interpretable nonlinear models such as Gaussian processes and decision trees; variable importance and Shapley values; connections to veridical data science principles. Also examines interpretability in artificial intelligence, covering probes, and concept activation, and sparse autoencoder analysis, with implications for model control and AI safety. Gain practical experience implementing methods and critically evaluating interpretability outputs.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: An in-depth analysis of the theory and computation of kernel methods, with particular emphasis on Gaussian processes, splines, reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, and foundational machine learning results like the kernel trick and representer theorem. The course will begin with detailed coverage of Gaussian process regression and the interplay between kernel design and the associated theory of best linear predictors, then transition to concrete mathematical connections and equivalences with splines and radial basis functions, and finish with modern machine learning tools. Throughout the semester, details for practical numerical implementations and example applications will be emphasized. Assignments will take the form of small reports or class presentations on specialized topics that will be collected into a growing reference for all students.

title: Bayesian Statistics
description: Introduces the theory, methods, and computational procedures needed to perform advanced Bayesian data analyses. Predictive and decision-theoretic motivations including subjective probability, risk, admissibility, and exchangeability; highlights key components of Bayesian analysis (i.e., prior, likelihood, posterior, and predictive distributions) within standard parametric models and advanced hierarchical and multilevel models; demonstrates the iterative process of model specification, implementation, criticism, and revision with applied case studies; implements computational techniques (e.g., Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference) in modern probabilistic programming languages.

description: Special topics in statistics at the graduate level. Subject matter varies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: An in-depth analysis of the theory and computation of kernel methods, with particular emphasis on Gaussian processes, splines, reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, and foundational machine learning results like the kernel trick and representer theorem. The course will begin with detailed coverage of Gaussian process regression and the interplay between kernel design and the associated theory of best linear predictors, then transition to concrete mathematical connections and equivalences with splines and radial basis functions, and finish with modern machine learning tools. Throughout the semester, details for practical numerical implementations and example applications will be emphasized. Assignments will take the form of small reports or class presentations on specialized topics that will be collected into a growing reference for all students.

title: Surgery Internship Preparation
description: High-yield topics that a surgery intern should know to start of residency. Routine communication skills  needed in residency, including writing comprehensive orders and effectively handing off patients. Communication and teamwork skills with healthcare team members. Communication and interpersonal skills in difficult situations, including obtaining informed consent, talking with parents of patients who choose to decline recommended management options, and disclosing complications. Based on the national Educational Curriculum that was developed by the American College of Surgeons, American Program Director Society, and the Association for Surgical Education, which focuses on focused on essential skills for medical students and PGY-1 residents to successfully navigate the first year of surgical residency.

title: Optimizing Value, Quality and Safety in Healthcare
description: An in-depth understanding of the key concepts of value, quality and safety is critical to the education of future physicians. The majority of adverse events experienced by hospitalized patients occur in surgery. Surgery offers the ideal setting to explore these three components critical to improving the US healthcare system. Examine factors that influence the care we provide and critically consider the value of this care. Observe efforts to improve value in surgery focusing on quality, safety and appropriate utilization of critical resources and consider areas for improvement. Follow patients in all processes of care from clinic, to the operating room, through their postoperative course, to discharge, and consider how important measures to secure safety and quality are encountered and impact care in the clinical arena. Consider price and allocation of scarce resources. Gather information for their analysis of the patient experience.

input: Optimizing Value, Quality and Safety in Healthcare

title: Multidisciplinary Approaches to Colon Cancer Prevention/Treatment
description: Explore the reasons behind failure of colorectal cancer screening programs. Learn the standard of care for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of colorectal cancer. Focus on all facets of the disease, with active engagement in dialogue to improve screening programs for colorectal cancer. Learn to identify methods to improve medical care and population health. Explore background studies to integrate emerging information on individual's biologic and genetic risk with population-level factors when deciding upon prevention and treatment options. Work with the various members of the healthcare team involved in treating colorectal cancer and educate the public on the importance of colorectal cancer screening.

title: The Science of Obesity and Diabetes
description: The science of diabetes and obesity as it correlates to the clinical setting. The history of endocrinology and discovery of insulin will provide the basis for understanding hormonal mechanisms controlling fuel metabolism and how these processes become dysfunctional in different disease states. Topics will include pancreatic and extrapancreatic control of metabolism, and diseases linked with obesity, including PCOS, type 2 diabetes, and cancer. Lifestyle, medical, and surgical treatments of obesity and diabetes, including pharmacologic mechanisms of insulin and non-insulin diabetes therapeutics and bariatric surgery, will be highlighted. The public health perspective will shine light on societal factors that influence obesity and diabetes care. Provides an advanced scientific foundation with which to approach evidence-based care and treatment of individuals with obesity and/or diabetes.

input: The Science of Obesity and Diabetes

title: Common Anorectal Diseases
description: The diagnosis and treatment of common anorectal diseases in the context of anatomical and physiological basis as it correlates to the clinical setting. The medical and surgical treatment of anorectal disorders will be discussed from the historical background to modern management algorithms. Topics will include fissures, perirectal abscess, fistula-in-ano, external and internal hemorrhoidal diseases, pruritus ani, fecal incontinence, rectal prolapse, obstructive defecation, sexually transmitted infections, and various anorectal manifestations of irritable bowel disease. Symptomatic presentation and natural progression of each of these disease processes will be discussed. Provide a sound scientific foundation with which to approach evidence-based diagnosis, triage, and treatment of patients with acute versus chronic anorectal disorders.

title: In Translation: The Drama of Henrik Ibsen
description: Often considered "the father of modern drama," the Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen (1828-1906) is a major figure of world literature whose dramatic works remain fascinating and globally influential, both as texts and through performance and adaptation. Read and discuss Ibsen in English translation, with a focus on Ibsen's historical contexts, dramatic techniques, social and political thought, and the reception and adaptation of his work in modern culture.

title: Postcolonial Theatre: Drama, Theory and Performance in the Global South
description: Study of drama, dramatic theory and theatrical practices in postcolonial cultures, primarily in Asia, Africa and the Caribbean. Considers status of drama/theatre in postcolonial studies and focuses on issues of form, language, intertextuality, trans-culturation, material organization and reception.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The formal end of European colonialism in various parts of Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean since the 1940s has initiated a new phase in literary-cultural production that is now widely recognized as both chronologically and qualitatively "postcolonial.  For more than four decades, however, the field of postcolonial studies has been dominated by the genres of fiction, non-fiction, and theory, deflecting attention away from the genres of drama, theatre, and performance. The main objective of this course, therefore, is to consider post-independence urban drama and theatre in such locations as India, Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, and the Caribbean as specifically postcolonial cultural formations that "perform  (rather than merely textualize) the tensions definitive of postcolonialism. The primary materials for the course will focus on such leading postcolonial playwrights as Wole Soyinka, Derek Walcott, Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Femi Osofisan, the Sistren Theatre collective, Ama Ata Aidoo, Mustapha Matura, Utpal Dutt, and Girish Karnad.For students unfamiliar with postcolonial studies, the class will provide an introduction to major theoretical issues and problems while also covering a range of significant authors. For students already familiar with postcolonial issues and interested in theatre, it will offer new perspectives on genre, language, textuality, intertextuality, sociopolitical contexts, performance, and reception.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: The course will begin by identifying key issues in colonial and postcolonial studies that appear more or less consistently in all the countries covered by our reading: Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Trinidad and Tobago, Martinique, Jamaica, and India. The discussion of each play and playwright will take into account the specific history and politics of each postcolonial location, producing carefully contextualized analyses. Students will write two medium-length papers, take mid-term and final exams, and participate actively in class discussions throughout the semester.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Lecture, discussion, in-class writing, presentations.

title: Welcome to Your Urban Future
description: We live in an increasingly urban world and anticipate that 70% of the world's population will live in urban areas by 2050. For many of us, our shared future experience will be urban and interconnected. How can we make the future of urban areas as bright as possible for everyone? The answer begins with us. Building equitable and sustainable urban futures for everyone will require the efforts of a diverse group of people from many disciplines, backgrounds, and ways of thinking. Guest presenters introduce different disciplines and perspectives through major themes related to the planning and design of urban systems and environments. Imagine and develop your plan to effect positive change in an urban area focused on relevant topics like community food systems, water conservation, multimodal and active transportation, affordable housing, and urban nature.

description: Investigates urbanization as a general process, as well as the resulting contemporary physical, social, cultural and political- economic forms of cities. Emphasis will be placed on the history and current forms of spatial and social segregation of cities by race, class, ethnicity, and gender. The myriad ways that cities have addressed the tensions emerging from this history of spatial and social segregation will be highlighted. Further, emphasis will be placed on understanding the experiences of those most-affected by historical and continuing segregation.

title: Energy Markets
description: Energy resources are an essential element of the world's business, political, technical and environmental landscape. Analytic tools provided by the discipline of economics expands our understanding of this critical issue. Energy supply markets reviewed include both fossil fuels and renewable resources. Energy demand sectors include residential, commercial, industrial and transportation. Electricity represents an intermediate energy market. The interactions among these markets participants indicate how scarce resources are allocated among competing needs in the world economy.

title: Animal Biology Laboratory
description: General concepts of animal biology at an introductory level emphasizing the evolutionary relationships between animals. Learn about general body plans and strategies used to accomplish the basic tasks of staying alive in major animal groups using preserved and live animals. Study the diversity within each group of animals by integrating the body plans with the lifestyle and ecology of animals. Dissections of earthworm, freshwater mussel, squid, sea star, and rat aid the study of these general principles.

title: Tiny Earth: Antibiotic Discovery Research
description: Learn basic methodology in scientific research and discovery, including laboratory techniques, quantitative reasoning, scientific communication, and collaboration. Gain hands-on laboratory experience working with microbes to test original hypotheses concerning the discovery of potential antibiotic compounds while addressing the world's antibiotic resistance crisis by contributing data to the global "Tiny Earth" network of researchers to advance potential drug development. Tiny Earth seeks to encourage students to pursue careers in science through real-world, applied research experiences and aims to address a worldwide health threat of the diminishing supply of effective antibiotics by "student-sourcing antibiotic discovery." Concurrent enrollment in ZOOLOGY/BOTANY/BIOLOGY 152 is required for permission to enroll.

title: Genetics of Human History
description: Covers a range of topics related to human genetics and evolution. Explores questions about what genetic differences between humans tell us about our species' evolutionary and demographic history, and conversely, how our history has shaped the genetic diversity of people living today. At a time of rapidly increasing ability to sequence huge numbers of genomes such questions play a central role in understanding how genetics impacts individuals' disease risks, how to interpret reported ancestry and family history from direct-to-consumer genotyping kits, and how genetics can (or importantly, cannot) inform descriptions of human diversity and concepts of race. Includes topics of diversity and inclusion in genomics studies, with a focus on the application and limits of results obtained from one group to our understanding of other groups.

title: Ecosystem Simulation Modeling
description: Introduces process-based mathematical models of ecosystems that are simulated on the computer. Ecosystem simulation models describe the major pools and fluxes in an ecosystem and the factors that regulate those fluxes. Mathematical equations are used to represent the processes that control how major pools (state variables) of an ecosystem change over time. Mechanistically rich, process-based ecosystem models are increasingly seen as critical for anticipating ecosystem change in a no-analog world. Learn why and how ecosystem simulation models are used in ecology. Knowledge of general ecology such as (e.g. BOTANY/F&W ECOL/ZOOLOGY 460) is strongly encouraged.
